title: Late Charges in Oregon
bodyText:
You may charge a late charge only if the rent is not received by the fourth day of the weekly or monthly rental period, and only if your written rental agreement states the tenant's obligation to pay it, its type and amount, the date rent is due and the date the late charge becomes due.

Oregon allows three structures, and each is a ceiling:
- a reasonable flat amount (what landlords customarily charge in that rental market), once per rental period;
- a reasonable daily charge from the fifth day through the end of that rental period, each day's charge no more than 6% of a reasonable flat amount;
- or 5% of the periodic rent for each five-day period (or part) the rent stays unpaid, from the fifth day through the end of that rental period.

In a periodic tenancy you may change the type or amount on 30 days' written notice. You may not deduct an earlier late charge from a later rent payment to make that rent late; unpaid late charges may earn simple interest at the judgment rate.

Nonpayment of a late charge alone does not support a nonpayment notice, though it is a cause for a for-cause notice; you may list a late charge on a nonpayment notice only if the notice makes clear the tenant can cure by paying the delinquent rent alone.

A discount for paying early counts as a late charge. Since June 5, 2026, you may not charge a late charge if you refused a payment the tenant offered by check or another commercially reasonable method.

title: Bounced Rent Checks
bodyText:
For a dishonored check you may charge a fee of up to $35 plus whatever your bank charged you for processing it, and only if your written rental agreement describes the fee.

The fee covers a check returned for insufficient funds or credit, no account, or a stop payment without good cause; Oregon's fee list has no fee for a failed card or electronic payment (whether a returned electronic check counts as a 'check, draft or order for the payment of money' is not settled by the text).

A rent check that bounces is not an acceptance of rent for waiver purposes.

If you sue on the check, statutory damages (the greater of $100 or three times the check, but not more than $500 over the check amount) and attorney fees are available only after a written demand at least 30 days before suing and only if the tenant didn't pay the check amount, accrued interest and the fee before you sued; a fee you collected reduces those damages; no statutory damages if the tenant pays the check, interest, fee, costs and your attorney fees after suit but before trial, and a court may waive them for economic hardship.

Oregon requires you to let a tenant pay by check or another commercially reasonable method and bars requiring electronic payment; whether you may insist on certified funds after a check bounces is not settled by the statute, so the library's clause doesn't claim that right.

title: How Tenants May Pay
bodyText: Since June 5, 2026, you must let a tenant pay by check or another commercially reasonable method, and you may not require payment by debit card, credit card, electronic check, tenant portal or any other electronic payment. The rule applies to leases signed before that date too. If you refuse a payment the tenant offers that way, you may not charge a late fee or end the tenancy for nonpayment of that rent or charge. You may pass a card or electronic-payment processing fee through to a tenant who chooses to pay that way only if the processor allows it, you also accept non-electronic payment, and you make your records of the fees available within a reasonable time after the tenant's written request.

title: Tenant Portals
bodyText: If you take rental applications through a tenant portal (an app, website or platform you provide for applying, setting up, keeping or ending a tenancy, not ordinary e-mail or text), you must either post a printable application on your website or send a printed or printable copy within seven days of a written request, and you must process applications received outside the portal. If an applicant or tenant asks in writing for an alternative, you may not make the portal the only way to verify identity, review and sign addenda or other legal agreements, or submit tenancy documents. A violation entitles the person to damages or $100, whichever is greater. Separately, from June 5, 2026, the habitability list requires a means of unlocking the unit's locks and of reaching every common area the tenant may use, at least one of which is not a tenant portal.

title: Rent Receipts
bodyText: A tenant who asks for a written record of a payment is entitled to one as a condition of making the payment: a receipt, account statement or other acknowledgment showing the amount, the date and information identifying you or the property. If the tenant pays by mail, deposit or another method not in person and asks for the record, you must provide it within a reasonable time. If a licensed property manager collects rent in cash for you, the manager must also write a numbered receipt for it and keep a copy (OAR 863-025-0060).

title: Statewide Rent Increase Limit
bodyText: For tenancies other than week-to-week, you may not raise the rent during the first year of the tenancy, more than once in any 12-month period, or by more than the maximum percentage the Department of Administrative Services publishes each September for the next calendar year: the lesser of 10% or 7% plus the annual West-region CPI change. The cap, and the limit on the next tenancy's rent after a first-year no-cause termination, do not apply if the unit's first certificate of occupancy was issued less than 15 years before the date of the increase notice, or if the unit is regulated or certified affordable housing and the change doesn't increase the tenant's share of the rent or is required by the program or a change in the tenant's income. Notice periods and contents: "Rent Increase Notice". Exceeding the cap costs three months' rent plus actual damages. If you end a tenancy without cause in its first year, the next tenancy's rent is held to what you could have charged the tenant you removed. Cities and counties may not control rent, apart from narrow exceptions.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: A week-to-week rent increase needs written notice at least seven days before it takes effect. Any other tenancy needs written notice at least 90 days before the effective date, and no increase is allowed in the first year. The notice must state the amount of the increase, the new rent, the effective date and, if the increase is above the statewide cap, the facts supporting the exemption you rely on. The terms of a fixed term tenancy, including the rent, can't be changed by either party alone during the term.

title: Local Rent Control Is Preempted
bodyText: Oregon bars cities and counties from enacting rent control on residential property, with exceptions: rent limits a state agency, city, county or urban renewal agency reserves on property it has contracted to benefit (for example with tax exemptions, financing or subsidies) to provide reduced rents for low-income tenants; condominium conversion ordinances limiting increases during the conversion notice period; temporary controls after a natural or man-made disaster that materially eliminates a significant part of the rental housing supply, removed once supply is substantially normal again; and inclusionary-zoning requirements that set the price of new multiunit housing. ORS 91.225 preempts only rent control; some cities, such as Portland, have other rental ordinances (relocation assistance, screening, notice rules), so check local law.

title: What Counts as Rent
bodyText: In Oregon, rent does not include security deposits, fees or utility and service charges you bill under the utility statute. Fees, late charges and utility charges are not rent for a nonpayment notice: unpaid, they support only a for-cause notice with its own cure period. The fees you may charge are limited to those the fee statute lists, each described in your written rental agreement. Recurring charges you set as part of the rent (such as pet rent or a parking charge you call rent) are rent and count toward the rent-increase limits.

title: Fees You May Charge
bodyText:
Oregon lets you charge **only the fees its fee statute lists**, and each must be described in your written rental agreement.
- Per-occurrence fees: late charges (as the late-charge rules allow); a dishonored check (up to $35 plus your bank's charge); removing or tampering with a working smoke or carbon monoxide alarm (up to $250, unless the State Fire Marshal fines the tenant); and, for a tenant who leaves a fixed term early without cause, a fee of no more than one and one-half times the monthly rent (not allowed when the tenant leaves under the victim or servicemember termination rights, or when, after you give a qualifying-reason notice ending a fixed term, the tenant ends the tenancy early with the tenant's own written notice of at least 30 days), in which case you give up rent after the date you knew or reasonably should have known of the departure, and reletting costs.
- Rule-violation fees: after a written warning notice, for the second violation of the same kind within a year (up to $50) and later ones (up to $50 plus 5% of that period's rent), but only for late utility charges, pet or service-animal waste or garbage left outside the unit, parking violations and improper vehicle use, smoking in a clearly designated nonsmoking area (up to $250, 24 hours after the warning) or an unauthorized pet capable of causing damage (up to $250, 48 hours after the warning).

You may not charge a fee at the start of the tenancy for an expected expense, any other liquidated damages, or both a fee and a termination for the same violation.

Outside the fee rules: attorney fees awarded by a court, screening charges, charges for improvements or other actions the tenant asks for that the lease or law doesn't require of you (including replacing a lost key), processing fees passed through under the payment rules, renter's insurance requirements and association assessments passed through as the statute allows, and, if a nonpayment eviction is dismissed because rental assistance or another payment covering the amount owed was tendered, the court filing fee you paid (paying it is not a condition of the dismissal).

A fee not allowed by the statute costs twice your tenant's actual damages or $300, whichever is greater (this penalty doesn't apply to the per-occurrence fees listed above).

title: Interest on Money a Tenant Owes
bodyText: Oregon's legal interest rate is 9% a year on money after it becomes due, unless the parties agreed to a different rate, and judgments carry 9% simple interest unless the law or the agreement sets another rate. The landlord-tenant act lets you charge simple interest at the judgment rate on an unpaid late charge, from the date you imposed it. Whether a lease may set its own interest rate on unpaid rent or damages without running into the act's fee and liquidated-damages limits is not settled by the statutes, so the library doesn't offer a contractual rate.

title: Accepting Rent After a Violation or Notice
bodyText: If you accept rent knowing of a tenant's violation during three or more separate rental periods, or accept performance that departs from the lease, you waive the right to end the tenancy for that violation. You avoid waiver by refunding the rent within 10 days, by agreeing otherwise with the tenant after the violation, or by giving a written warning notice before the third period that describes the conduct or the money owed, says the tenant must stop the conduct, correct the violation or pay, and says it may lead to termination; a warning for ongoing conduct lasts 12 months and can be renewed. There is no waiver for a 24-hour termination, a last month's rent deposit, rent released by a court, or rent paid more than one period in advance, and a dishonored check is not accepted rent. Accepting a partial payment waives a nonpayment termination unless you follow the statute: before the notice, on an agreement to pay the balance by a set time, serving the notice no earlier than allowed, and letting the tenant avoid termination by paying the balance within the notice period or by the agreed date, whichever is later; after the notice, only with a written agreement that acceptance is not a waiver. After a termination notice, accepting rent waives it unless the statute's refund or written-notice conditions are met. A lease clause written before the violation does not do this for you.

title: Changing Terms During a Tenancy
bodyText: A fixed term lease can't be changed by either party alone during the term. In a periodic tenancy, Oregon sets specific notice periods for some changes: rent increases (seven days week-to-week; 90 days otherwise, and none in the first year); the type or amount of a late charge (30 days); adding a renter's liability insurance requirement to an existing month-to-month tenancy (30 days, with the exceptions summary); requiring a public service charge adopted by a provider or local government within the previous six months, in a month-to-month tenancy (60 days); and a new or increased security deposit (none in the first year except with an agreed change such as a pet; after the first year, at least three months to pay). A new house rule that substantially modifies the bargain needs the tenant's written consent. From January 1, 2027, a landlord may adopt a smoking ban inside units or interior common areas without that consent only under the 2026 act's conditions, including 180 days' written notice.

title: Rent Concessions and Discounts
bodyText: Oregon treats an increase or decrease in the regular rent based on whether the tenant pays by a certain date as a late charge, so an early-payment discount has to meet the late-charge rules. No statute addresses move-in concessions such as a free month; if you offer one, state in the lease whether the stated rent is the rent before or after the concession, since the rent-increase limit is measured from the rent.

title: No Sales Tax on Rent
bodyText: Oregon has no general sales tax, so long-term residential rent is not taxed. The state transient lodging tax doesn't apply to a dwelling the same person rents for 30 consecutive days or more; shorter stays may be taxed, and vacation and transient occupancies fall outside the landlord-tenant act anyway.

title: Screening Charges for Applicants
bodyText: You may charge an applicant a screening charge only to cover the cost of screening, no more than your average actual cost or the customary charge of a screening company or credit agency for comparable screening, and only after you adopt written screening criteria and give the applicant written notice of the matters the statute lists (the charge, your criteria and process, dispute and appeal rights, nondiscrimination, the rent and deposits, any renter's insurance requirement and refund rights) and an estimate of available units and applications already under consideration. Give a receipt and confirmation of any outside screening; charge only one screening charge in any 60-day period across all your units; don't charge when you know no unit is or will soon be available; and refund within 30 days if you fill the unit before screening or haven't screened before the applicant withdraws in writing. Violations cost twice the screening charge plus $250.

title: Deposits to Secure a Rental Agreement
bodyText: Apart from a screening charge, you may take money from an applicant only as a deposit to secure the execution of a rental agreement, after you approve the application and before you both sign, and only after giving a written statement of the rent, fees and deposits, the terms of the agreement to sign and the conditions for refunding or keeping the deposit. When the agreement is signed, you must apply the deposit to the money due under it or refund it immediately. If the applicant fails to sign as agreed, you may keep the deposit, unless the applicant rejected the agreement because of material habitability defects. If you fail to sign, or the applicant rejects for habitability, you must return the deposit within five business days; the applicant can recover the deposit, and late return (unless caused by an act of God) adds a penalty equal to the greater of the deposit or an amount you agreed on.

title: Screening Rules and Denials
bodyText: In evaluating an applicant you may not consider an eviction action that was dismissed or ended in the applicant's favor, an eviction judgment entered five or more years before the application, judgments for claims that arose between April 1, 2020 and March 1, 2022, arrests unless they led to charges in the listed categories and the applicant was convicted, or the charges are pending and the applicant isn't in a diversion, conditional discharge or deferral program; convictions or charges outside the listed categories (drug-related crimes other than marijuana use or possession alone, person crimes, sex offenses, financial fraud, and crimes affecting property, health, safety or peaceful enjoyment) or for conduct no longer illegal; possession of a medical marijuana card or status as a medical marijuana patient; or rent unpaid during the emergency period; you may not ask about immigration status, and you must accept the identification documents the statute lists in place of a Social Security number. If you deny an applicant after applying your criteria, give a written statement of one or more reasons within 14 days (a $100 remedy if you don't); before denying on criminal history, let the applicant submit supplemental evidence and make an individualized assessment. From January 2, 2028, the emergency-period limits drop out of the screening statute.

title: Algorithmic Rent-Setting Tools
bodyText: No Oregon statute specifically regulates the use of algorithmic or other software to set rents. General antitrust law still bars agreements among competing landlords to fix rents.

title: Government Shutdowns
bodyText: Oregon has no statute giving tenants affected by a federal or state government shutdown extra time to pay rent or a defense to eviction.

title: Reporting Rent Payments to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: No Oregon statute requires or limits a landlord's reporting of rent payments to a credit bureau or makes a tenant join a rent-reporting program; general consumer reporting and debt collection law still applies.

title: Disclosing Rent and Fees
bodyText: Before taking a screening charge you must give the applicant written notice of the charge, the rent and the deposits you will require, and any renter's insurance requirement, among other items. Before taking a deposit to secure a rental agreement you must give a written statement of the rent, the fees you will charge and the deposits. Every fee you charge must be described in the written rental agreement. Oregon has no statute requiring an all-in rent figure in advertisements or a fee box on the first page of the lease.

title: No Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: Oregon sets no maximum security deposit. The limits that apply: the deposit must be listed in the written rental agreement and receipted; a last month's rent deposit counts as a security deposit; no pet deposit for an assistance animal; no new or increased deposit during the first year unless you and the tenant agree to a change (such as adding a pet) that the deposit relates to, and after the first year the tenant gets at least three months to pay a new or increased deposit; no fee at the start of the tenancy for an expected expense. Some cities limit deposits or move-in costs; check local law.

title: New or Increased Deposits
bodyText: During the first year of a tenancy you may not change the rental agreement to require a new or larger security deposit, except where you and the tenant agree to change the terms (for example to allow a pet) and the extra deposit relates to that change; a deposit the original agreement required but that was unpaid when the tenancy began may still be collected. After the first year, you must give the tenant at least three months to pay a new or increased deposit. Oregon has no general right to pay the initial deposit in installments.

title: Last Month's Rent Deposits
bodyText: A last month's rent deposit is a security deposit in Oregon. You must apply it to the rent for the last month of the tenancy when either of you gives a termination notice (other than a nonpayment notice), when you agree to end the tenancy, or when a fixed term ends under the written agreement, and account for and refund any part you don't apply. Unless you both agree otherwise, the tenant can't make you apply it to any other month, and it does not cap the rent you may charge unless the written agreement says so. Accepting one collected at the beginning of the tenancy is not acceptance of rent that waives a violation.

title: Penalties for Deposit Mistakes
bodyText: If you don't return the deposit or prepaid rent within 31 days with a written accounting, or withhold it in bad faith, the tenant may recover twice the amount withheld without an accounting or in bad faith. The tenant's creditors can't garnish a deposit or prepaid rent from you, and the tenant's claim to it comes ahead of your own creditors, including a bankruptcy trustee.

title: Deposits When the Property Changes Hands
bodyText: Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is responsible to the tenant for the security deposit and prepaid rent and bound by the deposit rules, so a buyer takes on the deposits of tenants in place; a purchaser at a foreclosure sale has a separate rule. Agree with the buyer on transferring deposits at closing.

title: No Deposit Interest or Trust Account Rule
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to pay interest on security deposits. If you manage your own rental, no statute requires a separate or trust account; a licensed property manager must deposit tenant security deposits in a federally insured security deposits account and keep them there until they are forwarded to the owner, disbursed or refunded under the lease and management agreement ("Where to Keep the Deposit"). You hold the deposit for the tenant: the tenant's claim to it comes before your creditors', including a bankruptcy trustee, and the tenant's creditors can't garnish it from you.

title: Where to Keep the Deposit
bodyText: Oregon law doesn't tell a landlord who manages their own rental where to keep a security deposit, require a separate account, or require notice of the bank. You must give the tenant a receipt and hold the deposit for the tenant, and the tenant's claim to it comes ahead of your creditors. If a licensed property manager collects deposits for you, the manager must put them in a federally insured trust account labeled for security deposits (or, where the management agreement and lease say the owner holds the deposit, pass it to you the month it arrives), keep records and not mix the money with the manager's own funds.

title: Move-In Condition Records
bodyText: Oregon does not require a move-in inspection or condition checklist for ordinary tenancies. Because your written accounting must state specifically the basis of any deposit claim and you may charge only for damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, a dated, signed condition report and photos at move-in are the practical way to support a claim.

title: Fees Instead of a Deposit
bodyText: Oregon has no statute authorizing or regulating a monthly fee or insurance product in place of a security deposit, and its fee statute lets you charge only listed fees, none of which is a fee in lieu of a deposit. The library offers no such clause.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: No Oregon landlord-tenant statute addresses a deposit refund the tenant never cashes or claims. Under Oregon's unclaimed property law, money held or owed in the ordinary course of business and unclaimed for more than three years after it became payable is presumed abandoned, and the holder must report it and pay it to the State Treasurer, after first trying to reach the owner. Don't keep or write off an uncashed refund.

title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText: A pet deposit is a refundable security deposit in Oregon: list it in the written agreement, and claim from it only as the deposit rules allow. You may not charge a pet deposit for an assistance animal a tenant with a disability needs. Oregon's fee statute has no one-time pet fee for ordinary tenancies, so a nonrefundable pet fee isn't allowed; pet rent you set as part of the rent is rent. For repeat problems you may use the rule-violation fees for pet waste or an unauthorized pet (after a warning).

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText:
Every rental dwelling must have approved smoke alarms or detectors, and you must supply, install and maintain them and give written testing instructions when the tenant first takes possession. Your maintenance duty, including working batteries, arises before each new tenancy and during the tenancy only when the tenant gives written notice of a deficiency other than dead batteries; the tenant tests at least every six months and replaces dead batteries.

If the unit contains a carbon monoxide source, or is in a structure with one and connected to its room by a door, ductwork or ventilation shaft, you may not start a new tenancy without properly installed, working carbon monoxide alarms, and the same instruction, battery and repair rules apply. Both are habitability items.

Removing or tampering with a working alarm is prohibited; you may charge a fee of up to $250 for it if your lease describes the fee, unless the State Fire Marshal has assessed the tenant a civil penalty for the same conduct. Placement and type follow State Fire Marshal rules and the state building code.

title: Flood Plain Notice and Insurance
bodyText: If the dwelling unit is in a 100-year flood plain as mapped by FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program, the rental agreement itself must say so. If you leave it out and the tenant suffers an uninsured flood loss, you owe the lesser of the tenant's actual uninsured loss or two months' rent. Oregon has no other flood disclosure for rentals; renter's insurance policies generally exclude flood, which tenants may not realize.

title: Affordable Housing Restriction End Date
bodyText: If the unit is subject to an affordability restriction (as defined in ORS 456.766), before charging a screening charge or entering into a rental agreement you must give the applicant or prospective tenant the notice ORS 456.788(4) requires or, if that doesn't apply, a written notice of the earliest date the restriction could end, in the form the Housing and Community Services Department prescribes. It is a separate form, not a lease clause. The notices must also be posted onsite in a common area.

title: Drinking Water Wells (from 2027)
bodyText:
From January 1, 2027, if a rental's drinking water comes from an exempt well and the unit is in a ground water quality management area, you must have the water sampled from the primary drinking faucet and tested by an accredited laboratory for arsenic, coliform bacteria, lead and nitrates (arsenic within 30 days of installing a new well; otherwise at least yearly, with a four-year break after a passing first test), complete the first round before June 1, 2027, give the tenant the results within 30 days after receiving them, and, before entering into a rental agreement, give written notice of the well, the latest results and the next test date.

If a test fails, give the results and the Oregon Health Authority's handout as soon as practicable and retest on the Authority's schedule. You may delegate sampling to the tenant only by a written, good-faith agreement for adequate consideration.

title: Lead-Based Paint
bodyText: For housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet apply in Oregon (the library's federal disclosure clause). Oregon adds no lease disclosure, but renovation for compensation (as federal rules define renovation) must be done by a firm certified by the Oregon Health Authority and, for contractors, by a Construction Contractors Board certified lead-based paint renovation contractor (see "No Lead-Safe Building Certificate; Who Must Be Certified for Lead Work" for whether this reaches work you do yourself). Lead-based paint alone doesn't support a tenant's 48-hour termination for an imminent and serious threat, and a tenant may not use the minor-repair deduction for it.

title: Radon
bodyText: Oregon has no radon disclosure or testing requirement for residential rentals. Radon is excluded from the conditions that let a tenant end the tenancy on 48 hours' notice for an essential-service failure, and from the minor-repair deduction.

title: Mold
bodyText: Oregon has no mold disclosure requirement for rentals. Mold problems fall under your general duty to keep the unit habitable (weatherproofing, plumbing, clean and sanitary conditions), and mold is excluded from the tenant's $300 minor-repair remedy.

title: Bed Bugs and Pests
bodyText: Oregon has no bed bug disclosure or treatment statute. Pests are covered by the habitability duty: at the start of the tenancy, buildings and grounds must be free of rodents and vermin, and areas under your control must stay that way. The tenant must keep areas under the tenant's control free of vermin to the extent the tenant caused the problem and must cooperate with your reasonable efforts to remedy it.

title: Drug Lab Contamination
bodyText: Oregon bars renting property you know, or have reasonable grounds to believe, was used as an illegal drug manufacturing site unless it has been determined fit for use under the Oregon Health Authority's decontamination process, and a lease made in violation is voidable by the tenant. A property officially determined not fit for use stays that way until it is decontaminated by a licensed contractor (or, with the Authority's approval, by the owner or the owner's agent) and certified, or it is assessed, found not contaminated and issued a Certificate of Fitness, or the determination is reversed on appeal. Oregon has no tenant disclosure form for rentals; the full written disclosure rule applies to sales and transfers. The abandoned property statute has special handling for property left in a unit determined unfit because of a methamphetamine lab.

title: Deaths or Crimes on the Property
bodyText: Oregon's statute on facts that are not material to a real property transaction lists a death on the property or a neighboring property (by violent crime, suicide or otherwise), a crime or other occurrence that doesn't affect the property's physical condition or title, an owner's or occupant's blood-borne infection, a registered sex offender living in the area, and notice that a neighboring property was found unfit because of a drug lab. Separately, you may not disclose that an occupant has or died from a blood-borne infection.

title: Military Installations Nearby
bodyText: Oregon has no disclosure requirement for rentals near a military installation.

title: Registered Sex Offenders
bodyText: Oregon does not require landlords to disclose registered sex offenders living nearby, and has no occupancy rule for registrants in ordinary tenancies (a manufactured dwelling park or marina landlord may terminate a level three sex offender, a facility rule outside this library's scope). When screening, a sex offense is one of the criminal categories you may consider, with the individualized assessment the screening statute requires before a denial.

title: When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause
bodyText: Either side may end a week-to-week tenancy on 10 days' written notice at any time. During the first year of occupancy you may end a month-to-month tenancy without cause on 30 days' written notice, and a fixed term ending within the first year on 30 days' written notice before its end date. The first year of occupancy lasts as long as any tenant has lived in the unit for one year or less. After the first year of occupancy, you may end a month-to-month tenancy only for a tenant cause under the notice statutes or for a qualifying landlord reason, and a fixed term ending after the first year becomes month-to-month unless you agree a new term, the tenant gives 30 days' notice, or you have a qualifying reason. The qualifying reasons, each needing at least 90 days' written notice stating the reason and supporting facts: demolition or conversion to a non-residential use; repairs or renovations within a reasonable time where the premises are unsafe or unfit for occupancy, or the unit will be unsafe or unfit during the work; you or an immediate family member moving in as a primary residence when you have no comparable vacant unit in the same building; or a buyer who will live there and whose accepted offer you document. With a qualifying-reason notice you must also pay the tenant one month's rent, unless you own an interest in four or fewer dwelling units. For the buyer reason you may give 60 days' notice instead of 90 if you pay the tenant one more month's rent with the notice, on top of any payment already required. A fixed term also doesn't convert if the tenant had three violations in 12 months, each with a written warning in the statutory form, and you give 90 days' notice. In a building or property with no more than two units where you live, you may end a month-to-month tenancy after the first year on 60 days' notice without cause (30 days for a documented owner-occupant buyer) and a fixed term at its end on 30 days' notice. Terminating in violation of the qualifying-reason, payment or three-violation rules costs three months' rent plus actual damages and gives the tenant a defense to possession; claims must be brought within one year. Some cities add relocation-payment and notice rules.

title: Notice Periods to End a Tenancy
bodyText: Without cause: week-to-week, 10 days' written notice by either side; month-to-month, the tenant may give 30 days' written notice at any time, and you may give 30 days' notice only in the first year of occupancy (after that, see the for-cause rules); a fixed term ending after the first year continues month to month unless ended as the statute allows, and a tenant who wants it to end must give 30 days' written notice before the end date. For cause: 30 days for a material violation with a cure period of at least 14 days (7 and 4 days in a week-to-week tenancy; the cure date can be the delivery date for a separate, completed act that isn't ongoing), 10 days for a repeat within six months (4 in a week-to-week tenancy), 72 hours or 10 or 13 days for nonpayment, 24 hours for serious threats or violence, intentional substantial damage, certain false application information, or acts outrageous in the extreme, 10 days for an unpermitted pet capable of causing damage to persons or property (curable by removing it; 10 days without cure for a repeat within six months), and the special 24- and 48-hour notices for a household member's violence, a unit posted unsafe, drug and alcohol free housing and group recovery homes. Every termination notice must include the veterans' information the statute requires, a nonpayment notice must come with the court's rental-assistance notice, and a notice served by first class mail alone adds three days.

title: Cure Periods for Lease Violations
bodyText:
For a material violation of the lease or of the tenant's statutory duties, your 30-day notice must describe the violation and, if it can be cured, say so, describe at least one way to cure it and set a cure date at least 14 days after delivery; if the tenant cures by that date the tenancy continues. For a separate, completed act that isn't ongoing, the cure date can be the date of delivery, so the act can't be cured by waiting.

If substantially the same violation recurs within six months after a notice, a 10-day notice with no right to cure is allowed (its termination date can't be earlier than the one in the earlier notice), but not when the only violation is failing to pay the current month's rent. In a week-to-week tenancy the 30, 14 and 10 days become 7, 4 and 4 days.

Nonpayment of a late charge, fee or utility charge is a for-cause matter, not a nonpayment-of-rent matter. A 24-hour notice has no cure, except that a pet-based notice is cured by removing the pet.

Accepting rent with knowledge of a violation during three or more separate rental periods, or accepting performance that varies from the lease, waives termination for that violation unless an exception applies, such as a written warning with the statutory content given before the third period; 24-hour causes are not waived.

title: Nonpayment of Rent Notices
bodyText:
For week-to-week tenancies, give at least 72 hours' written notice, no sooner than the fifth day of the rental period (counting the day rent is due). For other tenancies, give either at least 10 days' written notice no sooner than the eighth day, or at least 13 days' notice no sooner than the fifth day.

The notice must state the amount of rent that must be paid and the date and time by which it must be paid to cure, must include the veterans' information, and must be delivered with a copy of the Oregon Judicial Department's rental assistance notice (also required with any summons for nonpayment).

A tenant's payment mailed within the notice period is timely unless you served the notice personally, by mail and attachment or by mail and e-mail, both the written rental agreement and the notice name a payment location on the premises or where the tenant has always paid in person, and that place is available to the tenant throughout the notice period.

Since June 5, 2026, you must let tenants pay by check or another commercially reasonable method and may not require electronic payment; if you refuse a payment made that way, you may not charge a late fee or terminate for nonpayment.

A court will dismiss a nonpayment case if the rental-assistance notice wasn't delivered, if you caused the tenant not to tender rent (including by not reasonably cooperating with a rental assistance program), or if the tenant tenders rental assistance or other payment covering the amount owed; after a dismissal for tender you may charge the tenant the court filing fees, though paying them isn't a condition of the dismissal.

**Only rent supports this notice**: late charges, fees and utility charges don't.

title: Rental Assistance and Nonpayment Cases
bodyText: Every nonpayment termination notice and every summons in a nonpayment case must be delivered with the rental assistance notice the Oregon Judicial Department posts on its website. 'Nonpayment' for this purpose includes rent, late charges, utility charges and other fees, but not payments owed for damage to the premises. The court must dismiss the case if you didn't deliver the rental assistance notice, if you caused the tenant not to tender rent (for example by not reasonably participating in a rental assistance program), or if the tenant has tendered rental assistance or other payment covering the amount in the notice. Victims' calls for police or emergency help are protected separately ("No Adverse Action Against Victims").

title: 24-Hour Terminations
bodyText:
You may end a tenancy on at least 24 hours' written notice, specifying the cause and the date and time of termination, if the tenant, someone in the tenant's control or the tenant's pet seriously threatens or inflicts substantial personal injury on someone other than the tenant on the premises (or injures a neighbor living nearby); the tenant or someone in the tenant's control recklessly endangers others; the tenant or someone in the tenant's control intentionally causes substantial damage (a pet, on more than one occasion); the tenant intentionally gave substantial false information on the application within the past year about the tenant's own criminal conviction that would have been material to your acceptance of the application, and you act within 30 days of discovering it; or there is an act outrageous in the extreme, on the premises or in the immediate vicinity, such as prostitution, unlawful manufacture, delivery or possession of a controlled substance, unlicensed cannabis extract manufacture, a bias crime or burglary.

A pet-based notice can be cured by removing the pet.

Four more 24-hour notices:
- (1) to a tenant who commits a criminal act of physical violence related to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking against a household member who is a tenant (only the perpetrator's tenancy ends);
- (2) to an unauthorized person in possession after the tenant has vacated, if the rental agreement prohibited subletting or other occupants without your written permission and you haven't knowingly accepted rent from that person;
- (3) to a tenant after an agency posts the unit unsafe for conditions you didn't cause; and
- (4) in group recovery homes.

Someone is in the tenant's control if the tenant lets them enter or stay after the tenant reasonably knows or should know of their act or likelihood to commit such an act.

Drug and alcohol free housing programs have a separate 48-hour rule for tenants there less than two years (curable within 24 hours), with a 24-hour notice and no cure for a repeat within six months.

title: Early Termination by Victims
bodyText: A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking may give you at least 14 days' written notice asking to be released from the rental agreement, naming the release date and any immediate family members to be released, with verification: a protective order, a police report, a conviction, or a statement signed by the tenant and a qualified third party (law enforcement officer, attorney, licensed health professional, Department of Justice victim-services employee or victim's advocate) in the statute's form, showing an incident within the previous 90 days (not counting time the perpetrator was incarcerated or lived more than 100 miles away) or a valid protective order. You must release them. They owe no rent or damages incurred after the release date and no fee solely for the termination, and you may not charge an early termination fee. Other tenants remain bound. You may not disclose the information provided except with the tenant's written consent, for an eviction proceeding, to a qualified third party or as the law requires.

title: No Adverse Action Against Victims
bodyText: You may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy, serve a termination notice, sue or threaten to sue for possession, raise rent, cut services or refuse to rent because a tenant or applicant is or was a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking, because of a lease violation that consists of an incident against them, or because of criminal activity or a police or emergency response in which they are the victim; nor may you apply different rules to them. The one exception: after a prior written warning about the perpetrator's conduct, you may end the victim's tenancy if the tenant lets the perpetrator on the premises and the perpetrator is an actual and imminent threat to others, or lets the perpetrator live there as an unauthorized occupant. Violations cost up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, and give the tenant a defense. A tenant isn't responsible for damage caused by the perpetrator, though you may require verification of victim status as ORS 90.453 provides. If one tenant commits physical violence related to these crimes against a household member who is also a tenant, you may end the perpetrator's tenancy alone on 24 hours' written notice, without new rent, deposits or fees for the others.

title: Lock Changes for Victims
bodyText: A tenant who gives you actual notice of being a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking may ask you to change the locks; no verification is needed. You must promptly change them at the tenant's expense or let the tenant do it; if you don't act promptly, the tenant may change them and must give you a key. If the perpetrator is a tenant of the same unit, the tenant must first give you a court order requiring the perpetrator to move out; you then owe the perpetrator no access or keys, the perpetrator stays jointly liable for rent and damages incurred before exclusion, you may not charge the others extra rent, deposits or fees because of the exclusion, and the perpetrator's tenancy ends when the order becomes final.

title: Servicemember Termination Rights
bodyText: A tenant may end a rental agreement on written notice with proof of official orders if enlisting in the Armed Forces, ordered to active service outside the area for more than 90 days as a member of the National Guard, a reserve component or an active component, ending active service, or on qualifying Public Health Service or NOAA commissioned-corps duty; the termination takes effect on the earlier of any date federal law sets or the latest of 30 days after the notice, 30 days before the reporting date, the date in the notice, or (for ending service) 90 days before the orders take effect. A member of the Oregon organized militia called into state active service for 90 or more consecutive days may end the agreement on written notice with orders, effective the earlier of 30 days after the next rent is due or the last day of the month after the notice month. Neither owes a penalty, fee, charge or loss of deposit for the termination, or rent after the effective date. A court may stay for up to 90 days the eviction of a member of the organized militia called into state active service for 30 or more consecutive days, if the rent is $1,200 a month or less, the dwelling is occupied chiefly by the member's spouse, children or other dependents, and the service materially affects the member's ability to pay. Federal law adds cases Oregon's statute doesn't list: under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act a servicemember may end a residential lease signed before entering military service, or signed while in service and followed by orders for a permanent change of station or a deployment of 90 days or more, or signed on such orders and followed by a stop-movement order, indefinite or for 30 days or more, that prevents occupancy; a spouse or dependent may end it within one year after the servicemember dies in service; and within one year after a catastrophic injury or illness in service the servicemember (or, if the servicemember lacks mental capacity, a spouse or dependent) may end it; you may not charge an early termination charge in any of these cases (FEDERAL: 50 U.S.C. § 3955).

title: Other Ways a Tenant May Leave Early
bodyText: Besides the victim and servicemember rights, an Oregon tenant may end the tenancy: on written notice ending the tenancy at least 30 days later (7 for week-to-week) if you materially fail to comply with the lease, or fail to comply with the habitability duty, and don't remedy it (within 7 days for an essential service, 30 days otherwise); on 48 hours' notice if a failure to supply an essential service poses an imminent and serious threat; immediately if the unit is posted unsafe for conditions the tenant didn't cause, or if conditions existing at the start that the tenant didn't cause pose an imminent and serious threat within six months; on 72 hours' notice (or immediately before move-in) if a utility the tenant must pay can't be obtained because of a prior tenant's or the owner's debt, or a landlord-paid utility is shut off for nonpayment; after an unlawful lockout or a willful utility shutoff; after an unlawful or unreasonable entry, or repeated harassing demands for entry, through the 30-day notice-and-remedy procedure for landlord noncompliance; during a fixed term, on 30 days' notice after you give a qualifying-reason notice for the end of the term; and during a fixed term after a foreclosure notice, on 60 days' notice unless within 30 days you give written evidence from a lender or trustee that the property is no longer in foreclosure, or written evidence that a court has appointed a receiver. A tenancy in a unit destroyed in a natural disaster (including a disaster resulting in a state of emergency declared under ORS 401.165 or 401.309 for wildfires, floods, tsunamis, earthquakes or similar events) ends immediately unless the parties agree otherwise after the disaster (not for facility space rentals). The lease can't waive these rights.

title: Property Left Behind After a Tenancy
bodyText:
When a tenancy has ended and you reasonably believe the tenant left personal property with no intention of claiming it, or the tenant has been absent seven days after an unexecuted court order, or the sheriff has given you possession, you must store, sell or dispose of the property only as the statute provides.

First give written notice, personally delivered or by first class mail to the tenant at the premises, any known post office box and any forwarding address, saying the property is considered abandoned and must be claimed by a date at least five days after personal delivery or eight days after mailing (45 days for a manufactured dwelling or floating home), where it is stored and how to arrange removal.

Store it with reasonable care in a place of safekeeping; you may require payment of removal and storage charges before releasing it, except where the sheriff gave you possession.

If the tenant responds by the date, you must make it available for removal by appointment during the next 15 days (30 for a dwelling or home); otherwise it is conclusively presumed abandoned and you may sell it at a public or private sale, or dispose of it if its reasonable value is $1,000 or less or so low that storage and sale costs would probably exceed what a sale would bring, deducting notice, storage and sale costs and unpaid rent from any proceeds.

Special rules apply to a sole tenant's death, drug-lab sites and vehicles. A rental agreement may not waive these rights.

If you don't comply, the tenant is relieved of liability for unpaid rent and for damage that wasn't deliberate, intentional or grossly negligent and may recover up to twice actual damages; a deliberate and malicious violation also costs twice actual damages.

title: When a Sole Tenant Dies
bodyText: Oregon has no special termination rule for a tenant's death; the tenancy and the estate's obligations follow the rental agreement and general law. When a sole tenant dies and leaves property, the abandoned property statute applies with changes: an heir, devisee, personal representative or a person the tenant designated in writing to be contacted on death has the tenant's rights to the property, and your notice must go by first class mail to the tenant at the premises, to any of those people you actually know of, and to an estate administrator of the State Treasurer.

title: Rent Owed After a Tenant Abandons
bodyText: If a tenant abandons the unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental. Renting it to a new tenant for a term starting before the old agreement would have ended terminates the old agreement as of the new tenancy's start. If you don't make reasonable efforts, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the agreement is treated as ended by you as of the date you knew or should have known of the abandonment. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, the remaining term is treated as one month or one week. Taking back the keys, or trying to re-rent, is not by itself acceptance of a surrender. If you charge the early-termination fee Oregon allows for a fixed term, these rules don't apply and you can't also recover later rent or re-renting costs.

title: The Eviction Court Process
bodyText: After a valid termination notice expires, you may recover possession only through a court action for possession (forcible entry and detainer). You may not file until the notice period (or fixed term) has run. The complaint and summons follow statutory forms; the summons must include the veterans' information and, for nonpayment, the rental-assistance notice. The clerk sets the first appearance seven days after the judicial day following payment of the filing fee (15 days for nonpayment cases), and may delay it up to seven days; if the tenant contests, trial is usually set within 15 days (15 to 30 days for nonpayment claims), and a continuance of more than two days requires the tenant to give security for or pay accruing rent into court. Until September 28, 2027, a nonpayment trial can be rescheduled to 90 to 104 days out for a tenant who is the parent of a child under 12 months living in the unit, receives medical assistance and has been approved for health-related social needs housing supports. If you win, the sheriff executes a writ after a four-day notice of restitution; the judgment can't be enforced if you later sign a new agreement or accept rent for occupancy after the judgment. The court may award attorney fees to the prevailing party, but not to a landlord whose tenant does not contest. The filing fee is set by statute. Under the 2026 court rules, your complaint's caption must say whether the case is subject to the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the complaint and judgment must follow the statewide forms on the Oregon Judicial Department's website, and a judgment against several tenants must state the result for each (UTCR 18.020 to UTCR 18.040, court rules); some counties also have supplementary local rules.

title: Setting Aside and Sealing Eviction Records
bodyText: On a former tenant's motion, the court must set aside the judgment and seal the records of an eviction case that ended in the tenant's favor or in dismissal, a stipulated judgment the tenant complied with (with any money award satisfied), or a judgment of restitution (with any money award satisfied) entered at least five years earlier or, until January 2, 2028, based on claims arising between April 1, 2020 and March 1, 2022. Each court also sets aside and seals, once a year, judgments with no unexpired or unsatisfied money award: restitution judgments at least five years old and dismissals or judgments for the tenant at least 12 months old. A set-aside judgment is treated as never entered. When screening you may not consider dismissed actions, judgments for the applicant or judgments five or more years old, and, until January 2, 2028, judgments on claims arising between April 1, 2020 and March 1, 2022.

title: Tenant Property After a Writ
bodyText: When the sheriff returns possession to you, you must remove, store and dispose of the tenant's personal property under the abandoned property statute, and in that case you may not require payment of storage charges before releasing it. Execution, removal, storage and sale costs you don't recover from sale proceeds are added to the judgment. If you don't let the tenant recover the property, the tenant may recover twice the actual damages or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater.

title: No Lockouts, Utility Shutoffs or Property Seizures
bodyText: You may take possession only after an abandonment or relinquishment or through the court process. Removing or excluding a tenant, or seriously attempting or threatening to, or willfully cutting heat, running water, hot water, electricity or another essential service, lets the tenant get a court order restoring possession or end the tenancy and recover up to two months' rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater; the tenant can also recover damages without ending the tenancy. Distraint for rent is abolished, and a lien on the tenant's household goods is unenforceable unless perfected before October 5, 1973.

title: No Landlord Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: A landlord's lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods is unenforceable (unless perfected before October 5, 1973), and distraint for rent is abolished. The possessory liens of ORS 87.152 to 87.212 don't apply to tenancies under the act, and a lease can't create a lien in household goods. Abandoned property is handled under the abandoned property statute, and a storage lien under ORS 87.152 can arise only after property is conclusively presumed abandoned.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: You may not raise rent, decrease services, serve a termination notice or bring or threaten an eviction in retaliation because a tenant complained (or said in writing they would complain) to a government agency about a building, health or housing code violation materially affecting health or safety, or about mail delivery or housing discrimination violations; made a complaint to you in good faith and related to the tenancy; organized or joined a tenants' union; testified against you; successfully defended an eviction in the last six months (other than on a notice-service or notice-period defect); uses a dwelling as a family child care home as the statute allows; or asserted any other right under federal, state or local law. 'Decreasing services' includes unreasonably restricting tenant meetings in common areas. The tenant gets the lockout remedies (up to two months' rent or twice damages) and a defense to eviction. You may still evict if a complaint to you or your agent was made unreasonably or harassingly, the code violation was caused mainly by the tenant's household or guests, the tenant was behind on rent when you served the notice (rent paid into court doesn't count), or compliance requires work that would deprive the tenant of the unit.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization is protected from retaliation, and unreasonably restricting tenants' use of common areas for meetings to establish a tenant organization counts as retaliatory decreasing of services. Oregon's broader assembly and canvassing rights apply only to manufactured dwelling and floating home facilities.

title: Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: If the tenant has moved out and someone else remains without permission, you may give that person at least 24 hours' written notice specifying the cause and the date and time to leave, and then recover possession through the court process, but only if the rental agreement prohibited subletting or letting someone else occupy without your written permission and you haven't knowingly accepted rent from that person. A squatter who never had permission is outside the landlord-tenant act; an owner or landlord may recover possession from a squatter through the court process after 24 hours' written notice stating the vacate date and time and that the cause is the person's status as a squatter. A temporary occupant under a written temporary occupancy agreement can be required to leave as that agreement allows and is treated as a squatter if it stays after the tenancy ends or after the tenant revokes permission by ending the agreement.

title: Fire, Casualty and Uninhabitable Units
bodyText: Oregon has no general casualty-termination statute. If a government agency posts the unit as unsafe and unlawful to occupy after the tenancy begins, a tenant who didn't cause the conditions may end the tenancy immediately, and you may end it on 24 hours' written notice if you and your failure to maintain didn't cause them; you must return deposits and prorated prepaid rent within 14 days. If the unit is destroyed in a declared natural disaster (wildfire, flood, earthquake and similar events, even if begun by negligent or intentional acts), the tenancy ends immediately unless you and the tenant agree otherwise afterward: return deposits and prepaid rent (prorated from the disaster), don't charge the tenant for cleanup unless the tenant was responsible for the disaster, and let the tenant search for valuables after the emergency; no rent is owed while the unit is inaccessible or destroyed. Otherwise, an uninhabitable unit triggers the tenant's repair and essential-service remedies. A lease clause letting you end the tenancy after a casualty would add a cause the termination statute doesn't list, so the library doesn't offer one; repairs that make the unit unsafe are a qualifying landlord reason after the first year, with 90 days' notice and a relocation payment where required.

title: Posted or Unlawful Units
bodyText: If an agency posts a unit as unsafe and unlawful to occupy, you may not continue or start a tenancy there until you correct the conditions; knowingly doing so lets the tenant leave immediately and recover two months' rent or up to twice actual damages, whichever is greater. If an agency notifies you that a unit is unlawful but safe for the existing tenant, you may not start a new tenancy until you correct it; a written pre-tenancy disclosure of the determination (with the agency's notice attached) protects you from the tenant's damages claim but not from the agency's penalties or your habitability duty, and the library doesn't offer it as a clause. You may not take a deposit to secure a rental agreement for a posted or noticed unit without that disclosure; if you knowingly do, or don't correct the conditions before the tenancy is to start, the applicant may end the agreement and recover twice the deposit. A city of more than 300,000 people may recover its tenant relocation costs from an owner whose multiple and material code violations for more than 30 days, through the owner's action or inaction, endanger tenants or the public and cause condemnation; as to a tenant's relocation costs, it is a defense that the condition was caused by that tenant's action or negligence.

title: Tenants and Foreclosure
bodyText: Before signing a lease for premises with four or fewer units, you must disclose in writing any outstanding notice of default or trustee's sale, pending foreclosure suit, pending declaration of forfeiture or suit for specific performance of a contract of sale, or pending tax-lien foreclosure. During a foreclosure, a tenant with actual notice of it may apply the deposit or prepaid rent to its obligation to you after written notice without that being grounds for termination, and a fixed-term tenant may end the tenancy on 60 days' notice unless within 30 days you give written evidence from a lender or trustee that the property is no longer in foreclosure, or that a court has appointed a receiver. After a trustee's sale (nonjudicial foreclosure), the purchaser must give the occupants written notice of the sale containing the information the statute lists (a notice in the statutory form complies) within 30 days after the sale, and before or with any 30-day termination notice; a bona fide tenant may stay for 60 days after a written termination notice under a fixed term lease, or at least 30 days for a periodic tenancy, though a purchaser who will live there may end even a fixed term on 30 days' notice. If the purchaser accepts rent, signs a new agreement or fails to terminate the tenancy as the statute allows within 30 days after the sale, the purchaser becomes the landlord. The purchaser's responsibility for deposits follows the foreclosure statute. After an execution sale on a judgment with priority over the lease, a tenant under an unexpired lease may stay until the redemption period expires by paying the purchaser (or redemptioner) each month the greater of the value of the use and occupancy or the lease payments.

title: Condominium Conversion
bodyText: Converting a rental building to condominiums brings the condominium statutes' notices to tenants. After the declarant's conversion notice, you may not give a 30-day no-cause notice ending the tenancy before the 120-day or 60-day periods in those statutes run out, or raise the rent beyond a scheduled increase in a written rental agreement or the West-region CPI increase; in the year before the declaration is recorded, no-cause notices or above-CPI increases given to avoid the conversion requirements are also barred. Either violation lets the tenant recover six times the monthly rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater. Cities may limit rent increases during the conversion notice period within the state cap.

title: Premium Holdover Rates (Barred)
bodyText: Oregon limits a holding-over tenant's liability to your actual damages, including the value of rent until you know or should know the tenant has given up possession, and bars liquidated damages in a rental agreement except the capped early-termination fee. A lease charge of a premium daily rate (for example 150% of rent) for holding over would be liquidated damages, so the library doesn't offer one; the holdover clause recovers actual damages only.

title: Moving to a Care Facility
bodyText: Oregon has no statute letting a tenant end a lease early because of a move to assisted living, a nursing facility or other care, or because of illness or incapacity. A month-to-month tenant can always leave on 30 days' notice; a fixed-term tenant who leaves early is subject to the lease and the early-termination rules.

title: Minors as Tenants
bodyText: A minor can be a tenant in Oregon. An unemancipated, unmarried minor living apart from parents or guardians who is 16 or 17 (or younger and a parent, or pregnant) may contract for a dwelling and utilities without parental consent, and the contract binds the minor; parents aren't liable unless they sign as guarantors. The act's definition of tenant includes such a minor, and a minor tenant may appear in an eviction case.

title: Drug and Alcohol Free Housing Programs
bodyText: Oregon recognizes drug and alcohol free housing run by a nonprofit or housing authority for people in recovery, with a written rental agreement that must contain specified terms. In such housing, if a tenant who has lived there less than two years uses, possesses or shares alcohol, marijuana, illegal drugs or unprescribed drugs, you may give a 48-hour termination notice that allows a 24-hour cure; a repeat within six months supports a 24-hour notice with no cure. The library's ordinary lease is not for these programs.

title: Drug, Prostitution and Gambling Nuisance Abatement
bodyText: Oregon's place-nuisance statutes declare places used for prostitution, for-profit gambling, unauthorized controlled-substance or unlawful cannabis activity, and drug-lab sites not decontaminated within 180 days to be nuisances. The Attorney General, a district, county or city attorney, or anyone living or doing business in the county may sue to abate one, and a court may order the place closed for up to a year, award damages, and secure the property at a cost that becomes a lien; violating an order is a crime. A court won't order abatement against an owner it finds in good faith had no knowledge of the nuisance or has been making reasonable efforts to abate it, isn't in contempt, and will make best efforts to abate it immediately. Separately, unlawful manufacture, delivery or possession of a controlled substance by the tenant or someone in the tenant's control, on the premises or in the immediate vicinity, supports a 24-hour termination, and a landlord whose good-faith 24-hour termination on such grounds fails in court is not for that reason in violation of a law requiring the tenant's removal, while it keeps making good-faith efforts.

title: How to Deliver Notices
bodyText:
Written notices under the landlord-tenant act must be served by personal delivery, by first class mail (adding three days to the notice period, and the notice must say so), or by first class mail plus attachment to the main entrance if the written rental agreement provides for it both ways.

E-mail service is allowed only under a written addendum both parties sign after the tenant has moved in, listing each side's e-mail addresses, letting either side end it or change the address on three days' written notice, and containing the statute's notice about receiving legal notices by e-mail; even then, a termination notice sent by e-mail must also go by first class mail.

Other methods may be used only in addition to these.

'Actual notice' (for entry, for example) may be given in person or by voicemail, by a written notice left as the statute describes, or by another method agreed and described in the written rental agreement.

Days are counted as consecutive calendar days, excluding the day of service and including the last day until 11:59 p.m. Deposit refunds, utility bills and abandoned-property notices have their own delivery rules.

Oregon's electronic transactions act applies only between parties who agreed to transact electronically, doesn't override a statute's required delivery method, and itself doesn't authorize electronic notice of default, eviction or a right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence; e-mail service rests only on the landlord-tenant act's addendum rule.

title: Oregon's Statutory Forms
bodyText: Oregon prescribes several forms landlords use: the notice that must appear in an e-mail service addendum ('THIS IS AN IMPORTANT NOTICE ABOUT YOUR RIGHTS REGARDING RECEIPT OF WRITTEN NOTICES'); the qualified third-party verification a victim may use to end a tenancy; the eviction complaint and summons forms; the notice of rental assistance from the Oregon Judicial Department that goes with nonpayment notices and summonses; the foreclosure purchaser's notice to residential tenants; and agency forms for affordability-restriction notices and (from 2027) well-water test results. Use the current versions; the court forms are on the Oregon Judicial Department's website.

title: Giving Tenants a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: You must give the tenant a copy of any written rental agreement and of all amendments and additions. Keep a copy of each agreement at the resident manager's office or the manager's disclosed address; when a tenant asks, make it available for inspection within a reasonable time and provide a copy for a charge no greater than 25 cents a page or the actual copying cost, whichever is less.

title: Written Leases and Long Terms
bodyText: An agreement to lease real property for longer than one year is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it expressing the consideration, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged or that party's authorized agent. A rental agreement may otherwise be oral, but a late charge, fees, a renter's insurance requirement, utility billing and several other terms are enforceable in Oregon only if they are in a written rental agreement, and a week-to-week tenancy needs a written agreement.

title: Entering a Tenant's Home
bodyText:
Except in an emergency, a written repair request, an agreed yard-work entry, an agreement with the tenant about a specific entry, a court order, abandonment, or an absence of the tenant of more than seven days (entry then only at times reasonably necessary), you must give at least 24 hours' actual notice and enter only at reasonable times.

After receiving your notice, the tenant may deny consent (by actual notice, or by a written notice securely attached to the main entrance), but may not unreasonably withhold it; an unreasonable refusal lets you seek a court order or end the tenancy for cause, plus damages.

After an emergency entry in the tenant's absence, give actual notice within 24 hours of the fact, date and time, nature of the emergency and the names of those who entered.

Entry without notice to show the unit to a buyer requires a separate signed writing, made while you are actively trying to sell, with separate consideration.

You may not abuse entry or use it to harass; unlawful or harassing entry lets the tenant seek an injunction or end the tenancy and recover at least one month's rent (one week's for week-to-week). A good-faith attempt to comply protects you if an agency requires entry and the tenant refuses.

title: Selling or Changing Management
bodyText: Keep the manager and owner information you disclosed current; the duty binds any successor landlord, owner or manager. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is responsible for the security deposit and prepaid rent, except a trustee's-sale purchaser, as the foreclosure statute provides. A sale doesn't end a tenancy. After the first year of occupancy you may end a month-to-month tenancy, or a fixed term at its end, for a sale only where the buyer will live in the unit as a primary residence and you document the accepted offer, with the statutory notice and payment (the one-month payment isn't required if you own four or fewer units, except on the 60-day sale option); in an owner-occupied building or property with two units or fewer, 30 days' notice is enough for such a sale (or 60 days without cause). Showing the unit to buyers needs 24 hours' actual notice and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent, unless the tenant signs a separate written agreement for showings without notice, made while you are actively selling and supported by separate consideration.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText:
You may require renter's liability insurance only in a written rental agreement, only if you carry comparable liability insurance and give documentation to a tenant who asks, and only up to $100,000 per occurrence or the customary amount for similar rentals, whichever is greater.

Before a new tenancy, tell the applicant in writing about the requirement, the amount and a summary of the exceptions. You may not require it of a household at or below 50% of area median income or for a unit subsidized with public funds (vouchers don't count as a subsidy). To add it to an existing month-to-month tenancy, give 30 days' written notice with the summary; a tenant who doesn't comply can be given a for-cause notice and cure by getting insurance.

You may require only interested-party status, not a particular insurer, additional-insured status or a subrogation waiver, and you may claim against the policy only for damage the tenant is liable for (not wear and tear, acts of God or your conduct), only if the claim is greater than the tenant's security deposit and only with a copy to the tenant.

Your written agreement must describe your own insurance requirements. Knowing violations cost actual damages or $250, whichever is greater; a frivolous claim costs actual damages plus $500.

title: Keeping Tenants' Information Confidential
bodyText: Since June 5, 2026, you may not disclose a tenant's, former tenant's, applicant's or household member's confidential information, which includes date of birth, Social Security, taxpayer or government ID numbers, phone number and e-mail, banking information, tax returns, W-2 statements, and sources of income or financial assistance, employer, immigration status or membership in a protected class, records of victim protections they used, and medical or disability records. The exceptions are narrow: the individual's separate written consent; a court order, judicial warrant or subpoena (not an administrative one); communications needed for affordable-housing compliance; screening background and credit checks; giving a phone number or e-mail to someone who needs it for repairs, maintenance or utilities; answering a reference request from a prospective landlord; and your insurance claims, collections, administrative or court actions. A knowing violation costs twice the monthly rent. Because consent must be separate, a lease clause can't supply it.

title: Keeping Victim Information Confidential
bodyText: Information a tenant gives you to be released from a lease as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking may be disclosed only with the tenant's written consent, for an eviction proceeding, to a qualified third party, or as required by law; giving a verification statement doesn't waive the confidentiality of the tenant's communications with the qualified third party. Since June 5, 2026, records of a tenant's use of the victim protections are also confidential information under the broader confidentiality law.

title: Lease Terms Oregon Voids
bodyText: A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant waives rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act, authorizes a confession of judgment, agrees to excuse or limit your liability for your own willful misconduct or negligence (or to indemnify you for it), or agrees to pay liquidated damages other than the capped early-termination fee; such a term is unenforceable. Other provisions Oregon voids or bars in leases: fees not on the statute's list, including any move-in fee for an expected expense; waivers of the abandoned-property procedure; renter's insurance terms outside the statute; requiring payment by electronic means; a lien on household goods; and receiving rent free of the habitability duty. A lease may include an informal dispute resolution provision despite the waiver ban.

title: Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term
bodyText: If you deliberately use a rental agreement containing a provision you know is prohibited and try to enforce it, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent. Charging a fee the fee statute doesn't allow costs twice the tenant's actual damages or $300, whichever is greater, and collecting a charge that neither the agreement nor the law authorizes can also be an unlawful collection practice.

title: Collecting Money From Tenants
bodyText: Oregon's unlawful collection practices statute reaches anyone collecting a debt arising from a consumer transaction, which includes a residential lease, and it can be read as reaching a landlord collecting its own rent and charges. Among other things, it bars collecting interest, fees or charges beyond the actual debt unless the agreement expressly authorizes them or a law expressly allows them, threatening action you can't take, contacting the tenant's employer about the debt, and harassing communications. A willful violation lets the tenant recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus possible punitive damages and attorney fees. Since Oregon's fee statute limits what a lease can authorize, a fee the statute doesn't allow is not 'expressly authorized'.

title: The Unlawful Trade Practices Act
bodyText: Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act largely does not reach residential tenancy conduct: its definition of 'real estate' excludes conduct covered by ORS chapter 90. So the act is generally not a separate route against a residential landlord for tenancy conduct, although its general standard's clause on collecting or enforcing an obligation may reach rent collection, though a tenant can't bring its own suit on that clause (only on the act's listed practices); a tenant the landlord sues may be able to counterclaim; otherwise only a prosecuting attorney enforces it (whether advertising before a tenancy is 'conduct covered by ORS chapter 90' is not settled by the text); the landlord-tenant act's own remedies, fair housing law and the unlawful collection practices statute apply instead.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: If a court finds a rental agreement or any provision of it unconscionable when made, it may refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the rest without that provision, or limit the provision to avoid an unconscionable result; the same applies to a settlement of a claim under the act. The parties get a reasonable opportunity to present evidence of the agreement's setting, purpose and effect.

title: Attorney Fees
