bodyText: In any action on a rental agreement or under the landlord-tenant act, the court may award reasonable attorney fees at trial and on appeal, with costs and disbursements, to the prevailing party (the party with the final judgment), whatever the lease says; a one-way fee clause works both ways. In an eviction, a landlord whose tenant does not contest the case doesn't get attorney fees, and some statutes deny fees in particular situations (for example a nonpayment case dismissed because the tenant tendered payment after filing, or a victim's successful defense in some cases).

title: Oregon Fair Housing Classes
bodyText: Oregon bars housing discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, marital status, familial status, source of income (including Section 8 and other housing assistance) and disability, in renting, terms, advertising, and coercion or interference. A facially neutral policy with a disparate adverse impact on a protected class can violate the law, considering its business purpose and less discriminatory alternatives. Exemptions are narrow: familial status for qualifying housing for older persons; sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and familial status for renting space in an owner-occupied single-family home with shared common space (but not for advertising a preference); and sex where the property requires shared bath or bedroom facilities by unrelated persons of the opposite sex. Except as a federal rent-subsidy or affordable-rent program requires, Oregon's landlord-tenant act also bars discrimination against an applicant, tenant or household member based on actual or perceived immigration or citizenship status, and asking about that status. Local ordinances may add classes.

title: Source of Income
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, discourage, advertise a preference or otherwise discriminate because of source of income, which includes federal rent subsidies (Section 8) and any other local, state or federal housing assistance; it doesn't include income from a particular occupation or illegal income. You may still refuse based on an applicant's inability to pay rent, but only after taking the value of the applicant's housing assistance into account, and only consistently with fair housing laws.

title: Citizenship and Immigration Status
bodyText: You may not ask about the immigration or citizenship status of an applicant, tenant or household member (except where a federal housing program requires it), and you may not reject an applicant for lacking a Social Security number or proof of lawful presence if the applicant offers the identification the statute lists, which includes an individual taxpayer identification number, a passport, a driver license or any government identification regardless of expiration, and certain non-government combinations. You may not discriminate based on actual or perceived immigration status, or disclose or threaten to disclose immigration status to harass, retaliate or intimidate; violations are treated like other discrimination and are unlawful practices under the civil rights law.

title: Questions You May Not Ask Applicants
bodyText: When screening, you may not ask about immigration or citizenship status, may not consider medical marijuana card status, may consider arrests only as the screening statute allows, and may not consider dismissed evictions, judgments in the applicant's favor or old judgments. A rental notice or advertisement may not indicate a preference based on a protected class.

title: Families With Children
bodyText: Familial status is a protected class in Oregon: you may not refuse to rent or set different terms because a household includes children, except for qualifying housing for older persons. An occupancy guideline you adopt may not be more restrictive than two people per bedroom (a room of at least 70 square feet meant for sleeping and laid out with a fire exit in mind) and must be reasonable, considering bedroom and unit size and any discriminatory impact.

title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Oregon sets no statewide maximum occupancy for rentals, but an occupancy guideline you adopt may not be more restrictive than two people per bedroom and must be reasonable for the bedroom and unit sizes, without discriminatory impact on a protected class. Local housing codes may set their own standards, but no local government may set or enforce a maximum occupancy limit based on the family or non-family relationships among occupants. Listing the occupants in the lease and barring unapproved occupants also gives you Oregon's 24-hour notice route for an unauthorized person who stays after the tenant leaves, if you haven't knowingly accepted rent from that person; possession is then recovered through the court process.

title: Temporary Occupancy Agreements
bodyText:
Oregon lets you, the tenant and a proposed occupant sign a written temporary occupancy agreement. The temporary occupant is not a tenant and has no tenant's rights; the tenant may end the agreement at any time, and you may end it only for a material violation, without a right to cure.

You may screen the occupant for conduct or criminal record, but not credit or income. The agreement must expressly state that the occupant is not a tenant and has no tenant's rights and the termination rules, without a right to cure, may require compliance with the rules and may have an end date.

If the occupant doesn't leave when it ends, you may give the tenant a for-cause notice (unless the victim protections apply), and an occupant who stays after the tenancy ends, or after the tenant ends the agreement, is treated as a squatter; no written termination notice to the occupant is required. You may not use it to evade your duties, and every tenancy needs at least one tenant.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: You must allow reasonable modifications of the premises at the tenant's expense when necessary for full enjoyment by a person with a disability (you may, where reasonable, condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior at the end, reasonable wear and tear excepted), and make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services. You may not charge a pet deposit for an assistance animal. You may not disclose that an occupant has or died from a blood-borne infection.

title: House Rules
bodyText: A rule about the tenant's use and occupancy is enforceable only if it promotes tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects your property from abusive use or fairly distributes services and facilities; is reasonably related to that purpose; applies fairly to all tenants; is explicit enough to tell tenants what to do; isn't meant to evade your obligations; and the tenant had written notice of it on signing or when it was adopted. A rule adopted later that substantially modifies the bargain needs the tenant's written consent; from January 1, 2027, an indoor smoking ban adopted under the 2026 act's conditions is an exception. Rules become part of the rental agreement. Fees for repeated rule violations are limited to the statute's list.

title: Smoking Rules
bodyText:
Every Oregon rental agreement (other than for a space in a manufactured dwelling or floating home facility) must disclose the smoking policy: prohibited on the premises, allowed on the entire premises, or allowed in limited areas (identified).

From January 1, 2027, the statute defines smoking as inhaling or possessing a lit tobacco product, and you may change the policy during a tenancy to ban smoking inside units or interior common areas without the tenant's written consent only if the unit shares a wall with another unit or was developed under a development agreement, it isn't an accessible unit, the change doesn't apply to a fixed term until the term ends, you provide at least one posted designated smoking area on the premises, and you give 180 days' written notice.

A fee for smoking in a clearly designated nonsmoking area is allowed only under the rule-violation fee statute (up to $250, 24 hours after a warning). Statewide indoor clean air rules may reach staffed or public common areas.

title: Your Duty to Keep the Unit Habitable
Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies
bodyText: If you materially fail to comply with the lease or the habitability duty, the tenant may give written notice ending the tenancy on a date at least 30 days later (seven days for week-to-week) unless you remedy the breach within seven days for an essential service or 30 days otherwise; a recurrence within six months allows termination on 14 days' notice. The tenant may also recover damages, but not for a condition you neither knew nor reasonably should have known of, if the tenant knew of it and failed to give you timely actual notice or it was caused after the tenancy began by the deliberate or negligent act of someone other than you or your agent. For an essential service you intentionally or negligently fail to supply, after written notice and a reasonable time the tenant may buy the service and deduct its cost, recover reduced-rental-value damages, or, if the unit is unsafe or unfit, get substitute housing and stop paying rent; if the failure poses an imminent and serious threat, the tenant may give 48 hours' notice ending the tenancy unless you remedy it within those 48 hours. For a minor defect costing $300 or less (not mold, radon, asbestos or lead-based paint), the tenant may give at least seven days' written notice and then have it repaired by someone other than the tenant (you may reasonably specify who) and deduct the cost with a written statement. In an eviction for nonpayment or an action for rent, the tenant may counterclaim if you knew or should have known of the problem before you filed, and the court may order rent paid into court. None of these remedies applies to a condition the tenant or a guest caused.

title: Heat, Water and Cooling
bodyText: Adequate heating facilities, hot and cold running water and working plumbing are habitability items and essential services. For buildings whose construction permits were issued on or after April 1, 2024, you must also provide adequate cooling in at least one room other than a bathroom (central air, a heat pump or a portable air conditioner you supply). If you're responsible for a utility and it's shut off for your nonpayment, the tenant may pay and deduct, or end the tenancy on 72 hours' notice unless you restore service within the 72 hours, and recover actual damages. Tenants may install portable cooling devices subject only to the restrictions the statute allows, and a restriction is enforceable only if it is in writing, delivered to the tenant and states whether there is a community cooling space.

title: Locks and Keys
bodyText:
You must provide working locks for all dwelling entrance doors and latches for all windows through which the unit can be entered, and a means of unlocking them and of reaching the common areas and common facilities the tenant has access to, which must include at least one means other than a tenant portal. Oregon has no statute requiring rekeying between tenants or peepholes.

A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking may require you promptly to change the locks at the tenant's expense or let the tenant change them (if you don't act promptly the tenant may change them and give you a key) (if the perpetrator is a cotenant, only after the tenant gives you a court order excluding the perpetrator). Your charge for replacing a key the tenant lost, at the tenant's request, is outside the fee rules.

title: Utilities in Your Name and Tenant Accounts
bodyText:
If you're responsible for a utility under the lease and it's shut off for nonpayment, the tenant may pay the balance and deduct it from rent, or end the tenancy on 72 hours' actual notice unless you restore service in that time, and you must then return, within four days, rent prepaid for that month prorated from the later of termination or move-out and any other prepaid rent, and the deposit as the deposit statute requires; the tenant may also recover actual damages from the shutoff.

If a tenant can't get service in the tenant's own name because of a previous tenant's or the owner's unpaid bill, the tenant may, before moving in, pay and deduct, agree a solution with you, or end the tenancy immediately; after moving in, pay and deduct or end the tenancy on 72 hours' notice, which fails if service becomes available within that time.

If the tenancy ends before move-in, you must return all deposits, rent and fees within four days; if it ends after move-in, all rent and fees within four days and the deposit as the deposit statute requires, and the tenant may also recover actual damages from the shutoff. Failing to return money owed in these cases costs twice the amount.

A utility company can't transfer a claim against a tenant to the property owner without the owner's written consent. A municipal utility can't transfer one unless it notified the tenant and mailed the owner or the owner's agent a copy of the delinquency notice within 30 days after the payment was due; the statute itself gives a municipal utility no authority to transfer.

title: Tenants' Duties Under Oregon Law
bodyText:
By statute, a tenant must use the rooms and the facilities and appliances reasonably; keep the areas under the tenant's control clean, sanitary and free of debris and vermin as the premises' condition permits and to the extent the tenant caused the problem, and cooperate with your reasonable efforts to fix it; dispose of waste safely and legally (never needles or syringes in the garbage); keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits; test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms at least every six months, replace batteries and report problems in writing; and behave, and make guests behave, so as not to disturb neighbors.

A tenant may not tamper with alarms or sprinkler heads or deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly let others do so, and is not responsible for damage from acts of God or from a perpetrator of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking. Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant uses the unit only as a dwelling.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging
bodyText: A tenant may apply to install an electric vehicle charging station for personal, noncommercial use in or near the tenant's assigned parking space or dwelling unit. You may prohibit it only if the premises don't have at least one parking space per dwelling unit; otherwise you must approve a completed application within 60 days (unless you reasonably ask for more information) and may require an application, architectural standards, reasonable review and permit charges and reasonable restrictions that don't significantly raise the cost or reduce performance. A licensed electrician (at least journeyman) must install and remove it; the tenant pays all costs, including electricity and damage; if the station's combined load requires electrical upgrades you may assess their cost to the tenants with stations; the station is the tenant's personal property unless you negotiate otherwise; and if it isn't a certified electrical product, its owner must carry renter's liability insurance of at least $100,000 covering it and name you as an additional insured.

title: Towing at a Rental
bodyText:
You may have a vehicle removed only as the landlord towing statute and the private-property towing statutes allow.

Without notice, only if it blocks emergency access or entry, violates a prominently posted prohibition, is in a disabled space or a non-parking area, is in a reserved but unassigned tenant space without a tag (and only if you provide tags and have the written agreements the statute requires), or is in a space assigned to a tenant with that tenant's agreement at the time of the tow (you may not require tenants to agree in advance).

An inoperable vehicle parked under your agreement may be removed after a prominent notice affixed at least 72 hours before.

You may not tow because a registration has expired or is invalid. Posted guest spaces need readable signs, and parking facilities need tow signs under the general towing law. You may not require a nonremovable tag that reveals where the tenant lives. No Oregon statute authorizes a landlord to boot a vehicle.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules
bodyText:
Whether association rules bind a tenant depends on the association's governing documents; no Oregon statute binds tenants to them generally.

You may pass association assessments through to the tenant only if the written rental agreement sets out that requirement at the start of the tenancy and you give the tenant a copy of the assessment before or when you charge it. The statute's conditions read together cover move-in and move-out charges most clearly; for a fine caused by the tenant's rule violation, the safer route is to recover it as damages for the tenant's breach of the lease.

You may prohibit a family child care use that the association's governing documents don't allow, even though a landlord otherwise can't bar a certified or registered family child care home the tenant has told you about.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText:
Oregon's adult-use cannabis statutes expressly do not change landlord-tenant law, so a lease may restrict cannabis use and growing on the property like other conduct, and your lease's smoking policy can cover cannabis smoking (from January 1, 2027 the statutory smoking disclosure covers lit tobacco only, and a cannabis restriction added mid-tenancy that substantially modifies the bargain still needs the tenant's written consent).

A tenant who wants the rental registered as a medical marijuana grow site or processing site needs the owner's notarized written consent (yours, if you own the property), and a renewal needs it again unless your earlier consent covers the renewal term (you may say how many annual terms it covers).

When screening applicants you may not consider a medical marijuana card or a person's status as a patient, or convictions based only on marijuana use or possession. Making a cannabinoid extract without a license or registration is one of the 'outrageous in the extreme' acts that allow a 24-hour termination notice.

title: Firearms in Rental Housing
bodyText: No Oregon statute addresses whether a residential lease or rule may restrict a tenant's lawful possession of firearms, either way. A restriction in the lease itself is a term the tenant agrees to; a restriction adopted later as a rule must meet the general conditions for rules and can't substantially change the bargain without the tenant's written consent.

title: Flags, Signs and Religious Displays
bodyText: Oregon has no statute giving tenants of ordinary rentals a right to display flags, political signs or religious items, or limiting a landlord's display rules. The statutory right to post political signs and to canvass applies only to tenants renting a space for a manufactured dwelling or floating home in a facility, or a rented lot in a park converted to a planned community subdivision. A display rule adopted after the lease must meet the general conditions for rules.

title: Tenant Security Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: Oregon has no landlord-tenant statute on tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. Treat them like other tenant installations under the lease's alterations terms; a camera rule adopted after the lease must meet the general conditions for rules.

title: Tenant-Installed Solar and Other Alternative Energy Devices
bodyText: Oregon gives tenants no right to install a solar panel or other alternative energy device without your written permission; your lease's alterations terms control. If you give permission, the device is not a fixture you own unless your written agreement says so, and as conditions you may require the tenant to waive your liability for injury from negligent installation, get lien waivers from everyone who works on it, and post a bond or deposit up to the cost of restoring the premises.

title: Cable, Internet and Satellite Service
bodyText: Oregon has no statute requiring a landlord to give cable, internet or satellite providers access to a rental, or barring exclusive provider arrangements. If the provider bills you for cable, satellite or internet service and you pass the charge to the tenant, it is a 'utility or service': the written rental agreement must provide for the charge, you must bill in writing within the statute's time limits, any markup (up to 10%) is allowed only on the statute's conditions, and you can't force a markup into an existing agreement.

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText: No Oregon statute or rule text sets a maximum or minimum water heater temperature for residential rentals (lodging rented daily or weekly to travelers has a 120°F minimum). Habitability requires a water supply approved under applicable law, capable of producing hot and cold running water, furnished to appropriate fixtures, and maintained in good working order to the extent the system can be controlled by the landlord; plumbing must conform to the law in effect when it was installed, which brings in the plumbing code.

title: Pools and Spas at Rentals
bodyText: Oregon licenses and regulates public pools and spas through the Oregon Health Authority: building one needs plan approval and operating one needs an annual license. The Authority's rules treat a pool at a residential housing facility with five or more living units, used only by the facility's residents, as a regulated 'limited-use' aquatic venue. A pool owned by no more than four people at a residential property with no more than four living units, for the occupants and their friends only, is a private swimming pool and is exempt from those rules. The rules set design standards for regulated pools, including enclosures at least 6 feet high. No Oregon statute sets pool rules specific to leases.

title: Jury Trial Waivers (Not Offered)
bodyText: The Oregon Constitution keeps the right to a jury in civil cases, and no Oregon statute addresses a jury waiver in a residential lease. The library does not include a jury waiver for Oregon, and Oregon's act bars any lease term in which the tenant agrees to give up rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act.

title: Waiving Exemptions From Collection (Not Offered)
bodyText: When you collect a money judgment, Oregon exempts some of the tenant's property from execution, including household goods, furniture, a radio, a television and utensils up to a set value. No Oregon statute addresses a lease clause waiving those exemptions, and the library does not include one. A landlord's lien on a tenant's household goods is unenforceable.

title: Landlord Registration and Rental Licensing
bodyText: Oregon has no statewide registration or licensing requirement for landlords of ordinary rentals. The state registration statute applies to landlords of manufactured dwelling parks and floating home marinas only. Cities may run their own rental registration or licensing programs (flagged, not resolved). A licensed property manager is regulated separately by the Real Estate Agency. Two general business-registration laws can still reach you. Leasing real estate counts as carrying on business under Oregon's assumed business name law. So if you rent under a name that does not conspicuously disclose your real and true name (for an entity, its name on file with the Secretary of State), you must register that name with the Secretary of State. Until you do, you lack standing to maintain a court action for the business, an eviction included. You can cure that at any time by registering. A tenant who sues you and has to track down your real name can recover $500 or the actual cost, whichever is greater, and a civil penalty of up to $100 applies (ORS 648.005, 648.007, 648.135, 648.990). An out-of-state LLC or corporation must get the Secretary of State's authority, naming an Oregon registered agent, before transacting business in Oregon. Until it does, it may not maintain a proceeding in an Oregon court, though its acts stay valid and it may defend a suit. Owning real property without more is not transacting business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts and on case law; get advice before filing (ORS 63.701, 63.704, 63.707, 60.701, 60.704). An owner who lives outside Oregon and registers an assumed business name is deemed to appoint the Secretary of State as agent to receive legal papers (ORS 648.061, 648.070).

title: Rental Inspection Programs
bodyText: Oregon has no statewide rental inspection program for ordinary rentals. Some cities inspect rentals or require rental licenses (flagged, not resolved). If a city posts a unit as unsafe or unlawful to occupy, the tenant protections for condemned units apply.

title: Foreign Ownership of Rental Property
bodyText: Oregon has no statute restricting foreign persons, companies or governments from owning or leasing residential rental property.

title: Blank Spaces in the Lease
bodyText: No Oregon statute requires a residential lease to have every blank filled before signing. Fill or strike every blank anyway: a written rental agreement must list any security deposit and describe every fee you charge, and a late charge needs the written terms the late-charge statute requires.

title: Plain Language and Type Size
bodyText: Oregon sets no plain-language, readability or type-size standard for residential leases. Some notices you give must follow statutory forms, and a few terms must be in a separate signed writing (such as an agreement letting you show the unit to buyers without notice, which must be signed while you are actively selling and be supported by separate consideration recited in the agreement).

title: Translated Leases and Notices
bodyText: Oregon does not require a landlord to translate a lease or notices. The rental-assistance notice that must go with a nonpayment termination notice and with the summons in a nonpayment case tells tenants where to find information in Spanish, Korean, Russian, Vietnamese and Chinese.

title: What an Oregon Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Oregon has no single list of required lease contents, but specific rules require items in a written rental agreement: any security deposit, every fee you may charge, the late-charge terms if you charge one, the smoking policy, a flood plain notice if the unit is in a 100-year flood plain, utility or service charges you will pass through (common-area charges and any cable or internet markup described separately), an association-assessment pass-through, the renter's insurance description if you require it, and the landlord and agent disclosures (in the agreement or another writing). If a licensed property manager prepares the lease, it must also show the manager's registered business name and address, the tenant's name and address, the unit address, the rent amount and payment terms, the lease term, every amount the tenant pays the manager and why (including whether the manager or the owner holds the deposit), both signatures and the date, and the manager must give the tenant a copy.

title: Quiet Enjoyment
bodyText: Oregon's landlord-tenant act has no express covenant of quiet enjoyment. Its protections come from specific rules: limits on landlord entry, remedies for unlawful ouster, exclusion or diminished services, and the bar on retaliation. Tenants must behave, and make their guests behave, so as not to disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Breach Yourself
bodyText: Oregon's act gives a landlord no procedure to enter, fix a tenant's breach and bill the cost as rent. For a tenant's noncompliance you may give a for-cause termination notice with the right to cure, and recover damages or get an injunction; damage the tenant causes can be charged against the security deposit at the end of the tenancy. Entry to make repairs still requires the usual notice.

title: Assistance Animals
bodyText: Refusing a reasonable accommodation, including an assistance animal a person with a disability needs, is housing discrimination in Oregon. You may not ask for verification when the disability and the need are obvious or already known; otherwise you may ask only for what's needed to evaluate the disability-related need. You may not charge any deposit or fee for keeping the animal. You may refuse a specific animal only if it poses a direct threat to others' health or safety that can't be eliminated or significantly reduced, based on an individualized assessment of objective evidence. The tenant remains responsible for damage, and the rule-violation fee for not cleaning up an animal's waste outside the unit can apply.

title: Misrepresented Assistance Animals
bodyText: Oregon has no statute penalizing a tenant who misrepresents a pet as a service or assistance animal to get housing. Your protection is the verification you may request when the disability-related need isn't obvious.

title: Penalties for Refusing an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Oregon has no criminal penalty for a landlord who refuses a tenant's assistance animal; the refusal is an unlawful housing practice enforced through a civil rights complaint to the Bureau of Labor and Industries, which can assess civil penalties of up to $11,000 ($27,500 or $55,000 for repeat violators), or a lawsuit; a tenant may also raise it as a defense to a discriminatory eviction unless the tenant is in default in rent. There is no criminal penalty for the refusal itself, although willfully violating a commissioner's order is a Class A misdemeanor. Separately, it is a Class A misdemeanor to intentionally or knowingly injure, or attempt to injure, an assistance animal in the narrower sense of an individually trained dog or other animal designated by rule, or to interfere with one while it is assisting a person with a disability.

title: Liens From Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText: If a tenant hires someone to work on the property, the contractor's construction lien can reach the tenant's leasehold. Your own interest can be liened too: an improvement built with your knowledge is treated as built at your request unless, within three days after you learn of the work, you post a written notice in a conspicuous place on the land or the improvement saying you won't be responsible for it. Requiring your written consent for alterations doesn't by itself protect you once you know work is under way.

title: Receivership for Dangerous Rental Buildings
bodyText: If a city or county believes residential property violates building or housing codes badly enough to threaten public health, safety or welfare, it may ask the circuit court to appoint a receiver to do the repairs, after at least 60 days' written notice to the owner and other interested parties. The receiver's net losses, once the court approves them, can be recorded as a lien on the property that takes priority over most other liens and mortgages (not property tax or assessment liens, the mining, land-preparation, nursery-stock and irrigation-power liens of ORS 87.352 to 87.362, or a purchase-money interest recorded before the city's or county's notice, unless the notice was given to its holder and the buyer or borrower and the holder hadn't moved to foreclose or take possession before the receiver was appointed).

title: Utility Shutoffs and Tenants
bodyText: When the account holder isn't the occupant, regulated utilities must warn the tenants before shutting off service: an energy utility gives occupants a five-day notice addressed to 'tenant' or 'occupant' and, for a master-metered multifamily building, notifies the Public Utility Commission at least five business days ahead; a regulated water utility sends a duplicate notice to the service address and, for a master-metered building, a seven-day notice to each unit. If you are responsible for a utility under the lease and it is shut off for nonpayment, the tenant may pay it and deduct the amount from rent, or end the tenancy on 72 hours' notice unless you restore service within the 72 hours. A regulated water utility must also tell the Public Utility Commission seven days before shutting off a master-metered building.

title: Statement of Tenant Rights
bodyText: Oregon does not require a landlord to give tenants a state-prepared statement or summary of tenant rights with the lease. Specific notices carry their own statutory information, such as the rental-assistance notice with a nonpayment notice and the veterans information with termination notices.

title: Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Rent
bodyText: No Oregon statute requires the same rent or terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. The statewide rent increase limit and its notice rules apply to both. During a fixed term neither side can change the terms alone. In a month-to-month tenancy, specific changes need the notice the act sets (rent, late charges, renter's insurance, public service charges; "Changing Terms During a Tenancy"), other changes come through rules, and a rule that substantially modifies the bargain needs the tenant's written consent.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In an eviction for nonpayment, or an action for rent while the tenant is in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for any amount the tenant could recover under the lease or the landlord-tenant act, if the tenant proves you knew or should have known of the facts, or had actual notice, before you filed. On either side's request the court may order the tenant to pay accrued and accruing rent into court, applies it to whatever each side is owed, and enters judgment for the tenant on possession if no rent remains due. A tenant who doesn't pay rent into court as ordered can't pursue the counterclaim. A continuance of more than two days requires the tenant to pay rent into court (or give a bond), and if the tenant doesn't pay as ordered the case is tried immediately.

title: Settlements, Continuances and Stays in Eviction Cases
bodyText: Oregon eviction cases often end in a stipulated agreement: if the tenant keeps possession on condition of paying or doing something by set dates, the court enters an order, and if the tenant later complies, the case is dismissed. You can enforce such an order by affidavit of noncompliance only if it covers future conduct and payment of past-due amounts for no more than six months and future rent for no more than the next three months; the order is automatically dismissed 12 months after entry unless you've filed a noncompliance affidavit and won, and the tenant can ask for a hearing that delays the writ. A continuance longer than two days requires the tenant to give security for, or pay into court, the rent that accrues. A court may stay the eviction of a state service member for up to 90 days in the circumstances the statute lists. Until September 28, 2027, a nonpayment trial must be rescheduled to 90 to 104 days out if a tenant who is the parent of a child under 12 months living in the unit, receives medical assistance and has been approved for health-related social needs housing supports moves at least three judicial days before trial and has delivered documentation of the approval to you. Beyond these, there is no general statutory hardship stay.

title: Tenancies After a Natural Disaster
bodyText: Since June 5, 2026, if a tenancy is affected by a natural disaster (a disaster with a declared state of emergency for wildfire, flood, tsunami, earthquake or similar event, including one begun by negligent or intentional acts), unless you and the tenant agree otherwise after the disaster: a destroyed unit's tenancy ends immediately and neither side owes anything further under the agreement or the act, except that you must return the deposit and prepaid rent (including rent prorated from the disaster date) under the deposit statute, may not hold the tenant responsible for cleanup unless the tenant was responsible for the disaster, and after the emergency must notify the tenant and allow a chance to search the premises for valuables (you may require a release of liability for that visit). Anyone who stays after the tenancy ends can be given the 24-hour posted-unit notice. No rent is owed while the unit is inaccessible because of the disaster or destroyed; a unit posted unsafe or unlawful to occupy counts as inaccessible. A lease can't contract around this in advance.

title: Rights an Oregon Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Oregon has one general non-waiver rule for the whole landlord-tenant chapter, ORS chapter 90, which covers ordinary residential tenancies (ORS 90.100 to 90.465) and manufactured dwelling and floating home spaces in a facility (ORS 90.505 to 90.850): 'A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant' (ORS 90.245(1)) '(a) Agrees to waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.245(1)). Such a provision 'is unenforceable' (ORS 90.245(2)), and if you deliberately use a provision you know is prohibited and try to enforce it, the tenant may recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent ("Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term"). Several sections repeat the point for particular rights. A rental agreement may not let anyone receive rent free of your habitability duty (ORS 90.250). On abandoned property, you 'may not, as part of a rental agreement, require a tenant ... to waive any right provided by this section' (ORS 90.425(26)(b)); only a separate good-faith writing signed after the tenancy ends, or no more than seven days before, can let you dispose of property without the statutory procedure (ORS 90.425(26)(a)). You may not 'Require that a tenant waive the insurer's subrogation rights' (ORS 90.222(7)(c)). Attorney fees go to the prevailing party 'notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary' (ORS 90.255). The one waiver the chapter itself permits in an ORS 90.100 to 90.465 lease is a provision for informal dispute resolution (ORS 90.220(5)), which 'does not include mandatory mediation or arbitration' (ORS 90.100(24)). Settling an existing dispute is different: a settlement in which a party gives up a claim is not barred, but a court may refuse to enforce it if it 'was unconscionable when made' (ORS 90.135(1)(b)). Outside chapter 90, if a homeowner in foreclosure sells the home to an investor and stays on under a lease-back (an "equity conveyance"), a contract provision is void if it has the seller 'Waive any rights of the equity seller under ORS 646A.725 to 646A.750' (ORS 646A.735(2)). The full list of terms Oregon voids is in "Lease Terms Oregon Voids".

title: Which Habitability Duties an Oregon Lease Can Change
bodyText: Your Oregon habitability duty can't be switched off by the lease: 'A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with ORS 90.320 (1) or 90.730' (ORS 90.250), and a term by which the tenant waives rights or remedies is unenforceable (ORS 90.245(1)(a); ORS 90.245(2)). For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, the only flexibility is what the duty section itself builds in. Garbage: receptacles and removal are owed 'Except as otherwise provided by local ordinance or by written agreement between the landlord and the tenant' (ORS 90.320(1)(g)), the one listed item a written agreement may change. Water: the supply may be 'Under the control of the tenant or landlord' (ORS 90.320(1)(c)(A)), and the safe-drinking-water duty runs 'to the extent that the system can be controlled by the landlord' (ORS 90.320(1)(c)(D)), but a supply 'capable of producing hot and cold running water' (ORS 90.320(1)(c)(A)) is still required, and no Oregon statute lets a lease waive it where the property has no well or public water. Appliances: ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances are owed in good repair 'if supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord' (ORS 90.320(1)(i)), and you need not supply a cooking appliance or refrigerator you did not supply or agree to supply (ORS 90.365(4)). Cooling is owed only where building permits for the building were issued on or after April 1, 2024 (ORS 90.320(1)(n)). Where the tenant owns a recreational vehicle and rents the space, or owns a manufactured dwelling or floating home and rents a space outside a facility, provisions that reasonably apply only to a home do not apply (ORS 90.320(3)); spaces in a facility are governed by ORS 90.730 instead. Finally, a writing may have the tenant perform 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling' (ORS 90.320(2)) only if it is made in good faith and not to evade your obligations, does not diminish your obligations to other tenants, and its terms are clearly and fairly disclosed with adequate consideration specifically stated (ORS 90.320(2)(a)-(c)); that moves a task to the tenant, not the duty ("Tenant Maintenance Tasks Agreement" clause). On a lease waiver of the water or hot-water duty: A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: How Serious a Defect Must Be for Each Oregon Tenant Remedy
bodyText: Oregon uses a different seriousness test for each tenant remedy (tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465; a facility space uses ORS 90.360 and ORS 90.365 with the space duties of ORS 90.730, but the minor-defect remedy reaches only a failure to repair 'contrary to ORS 90.320' (ORS 90.368(2)), and ORS 90.320 does not govern facility spaces (ORS 90.320(3))). The duty itself: a unit 'shall be considered unhabitable if it substantially lacks' (ORS 90.320(1)) one of the listed items. Ending the tenancy on notice: the tenant may give the 30-day notice (seven days for you to cure an essential service, 30 days otherwise) 'if there is a material noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement or a noncompliance with ORS 90.320 or 90.730' (ORS 90.360(1)(a)), so a breach of a lease promise must be material, while a breach of the habitability duty is measured by the "substantially lacks" test. Damages and an injunction: available 'for any noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement or ORS 90.320 or 90.730' (ORS 90.360(2)), subject to the knowledge limits in that subsection. Essential services: the buy-and-deduct, reduced-rental-value and substitute-housing remedies apply only if you 'intentionally or negligently' fail to supply an essential service (ORS 90.365(1)), and you are not treated as failing if 'The landlord substantially supplies the essential service' (ORS 90.365(3)(a)) or are making a reasonable, good-faith effort and the failure is beyond your control (ORS 90.365(3)(b)). An essential service is heat, plumbing, hot and cold running water, gas, electricity, light fixtures, exterior door locks, window latches and any cooking appliance or refrigerator you supply or must supply, plus 'Any other service or habitability obligation imposed by the rental agreement or ORS 90.320, the lack or violation of which creates a serious threat to the tenant's health, safety or property or makes the dwelling unit unfit for occupancy' (ORS 90.100(15)(a)(B)). Substitute housing requires that the failure 'makes the dwelling unit unsafe or unfit to occupy' (ORS 90.365(1)(c)). The 48-hour termination notice requires an 'imminent and serious threat to the tenant's health, safety or property' (ORS 90.365(2)), which 'shall not include the presence of radon, asbestos or lead-based paint or the future risk of flooding or seismic hazard' (ORS 90.365(2)). Repair and deduct: only a minor habitability defect, one that 'may reasonably be repaired for not more than $300' (ORS 90.368(1)(a)), and not mold, radon, asbestos or lead-based paint (ORS 90.368(1)(b)). Code violations: the condemned-unit rules turn on conditions that violate state or local law and 'materially affect health or safety' (ORS 90.380(2)(a)), and a tenant may end the tenancy at once if conditions existing at the outset and not caused by the tenant 'pose an imminent and serious threat to the health or safety of occupants' (ORS 90.380(7)) within six months of the start. Details of each remedy: "Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies".

title: No Oregon Presumption on Habitability or Repair Time
bodyText: No Oregon statute or rule presumes that you breached the habitability duty because a unit violates a code or an inspector's citation is unabated, presumes that you had notice of a condition, presumes that a repair took too long after a set number of days, or presumes a unit habitable. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Whether a unit 'substantially lacks' (ORS 90.320(1)) a required item is proved like any other fact, and the remedy sections put the knowledge questions to proof instead. A tenant cannot recover damages for a habitability noncompliance you neither knew nor reasonably should have known of if the tenant knew or reasonably should have known of it and failed to give you actual notice in a reasonable time, or if it was caused after the tenancy began by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of someone other than you or a person acting on your behalf (ORS 90.360(2)(a)-(b)). In your action for possession for nonpayment or for rent, a tenant who counterclaims 'must prove that prior to the filing of the landlord's action the landlord reasonably had or should have had knowledge or had received actual notice of the facts that constitute the tenant's counterclaim' (ORS 90.370(1)(a)). The only presumptions in the residential tenancy sections concern abandoned property: property not claimed or removed in time 'is conclusively presumed to be abandoned' (ORS 90.425(9)). Repair timing is set by the tenant's notices, not a presumption ("Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies").

title: No Required Oregon Lease Statement on Habitability
bodyText: Oregon does not require your rental agreement to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation, or to state an agreed condition instead. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. You don't need the sentence for the duty to apply: 'A landlord shall at all times during the tenancy maintain the dwelling unit in a habitable condition' (ORS 90.320(1)), whatever the lease says, and the lease can't take that duty away (ORS 90.250). The library's maintenance clause restates it anyway ("Maintenance & Repairs" clause). Two Oregon writings touch habitability before a tenancy starts. If you take a deposit to secure the execution of a rental agreement, you must first give the applicant a written statement of the rent, fees and deposits, the terms of the agreement to execute and the conditions for refunding or keeping the deposit (ORS 90.297(2)), and you must return the deposit within five business days if the applicant rejects the agreement 'due to the discovery of material defects relating to the premise's habitability, as described in ORS 90.320 (1)' (ORS 90.297(4)); see ORS 90.297(5). And if a governmental agency has told you a unit is unlawful but not unsafe to occupy, a written disclosure of that determination, with the agency's notice attached, given before the tenancy begins, means you are not liable to the tenant for entering the new tenancy (ORS 90.380(3)(c)), but it 'does not release the landlord from the duties imposed by this chapter' (ORS 90.380(3)(e)) and does not stop the agency from imposing any penalty the law allows for entering the new tenancy (ORS 90.380(3)(e)); see "Posted or Unlawful Units".

title: An Oregon Tenant Can't Waive Habitability
bodyText: In Oregon no agreement can remove a habitability requirement itself. 'A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with ORS 90.320 (1) or 90.730' (ORS 90.250), and a term by which the tenant agrees 'to waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.245(1)(a)) is unenforceable (ORS 90.245(2)); deliberately using a term you know is prohibited and trying to enforce it can cost you up to three months' periodic rent on top of damages ("Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term"). This covers ordinary tenancies (ORS 90.320) and facility spaces (ORS 90.730). Only two sentences in the duty section let an agreement change anything. Garbage receptacles and their removal are owed 'Except as otherwise provided by local ordinance or by written agreement between the landlord and the tenant' (ORS 90.320(1)(g)). And the parties 'may agree in writing that the tenant is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling only if' (ORS 90.320(2)) the agreement is made in good faith and not to evade your obligations, does not diminish your obligations to other tenants, and its terms are clearly and fairly disclosed and adequate consideration is specifically stated (ORS 90.320(2)(a)-(c)); that moves who does the work, not whether the unit must be habitable ("Tenant Maintenance Tasks Agreement" clause). Oregon has no rule letting a tenant accept specified defects in exchange for a stated rent reduction, and none on a separate heat-level agreement. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. So an "as is" clause or a discount for living with a defect does not waive the duty or the tenant's remedies. Even a tenant who rents a unit after your written disclosure that an agency found it unlawful to occupy 'does not waive the tenant's other remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.380(3)(e)). Settling an existing claim is possible, but a court may refuse to enforce a settlement that 'was unconscionable when made' (ORS 90.135(1)(b)). Which built-in qualifiers limit the duty itself: "Which Habitability Duties an Oregon Lease Can Change".

title: Oregon Bars Lease Clauses Excusing Your Own Negligence
bodyText: A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability arising as a result of the other party's willful misconduct or negligence or to indemnify the other party for that liability or costs connected therewith' (ORS 90.245(1)(c)). The bar covers every tenancy under ORS chapter 90. Such a clause is unenforceable (ORS 90.245(2)), and deliberately using a clause you know is prohibited and trying to enforce it can cost you up to three months' periodic rent on top of the tenant's actual damages ("Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term"). So leave out broad "Landlord is not liable for any injury or loss" and indemnity clauses that would reach your own or your agents' negligence or willful misconduct. The bar is written against excusing "the other party's" fault, so a clause that only makes the tenant answer for the tenant's own conduct is outside it, though any charge to the tenant must still fit the fee and damage rules ("Fees You May Charge", "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause). Several statutes give you a protection directly, with no lease clause needed: 'A landlord is immune from liability for any claim for damages, injury or death caused by a portable cooling device installed by the tenant' (ORS 90.355(4)); as a condition of written permission for a tenant-installed alternative energy device, you may require the tenant to 'Provide a waiver of the landlord's liability for any injury to the tenant or other installer resulting from the tenant's or installer's negligence in the installation' (ORS 90.265(2)(a)); for a family child care home you may require the tenant, at your election, either to have the parents of children in care sign a document agreeing that the landlord 'is not liable for losses from injuries to their children or their guests connected with the operation of the family child care facility' (ORS 90.358(5)(a)(A)) and acknowledging that the provider carries no liability coverage for those losses (ORS 90.358(5)(a)(B)), or to carry a reasonable surety bond or liability policy that names you as an additional insured (ORS 90.358(5)(b)) ("Family Child Care Home Conditions" clause); for abandoned property, including property left when the sheriff returns possession to you after an eviction judgment (ORS 90.425(2)(c)), you are 'not responsible for any loss to the tenant, lienholder or owner resulting from storage of personal property in compliance with this section unless the loss was caused by the landlord's deliberate or negligent act' (ORS 90.425(15)), and 'Complete compliance in good faith with this section shall constitute a complete defense' (ORS 90.425(16)) to a claim over property disposed of under it ("Property Left Behind After a Tenancy"); and if you change locks for a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking in complete good-faith compliance with ORS 90.459, 'the landlord is not liable to a perpetrator excluded from the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.459(3)(b)) ("Lock Changes for Victims"). Oregon has no statute giving a landlord immunity from a tenant's claims for acting on a police notice of drug or other criminal activity, but two statutes protect a landlord who acts against such activity. If your good-faith 24-hour termination for an act outrageous in the extreme, such as unlawful manufacture, delivery or possession of a controlled substance (ORS 90.396(1)(f)(B)), fails in court, you 'may not be found in violation of any state statute or local ordinance requiring the landlord to remove that tenant upon threat of fine, abatement or forfeiture as long as the landlord continues to make a good faith effort to terminate the tenancy' (ORS 90.396(5)). And in a drug-house nuisance action the court enters no abatement order against an owner it is satisfied acted in good faith, had no knowledge of the nuisance or has been making reasonable efforts to abate it, is not in contempt and will make best efforts to abate it immediately and keep it from being a nuisance for a year (ORS 105.580(3)); see "Drug, Prostitution and Gambling Nuisance Abatement". A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no statute giving that immunity.

title: No Eviction Fees or Penalty Charges in an Oregon Lease
bodyText: No Oregon section names an eviction-penalty clause, but the fee statute bars one for every tenancy under ORS chapter 90. You 'may not require the payment of any fee except as provided in this section' (ORS 90.302(1)), and the list it allows (a late rent payment, a dishonored check, removing or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, violating a written pet agreement or a facility pet rule, abandoning a fixed term early, and capped fees for repeated violations of certain written rules) contains no fee for serving a notice, filing or winning an eviction case, or for any default the list does not name (ORS 90.302(2)-(3)). You also 'may not charge a tenant any form of liquidated damages, however designated' (ORS 90.302(5)), apart from the early-termination fee capped at one and one-half times the monthly rent (ORS 90.302(2)(e)), and a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant agrees to pay liquidated damages (ORS 90.245(1)(d)). So a flat "eviction fee", "notice fee" or "penalty rent" can't go in an Oregon lease. If you charge a fee the statute does not allow, 'the tenant may recover twice the actual damages of the tenant or $300, whichever is greater' (ORS 90.302(8)), and deliberately using a term you know is prohibited and trying to enforce it can add up to three months' periodic rent (ORS 90.245(2)). What you can recover instead: the court may award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party, 'notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary' (ORS 90.255), which the fee list does not reach (ORS 90.302(7)(a)), but in an eviction 'attorney fees may not be awarded to the plaintiff if the defendant does not contest the action' (ORS 105.137(3)); costs and disbursements come with the judgment (ORS 105.137(1)); and you may recover damages for the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement (ORS 90.401(2)), which you must mitigate (ORS 90.125(1)). Nonpayment of a fee is never grounds for a nonpayment-of-rent termination (ORS 90.302(6)). General fee rules: "Fees You May Charge".

title: An Oregon Residential Lease Can't Waive Termination Notice
bodyText: For a dwelling unit covered by ORS chapter 90, the lease can't waive or shorten the termination notices the chapter requires. A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.245(1)(a)), and such a term 'is unenforceable' (ORS 90.245(2)). The eviction statutes follow chapter 90: for a dwelling unit to which ORS chapter 90 applies, a holdover is an unlawful holding only 'after a valid notice terminating the tenancy pursuant to ORS chapter 90' (ORS 105.115(2)(a)(B)), you may not file until the fixed term has expired or the notice period has run (ORS 105.115(2)(b)), and the court applies chapter 90 to decide 'Whether a tenancy or rental agreement has been validly terminated' (ORS 105.115(3)(b)). Oregon's older notice-waiver rules don't reach these tenancies. ORS 105.120(2) says a tenant under a written lease 'may, by the terms of the lease, waive the giving of any notice required by this subsection' (ORS 105.120(2)), and ORS 91.100 lets a written lease waive the notices of ORS 91.050 to 91.070, but ORS 105.120(2) covers only the non-chapter-90 holdovers of ORS 105.115(1)(b) (a chapter 90 unit is under ORS 105.120(3), with notice served as ORS 90.155 provides), and ORS 91.010 to ORS 91.110, among other sections, 'do not apply to the rights and obligations of landlords and tenants governed by this chapter' (ORS 90.120(1)). Those waivers matter only for arrangements outside chapter 90 (ORS 90.110), such as vacation occupancy or agricultural premises; an employee whose occupancy depends on employment on the premises may be removed 'only pursuant to ORS 91.120' (ORS 90.110(7)). Notice periods for chapter 90 tenancies: "Notice Periods to End a Tenancy".

title: No Confession of Judgment in an Oregon Lease
bodyText: A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Authorizes any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement' (ORS 90.245(1)(b)). This covers every tenancy under ORS chapter 90, whether the confession is for rent, damages or possession. The clause is unenforceable (ORS 90.245(2)), and deliberately using a clause you know is prohibited and trying to enforce it lets the tenant recover actual damages plus up to three months' periodic rent ("Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term"). Oregon still knows judgment by confession as a procedure (a justice court may 'give judgment without action, upon the confession of the defendant' (ORS 51.075(1)(e)), and a party to a judgment given by confession has only a limited right to appeal (ORS 19.245(2))), but the ban means a lease can't set one up in advance. Oregon bars confession clauses contract by contract (also in retail installment contracts and in lease-purchase agreements for household personal property, ORS 83.670(1); ORS 646A.128(1)); it has no statute or court rule voiding confessions of judgment in every contract or abolishing confessed judgments for possession. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Once an eviction case is filed, the parties may still settle it: if they agree, in the manner provided for judgment by stipulation, that the tenant will perform or pay and keep possession, the court enters that stipulation, and on proof of compliance it 'shall enter a judgment of dismissal in favor of the defendant' (ORS 105.145(3)). That is an agreement made in the case, not a lease term.

title: Waiving Entry Notice for Showings in Oregon
bodyText: Oregon sets an entry-notice period, so the question of waiving it is real: except as the access statute provides, you must give at least 24 hours' actual notice of your intent to enter and may enter 'only at reasonable times' (ORS 90.322(1)(f)), and the tenant may deny consent after receiving the notice, though not unreasonably (ORS 90.322(1)(f); ORS 90.322(2)). Showing the unit is one of the purposes for entry, 'to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors' (ORS 90.322(1)), but notice can be waived in advance only for a buyer. You and the tenant may agree that you may enter without notice, at reasonable times, 'for the purpose of showing the premises to a prospective buyer' (ORS 90.322(1)(d)), and only if the agreement 'Is executed at a time when the landlord is actively engaged in attempts to sell the premises' (ORS 90.322(1)(d)(A)), 'Is reflected in a writing separate from the rental agreement and signed by both parties' (ORS 90.322(1)(d)(B)) and 'Is supported by separate consideration recited in the agreement' (ORS 90.322(1)(d)(C)). So it can't be a lease clause, can't be signed at move-in before any sale effort, and needs its own stated consideration. For showings to prospective tenants, lenders or contractors, no advance waiver is available: give the 24 hours' notice, or rely on an agreement with the tenant 'regarding a specific entry' (ORS 90.322(1)(f)). A lease term waiving entry notice in general is unenforceable (ORS 90.245(1)(a); ORS 90.245(2)), and 'A landlord has no other right of access except' (ORS 90.322(5)) by court order, during an extended absence (ORS 90.410(2)) or after abandonment or relinquishment. An unlawful or harassing entry lets the tenant seek an injunction or end the tenancy and recover actual damages of not less than one week's rent for a week-to-week tenancy or one month's rent otherwise (ORS 90.322(8)). ORS 90.322 does not apply to a space in a facility (ORS 90.322(3)). Entry rules in full: "Entering a Tenant's Home"; clause: "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause.

title: Oregon Deposit Rights Can't Be Waived
bodyText: The tenant's security deposit rights are rights under ORS chapter 90, so a rental agreement may not have the tenant 'waive or forgo' them (ORS 90.245(1)(a)); such a term is unenforceable (ORS 90.245(2)), and deliberately using a term you know is prohibited and trying to enforce it can cost you up to three months' periodic rent plus damages ("Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term"). That covers, among others: the receipt and the tenant's priority over your creditors (ORS 90.300(2)(a)); the limit on what you may claim, 'only the amount reasonably necessary' (ORS 90.300(7)(a)) to remedy the tenant's defaults and repair damage beyond ordinary wear and tear; the bar on forfeiting a deposit for not staying a minimum number of months in a month-to-month tenancy (ORS 90.300(8)); the written accounting and refund within 31 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant delivers possession (ORS 90.300(12)-(13)); and the tenant's right to twice the amount withheld without an accounting or in bad faith (ORS 90.300(16)). A lease can't turn a deposit into a nonrefundable payment either, because that is a fee, and fees are limited to the statutory list (ORS 90.302(1); "Fees You May Charge"). The statute itself lets an agreement matter in only a few places: the written rental agreement must list the deposit (ORS 90.300(3)); a carpet-cleaning deduction requires a written rental agreement providing for it (ORS 90.300(7)(c)(A)(iii); "Carpet Cleaning Deduction" clause); you must apply a last month's rent deposit to the last month's rent when either side gives a termination notice (other than a nonpayment notice), when you agree to end the tenancy, or when a fixed term ends (ORS 90.300(9)), and the tenant may not require you to apply it to any other period 'Unless the tenant and landlord agree otherwise' (ORS 90.300(10)); and you may refund electronically only 'If agreed to by both parties in an addendum executed after the tenancy begins and the tenant has occupied the premises' (ORS 90.300(13)). How deposits are used and returned: "Use of Security Deposit" clause, "Return of Security Deposit" clause.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Can't Be Waived in Oregon
bodyText: For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, neither the casualty rules Oregon has nor the duty to mitigate can be waived in the lease. Casualty: Oregon has no general fire-or-casualty statute for these tenancies, so there is no statutory surrender right for a fire-damaged unit that an express agreement could override. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Two statutes do cover a damaged unit. If, after the tenancy begins, a governmental agency posts the unit as unsafe and unlawful to occupy, a tenant who did not cause the conditions may end the tenancy immediately, and you may end it on 24 hours' written notice if the conditions were not caused by you or your failure to maintain the dwelling (ORS 90.380(5)(a)-(b)). Since June 5, 2026, if a natural disaster (a disaster resulting in a declared state of emergency for wildfire, flood, tsunami, earthquake or a similar event, as defined in ORS 197A.440(1)) destroys the unit, 'the tenancy is immediately terminated' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21(1)) and you return the deposit and prepaid rent, including rent prorated from the date of the disaster (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21(1)(a)). Whether or not the unit is destroyed, 'A tenant does not owe rent while the dwelling unit is inaccessible due to the natural disaster or the destruction of the dwelling unit' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21(3)), and a unit is inaccessible while an agency has posted it as unsafe or unlawful to occupy (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21(3)). That rule applies 'unless the parties agree otherwise following the natural disaster' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21), so only an agreement made after the disaster can change it; a lease term made in advance would waive a chapter 90 right and is unenforceable (ORS 90.245(1)(a); ORS 90.245(2)). Mitigation: 'The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages' (ORS 90.125(1)), and if a tenant abandons, 'the landlord shall make reasonable efforts to rent it for a fair rental' (ORS 90.410(3)). A lease term excusing you from that duty is unenforceable for the same reason. The statute's one substitute: if you charge the early-termination fee for abandonment of a fixed term (no more than one and one-half times the monthly rent), ORS 90.410(3) does not apply, and you may not recover rent past the date you knew or reasonably should have known of the abandonment, or the cost of re-renting (ORS 90.302(2)(e)(A)-(C)). Related: "Fire, Casualty and Uninhabitable Units", "Tenancies After a Natural Disaster", "Rent Owed After a Tenant Abandons", "Early Termination" clause.

title: No Liquidated Damages in an Oregon Lease, With One Exception
bodyText:
For every tenancy under ORS chapter 90, Oregon bars liquidated damages with one exception. A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to pay liquidated damages, except as allowed under ORS 90.302 (2)(e)' (ORS 90.245(1)(d)), and 'Except as provided in subsection (2)(e) of this section, a landlord may not charge a tenant any form of liquidated damages, however designated' (ORS 90.302(5)).

Calling the charge something else (a reletting fee, an administrative charge, a flat cleaning charge, a holdover premium) doesn't change that.

The exception is the early-termination fee: a fee, described in the written rental agreement, for 'The abandonment or relinquishment of a dwelling unit during a fixed term tenancy without cause' (ORS 90.302(2)(e)), which 'may not exceed one and one-half times the monthly rent' (ORS 90.302(2)(e)) and may not be charged for a release by a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking or the other statutory terminations named in that paragraph (ORS 90.302(2)(e)).

If you charge it, you give up rent after the date you knew or reasonably should have known of the abandonment and any re-renting costs, and the reletting rule of ORS 90.410(3) does not apply (ORS 90.302(2)(e)(A)-(C)); see "Early Termination" clause.

Otherwise, recover only your actual damages for the tenant's noncompliance (ORS 90.401(2)), subject to your duty to mitigate (ORS 90.125(1)).

A prohibited term is unenforceable, and deliberately using and trying to enforce one you know is prohibited can cost up to three months' periodic rent plus the tenant's actual damages (ORS 90.245(2)); collecting a charge the fee statute doesn't allow can also cost twice the tenant's actual damages or $300, whichever is greater (ORS 90.302(8)).

Oregon has no consumer-protection rule permitting you to keep an agreed damages amount, and no general contract statute on damages fixed in advance (the sale-of-goods and lease-of-goods rules, ORS 72.7180 and ORS 72A.5040, cover goods, not leases of dwellings). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

Holdover charges: "Premium Holdover Rates (Barred)".

title: What an Oregon Tenant Can Do When You Breach
bodyText: When you fail to keep the lease or the habitability duty, an Oregon tenant under ORS 90.100 to 90.465 has these statutory remedies, which the lease can't take away (ORS 90.245(1)(a)): a written notice ending the tenancy unless you remedy a material breach of the agreement, or a habitability noncompliance, in time (ORS 90.360(1)); damages and an injunction 'for any noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement or ORS 90.320 or 90.730' (ORS 90.360(2)); for an essential service you intentionally or negligently fail to supply, buying it and deducting the cost, reduced-rental-value damages, or substitute housing with rent excused, and a 48-hour termination notice for an imminent and serious threat (ORS 90.365); repair and deduct for a minor defect costing no more than $300 (ORS 90.368); a counterclaim in your action for possession for nonpayment or for rent (ORS 90.370(1)(a)); a defense and remedies if you retaliate against a complaint (ORS 90.385); immediate termination for a unit an agency posts as unsafe to occupy (ORS 90.380(2)(b), (5)(a)) or for conditions existing at the outset, not caused by the tenant, that pose an imminent and serious threat to health or safety within six months of the start (ORS 90.380(7)), with statutory damages where you knowingly continued or began a tenancy in a posted unit, knowingly began a new tenancy in a unit an agency has given you written notice is unlawful to occupy, or knew or should have known of those outset conditions (ORS 90.380(2)(b), (3)(b), (7)); and remedies for unlawful entry (ORS 90.322(8)). The details, deadlines and the tenant-fault bars are in "Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies". Oregon has no rent-withholding or rent-escrow statute, and no lead-hazard or health statute that directs rent to be withheld until you comply or bars eviction on that basis. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. A tenant who simply stops paying rent is in default unless one of the remedies above excuses or reduces it; rent goes into court only when the court orders it in your action, either on a counterclaim (ORS 90.370(1)(b)) or on a continuance or a delayed trial (ORS 105.140; ORS 105.137(7)), and 'a tenant who has paid rent into court pursuant to ORS 90.370 shall not be considered to be in default in rent' (ORS 90.385(6)) for the retaliation rule. The retaliation protection still covers a tenant who complains to a governmental agency about a building, health or housing code violation materially affecting health or safety (ORS 90.385(1)(a)(A)).

title: Repair Requests and Notice in Oregon
bodyText: Oregon separates the notices that start a tenant's repair remedies from the knowledge that decides damages (tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465). The remedies need written notice: the termination notice for your noncompliance (ORS 90.360(1)(a)), the essential-service notice (ORS 90.365(1)), the 48-hour notice (ORS 90.365(2)) and the minor-defect repair notice, which must give you at least seven days and be served as written notices are (ORS 90.368(3)(a)-(d)). Damages, though, turn on what you knew and on actual notice: the tenant can't recover damages for a habitability noncompliance only if you 'neither knew nor reasonably should have known of the condition' (ORS 90.360(2)) and either the tenant knew or reasonably should have known of the condition and 'failed to give actual notice to the landlord in a reasonable time' (ORS 90.360(2)(a)) before the loss, or the condition was caused after the tenancy began by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of someone other than you or a person acting on your behalf (ORS 90.360(2)(b)); and a tenant's counterclaim in your action for rent or possession requires that you 'reasonably had or should have had knowledge or had received actual notice' (ORS 90.370(1)(a)). Actual notice includes 'Verbal notice that is given personally to the landlord or tenant or left on the landlord's or tenant's telephone answering device' (ORS 90.150(1)). So your lease may ask the tenant to report repairs promptly in writing, as "Maintenance & Repairs" clause does, but it can't make a written request a condition of damages or a counterclaim when the tenant told you or you otherwise knew; that would waive a chapter 90 remedy (ORS 90.245(1)(a)), which is why that clause says its written-notice request "does not limit any notice Oregon law otherwise accepts". A tenant's written repair request also lets you enter without further notice to make the repairs, at the times the request allows or otherwise at reasonable times, for seven days, or longer while the repairs are in progress and you are making a reasonable effort to complete them in a timely manner (ORS 90.322(1)(c)). On how notice is given: a written rental agreement may add for actual notice 'Any other method reasonably calculated to achieve actual receipt of notice, as agreed to and described in a written rental agreement' (ORS 90.150(4)); written notices must use the methods of ORS 90.155, with mail and attachment only if the agreement provides it both ways (ORS 90.155(1)(c)), e-mail only under a separate addendum signed after move-in (ORS 90.155(1)(d)), and any other method only 'in addition to one of the service methods described in subsection (1) of this section' (ORS 90.155(3)). Naming an extra method in the lease doesn't turn a notice the statute requires in writing into an oral one, for you or the tenant. Notice clauses: "Agreed Method for Actual Notice" clause, "Service of Notices by Mail and Attachment" clause.

title: No Oregon Right to End a Lease Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: Oregon has no statute that lets you, or the tenant, end a residential tenancy because repairs would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value, and none that excuses a repair on cost grounds. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Your duty to keep the unit habitable has no cost limit, and no agreement may let you receive rent free of it (ORS 90.320(1); ORS 90.250). The only dollar figure in the repair remedies limits the tenant: the repair-and-deduct remedy covers a defect that 'may reasonably be repaired for not more than $300' (ORS 90.368(1)(a)). If a repair job is large, your routes out are the ordinary termination rules for tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465. During a fixed term you may terminate only for cause (ORS 90.427(4)(a)); in the first year of occupancy a month-to-month tenancy may be ended on at least 30 days' written notice without cause (ORS 90.427(3)(b)). For a month-to-month tenancy after the first year of occupancy, or at the end of a fixed term that ends after the first year, a qualifying landlord reason includes that you intend to 'undertake repairs or renovations to the dwelling unit within a reasonable time' (ORS 90.427(5)(a)(B)) and the premises is unsafe or unfit for occupancy, or the unit will be during the work (ORS 90.427(5)(a)(B)(i)-(ii)); that takes at least 90 days' written notice stating the reason and supporting facts and, unless you own an interest in four or fewer units, a payment of one month's periodic rent with the notice (ORS 90.427(5)(a), (6)); see "When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause". Getting that wrong costs three months' rent plus actual damages (ORS 90.427(9)(a)). Retaliation rules don't block an action for possession where 'Compliance with the applicable building or housing code requires alteration, remodeling or demolition which would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.385(4)(d)), but that does not release you from damages for the noncompliance (ORS 90.385(7)). If an agency posts the unit unsafe and unlawful to occupy, see "Posted or Unlawful Units"; local relocation ordinances may add payments.

title: Shifting Repairs and Maintenance to an Oregon Tenant
bodyText:
You can have an Oregon tenant take on chores, but not your habitability duty.

For any dwelling under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, single-family or not, 'The landlord and tenant may agree in writing that the tenant is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling only if' (ORS 90.320(2)): the agreement 'is entered into in good faith and not for the purpose of evading the obligations of the landlord' (ORS 90.320(2)(a)); it 'does not diminish the obligations of the landlord to other tenants in the premises' (ORS 90.320(2)(b)); and 'The terms and conditions of the agreement are clearly and fairly disclosed and adequate consideration for the agreement is specifically stated' (ORS 90.320(2)(c)).

In practice: list each task, state the consideration specifically (a stated rent reduction or other stated payment, not just "included in the rent"), and keep shared areas and other tenants' units your job.
