The statute asks for a writing, not a separate document, so the agreement may sit in the lease if it meets those terms; the library's clause does that ("Tenant Maintenance Tasks Agreement" clause).

A tenant or applicant who does repairs, routine maintenance or cleaning on the unit for a rent reduction is not your employee, but may not do electrical or plumbing installation, maintenance or repair unless properly licensed (ORS 90.145(1)-(2)), and 'Nothing in this section diminishes the obligations of a landlord to maintain the dwelling unit in a habitable condition under ORS 90.320 or 90.730' (ORS 90.145(3)).

One listed habitability item may be shifted by a plain written agreement without those conditions: garbage receptacles and their removal are owed 'Except as otherwise provided by local ordinance or by written agreement between the landlord and the tenant' (ORS 90.320(1)(g)).

The tenant's own statutory duties, such as keeping the unit clean and safe and not damaging it, apply without any agreement (ORS 90.325; "Tenants' Duties Under Oregon Law"). For a space in a facility, the same chores rule is ORS 90.730(7). Which duties can't be shifted at all: "An Oregon Tenant Can't Waive Habitability".

title: Yard, Landscaping and Irrigation Work in Oregon
bodyText: No Oregon statute assigns lawn, landscaping or irrigation upkeep to the tenant of a dwelling under ORS 90.100 to 90.465. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The grounds are part of your habitability duty: a unit is unhabitable if it substantially lacks buildings, grounds and appurtenances safe for normal and reasonably foreseeable uses, clean, sanitary and free of debris at the start of the tenancy, with 'all areas under control of the landlord' (ORS 90.320(1)(f)) kept that way. A tenant may take on mowing, watering or other yard tasks only under a writing that meets ORS 90.320(2): 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling' (ORS 90.320(2)), agreed in good faith and not to evade your obligations, not diminishing your obligations to other tenants, with terms clearly and fairly disclosed and 'adequate consideration for the agreement is specifically stated' (ORS 90.320(2)(c)). So list the yard tasks and state what the tenant gets for them; the library's clause is "Tenant Maintenance Tasks Agreement" clause, and the shared landscaping clause isn't used in Oregon because it assigns yard upkeep without stated consideration. If you keep the yard work, a written agreement requiring you to do it lets you agree to enter the yard without notice at reasonable times (ORS 90.322(1)(e); "Entry for Yard Maintenance" clause). Trees near power lines: Oregon's vegetation rules run to the electric utility, which may prune or remove vegetation near its facilities with notice to the property owner (ORS 758.282; ORS 758.284) and must plan vegetation management (ORS 757.963); no statute makes a tenant or renter keep trees clear of lines. Spaces in a manufactured dwelling park or marina have their own statutory yard and tree duties (ORS 90.740(4)(h)-(i); ORS 90.727). Local ordinances on yards, weeds or water use may also apply.

title: Snow and Ice Removal in Oregon
bodyText: No Oregon statute or rule says who clears snow and ice at a rental, and none statewide makes an owner or occupant clear a public sidewalk. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Cities often have sidewalk-clearing ordinances that name the owner or the person in possession, so check yours. Absent an agreement, shared walks, stairs, parking and other areas you control fall under your duty to keep 'all areas under control of the landlord' (ORS 90.320(1)(f)) safe for normal and reasonably foreseeable uses, and stairways and railings in good repair (ORS 90.320(1)(h)); you can't shift that duty for shared areas in a way that reduces what you owe other tenants (ORS 90.320(2)(b)). A tenant may take on snow and ice removal, for example the walk and driveway of a single-family home, only under a writing for 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling' (ORS 90.320(2)) that is made in good faith and not to evade your obligations, does not diminish your obligations to other tenants, and clearly and fairly discloses its terms with 'adequate consideration for the agreement is specifically stated' (ORS 90.320(2)(c)). So name the areas and state the consideration; the library's clause is "Tenant Maintenance Tasks Agreement" clause, which gives snow and ice removal on the walkways the tenant uses as an example. The shared snow-removal clause isn't used in Oregon because it assigns the work without stated consideration. Damage the tenant deliberately or negligently causes remains the tenant's responsibility under ORS 90.325(2)(b).

title: Collecting Rent Means Keeping the Unit Habitable
bodyText: In Oregon the right to receive rent can't be separated from the duty to maintain the unit: 'A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with ORS 90.320 (1) or 90.730' (ORS 90.250). That covers ordinary tenancies (ORS 90.320(1)) and spaces in a facility (ORS 90.730). So whoever collects the rent (you, a buyer, a lender holding an assignment of rents, a manager) takes it subject to the habitability duty, and no lease term, sale document or loan document can say otherwise; a term by which the tenant gives up the matching remedies is unenforceable too (ORS 90.245(1)(a); ORS 90.245(2)). Deposits follow the same idea: except as ORS 86.782(10) provides after a foreclosure sale, the holder of the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is responsible for the deposit and prepaid rent (ORS 90.300(2)(b)); see "Deposits When the Property Changes Hands". A different rule governs the effect of accepting rent on your own rights. If you accept rent knowing of a tenant's violation during three or more separate rental periods, or accept performance that varies from the agreement, you waive the right to terminate for that violation (ORS 90.412(2)), unless an exception applies, such as a timely written warning notice (ORS 90.412(4)(b)-(c)) or an agreement made 'after the violation has occurred' (ORS 90.412(4)(a)); after a termination notice, acceptance of rent waives it unless the conditions of ORS 90.414 are met. Because the agreement must come after the violation, a general non-waiver sentence in the lease does not protect you ("Accepting Rent After a Violation or Notice").

title: Substitute Housing Is the Tenant's Remedy in Oregon
bodyText: Oregon does not make you find or pay for other housing on your own while a unit under ORS 90.100 to 90.465 is repaired or after a casualty; substitute housing is a remedy the tenant chooses, triggered by the tenant's written notice. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. If, contrary to the rental agreement or the habitability duty, you intentionally or negligently fail to supply an essential service, the tenant may give you written notice 'specifying the breach and that the tenant may seek substitute services, diminution in rent damages or substitute housing' (ORS 90.365(1)). After you have had a reasonable time and reasonable access to supply the service, and only if the failure 'makes the dwelling unit unsafe or unfit to occupy' (ORS 90.365(1)(c)), the tenant may 'procure substitute housing during the period of the landlord's noncompliance' (ORS 90.365(1)(c)) and is excused from rent for that period, and may recover the reasonable cost of comparable substitute housing above the rent; if the tenant picks better housing, damages are limited to the cost of comparable housing (ORS 90.365(1)(c)). A tenant who proceeds under this section may not also use the 30-day termination remedy for that breach (ORS 90.365(5)), and has no right to it if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant or a person on the premises with the tenant's consent (ORS 90.365(6)). Other payments tied to moving: if you end a tenancy after the first year for a qualifying landlord reason, such as repairs that make the unit unsafe or unfit, you must pay one month's periodic rent with the notice unless you own an interest in four or fewer units (ORS 90.427(6)); in a city over 300,000 people, the city may recover from the owner its reasonable costs of relocating tenants when, due to the owner's action or inaction, multiple and material health or safety code violations lasting more than 30 days and endangering the tenants or the public cause condemnation, and it is a defense to the costs for any tenant that the condition was caused by that tenant's action or negligence, and you may not terminate a tenancy because you received the city's warning notice except for the reasons in ORS 90.385(4) (ORS 90.465(1), (2), (4)). Local relocation ordinances (Portland's among them) may add more. Remedies in full: "Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies".

title: Naming Who Makes a Tenant-Arranged Repair in Oregon
bodyText:
Oregon lets you name the repairers a tenant must use only for the minor-defect repair-and-deduct remedy, and only within limits. For a tenancy under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, if you fail to repair a minor habitability defect (one that can reasonably be repaired for $300 or less, not mold, radon, asbestos or lead-based paint) by the date in the tenant's written notice, the tenant may have it repaired and deduct the actual and reasonable cost, up to $300, from later rent (ORS 90.368(1)-(3)).

For that remedy, 'The landlord may specify the people to perform the repair work if the landlord's specifications are reasonable and do not diminish the tenant's rights under this section' (ORS 90.368(4)(b)). So a list of approved repairers works if the repairers can actually do the job in a reasonable time at a reasonable price; a list that leaves the tenant no one available, or only someone costing more than $300, would diminish the remedy.

The statute already says 'The tenant may not perform work to repair the defect' (ORS 90.368(4)(c)); the work must be done in a workmanlike manner and comply with state statutes, local ordinances and the state building code (ORS 90.368(4)(a)); and the tenant must give you a written statement from the repairer showing the actual cost (ORS 90.368(4)(d)).

No similar designation right exists for the essential-services remedy, where the tenant may procure reasonable amounts of the service and deduct its cost (ORS 90.365(1)(a)), so don't write a designation clause that reaches it; a term limiting that remedy would waive a chapter 90 right (ORS 90.245(1)(a)).

Optional clause: "Repair Contact and Approved Repairers" clause. All repair remedies: "Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies".

title: Promises to Clean, Repair or Improve in Oregon
bodyText: Oregon has no rule that your promise to clean, repair or improve a unit must be in writing, carry a completion date, or be made before the lease is signed. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. But a promise you make binds you, written or not. For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, a "rental agreement" means 'all agreements, written or oral' (ORS 90.100(42)) about the use and occupancy of the unit, so an oral promise to paint or fix something before move-in can become part of the agreement, and facilities 'the use of which is promised to the tenant' (ORS 90.100(37)(b)) are part of the premises. If you don't keep it, the tenant may recover damages and get an injunction 'for any noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement' (ORS 90.360(2)), and a material noncompliance supports the tenant's 30-day termination notice (ORS 90.360(1)(a)). Every duty under the chapter 'imposes an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement' (ORS 90.130). Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act lists a promise to deliver real estate, goods or services within a set time 'with intent not to deliver' (ORS 646.608(1)(q)) as an unlawful practice, but its definition provides that 'Real estate' does not cover 'conduct covered by ORS chapter 90' (ORS 646.605(6)(b)(A)), so it generally isn't a route for a tenancy promise ("The Unlawful Trade Practices Act"). Practical course: write any promised work, with a target date, into the lease or a signed addendum, so both sides know exactly what was promised. If you take a deposit to secure the execution of a rental agreement, the written statement you must give first has to describe the terms of the agreement to execute (ORS 90.297(2)(b)).

title: No Smoke-Drift Waiver in an Oregon Lease
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule on tobacco or cannabis smoke drifting between rental units, and none that lets a lease have the tenant accept smoke drift and give up claims about it. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The library doesn't offer a smoke-drift waiver for Oregon, for two reasons. A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.245(1)(a)), so a waiver could not bar a repair or habitability claim where smoke made a unit or area you control unsafe or unsanitary (ORS 90.320(1)(f)); and it may not provide that the tenant agrees to excuse 'any liability arising as a result of the other party's willful misconduct or negligence' (ORS 90.245(1)(c)). Such a term would be unenforceable, and deliberately using and enforcing a term you know is prohibited can cost up to three months' periodic rent plus damages (ORS 90.245(2)). What Oregon does require is a plain disclosure, which is lawful without any waiver: every rental agreement for a dwelling under ORS chapter 90, other than a space in a facility, 'must include a disclosure of the smoking policy for the premises' (ORS 90.220(4)), stating 'whether smoking is prohibited on the premises, allowed on the entire premises or allowed in limited areas on the premises' (ORS 479.305(1)) and identifying any areas where it is allowed. From January 1, 2027, that rule is ORS 479.305(2), and the section defines smoking as 'inhaling or possessing a lit tobacco product, as defined in ORS 431A.175' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 60, § 2). Use "Smoking Policy (Smoking Prohibited)" clause, "Smoking Policy (Limited Areas)" clause or "Smoking Policy (Allowed on Entire Premises)" clause; rules for changing the policy during a tenancy, including the version from January 1, 2027, are in "Smoking Rules". Common areas: Oregon's Indoor Clean Air Act bars smoking, aerosolizing or vaporizing an inhalant in a 'place of employment' or 'public place' (ORS 433.845(1)) and within 10 feet of their entrances, exits, opening windows and air intakes (ORS 433.845(2)). A place of employment is 'an enclosed area under the control of a public or private employer, including' (ORS 433.835(4)(a)) hallways, elevators and stairways, but not 'a private residence unless it is used as a child care facility as defined in ORS 329A.250 or a facility providing adult day care as defined in ORS 410.490' (ORS 433.835(4)(b)); a public place is 'an enclosed area open to the public' (ORS 433.835(5)). Neither the act nor the health authority's rules name apartment buildings, so whether a building's enclosed hallways count turns on whether an employer, such as you with on-site staff, controls them; treat staffed or public enclosed common areas as covered.

title: Subsidized Rent When an Oregon Unit Is Unfit
bodyText: No Oregon statute or rule says how a rent reduction is split between a subsidized tenant's share and the housing assistance payment when a unit is unfit, or lets a state agency abate its payment for a habitability defect. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Under Oregon law the tenant's own remedies apply to every tenancy under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, subsidized or not, for example damages 'based upon the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.365(1)(b)) when you fail to supply an essential service ("Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies"); the statute does not divide that figure between the tenant and the program. For a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, federal rules govern the agency's share. You must maintain the unit to the federal housing quality standards and correct a life-threatening deficiency within 24 hours of notification and any other within 30 calendar days or an approved extension (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(a)(3)). Once it has notified you in writing of a deficiency, the agency 'may withhold assistance payments' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)(1)) and must pay them back if you cure in time; if you don't, it 'must abate the HAP, including amounts that had been withheld' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)(2)(i)), and it terminates the payment contract if the unit still fails after 60 days or a longer period it sets (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)(5)). 'An owner may not terminate the tenancy of any family due to the withholding or abatement of assistance' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)(3)), and during an abatement the family may end the tenancy by notifying you and the agency. Payments abated are not made up later (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)(4)). If the agency finds a deficiency was caused by the tenant, a household member, a guest or another person under the tenant's control (beyond ordinary use), it may waive your responsibility to fix it, and then 'The HAP to the owner may not be withheld or abated if the owner responsibility has been waived' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(a)(4)). These rules apply to payment contracts executed on or after, or renewed after, June 6, 2024; older contracts follow the section as in effect on June 6, 2024 (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(f)). For Oregon's own notice and waiver rules, subsidy payments are not "rent" (ORS 90.412(1); ORS 105.120(1)). Voucher lease terms: "Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease".

title: No Small-Landlord Opt-Out From Oregon Repair Remedies
bodyText: Some states let tenants pay rent into escrow while repairs are outstanding and let a landlord with few units opt out by giving the tenant a notice. Oregon has neither. It has no rent-escrow procedure for repairs, and no notice or other procedure that excuses a landlord with few units, or an owner who lives on site, from the tenant's repair remedies. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The tenant's rights to end the tenancy after written notice, recover damages and an injunction, use the essential-services remedies, repair and deduct a minor defect, and counterclaim in your rent or possession case (ORS 90.360; ORS 90.365; ORS 90.368; ORS 90.370) apply to every tenancy under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, however few units you own, and a lease term waiving them is unenforceable (ORS 90.245(1)(a)). Rent goes into court only when the court orders it in your own action (ORS 90.370(1)(b); "Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court"). Oregon's small-landlord and owner-occupant rules are elsewhere and don't touch repairs: a landlord who has an ownership interest in four or fewer residential dwelling units need not pay the one-month relocation payment with a qualifying-reason termination notice (ORS 90.427(6)(b)); a landlord whose primary residence is in the same building or on the same property, with no more than two units, has wider termination rights after the first year (ORS 90.427(8)); and for premises with no more than four dwelling units, the foreclosure-disclosure duty in ORS 90.310 applies ("Disclosure of Pending Foreclosure or Forfeiture" clause).

title: Carpet Cleaning Charged to the Deposit
bodyText:
For a dwelling unit rented under Oregon's residential landlord-tenant law (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), carpet cleaning is something you may charge against the security deposit only on the deposit statute's conditions.

Carpet cleaning 'other than the use of a common vacuum cleaner' (ORS 90.300(7)(c)(A)) is a recoverable default or damage only if 'The cleaning is performed by use of a machine specifically designed for cleaning or shampooing carpets' (ORS 90.300(7)(c)(A)(i)), the carpet 'was cleaned or replaced after the previous tenancy or the most recent significant use of the carpet and before the tenant took possession' (ORS 90.300(7)(c)(A)(ii)), and 'The written rental agreement provides that the landlord may deduct the cost of carpet cleaning regardless of whether the tenant cleans the carpet before the tenant delivers possession' (ORS 90.300(7)(c)(A)(iii)).

Without that lease term, you can charge for carpet cleaning only as damage the tenant caused beyond ordinary wear and tear. The library's optional clause "Carpet Cleaning Deduction" supplies the term.

Every deduction is limited to 'the amount reasonably necessary' (ORS 90.300(7)(a)), labor 'must be based on a reasonable hourly rate' (ORS 90.300(7)(b)), and the charge must appear in the written accounting you give within 31 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant delivers possession ("Return of Security Deposit" clause).

You may not collect a nonrefundable carpet-cleaning fee instead: 'A landlord may not charge a fee at the beginning of the tenancy for an anticipated landlord expense' (ORS 90.302(1)).

The statute speaks only to a deduction for machine cleaning; it does not provide for requiring the tenant to hire a professional cleaner, and it sets no carpet-age or depreciation schedule. The limits are the reasonably-necessary test and the exclusion of 'ordinary wear and tear' (ORS 90.300(7)(a)(B)).

title: No Move-Out Notice Condition on the Deposit Refund
bodyText:
For a tenancy under Oregon's residential landlord-tenant law, the deposit deadline runs from the end of the tenancy and the tenant's delivery of possession, not from any notice of surrender.

You must give the written accounting of any claim, and return what you don't claim, 'not later than 31 days after the tenancy terminates and the tenant delivers possession to the landlord' (ORS 90.300(13)). Delivery of possession happens, for example, when the tenant gives you actual notice of giving up the right to occupy, which 'may be implied by actions such as the tenant’s return of the keys to the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.147(2)(a)).

No Oregon statute lets you make the refund depend on advance notice of moving out or on a forwarding address, and a lease term by which the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.245(1)(a)) is unenforceable (ORS 90.245(2)).

Advance notice matters for rent instead: a month-to-month tenant who leaves without notice owes rent until, at the latest, 'Thirty days after delivery of possession without prior notice of termination of a month-to-month tenancy' (ORS 90.220(8)(f)), and you may claim unpaid rent from the deposit through the accounting. You also may not make a month-to-month tenant forfeit a deposit for not staying a minimum number of months (ORS 90.300(8)).

The library's clause "Return of Security Deposit" sets out the timeline and asks for a forwarding address as a tenant duty, not a condition of the refund.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: Oregon has no rule requiring you to post or hand out the standards you use to set security deposit amounts, however many units you rent. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. What Oregon does require is disclosure of the amounts themselves. Before you take a screening charge, your written notice to the applicant must include 'The amount of rent the landlord will charge and the deposits the landlord will require' (ORS 90.295(3)(b)(G)), and before you take a deposit to secure a rental agreement your written statement must describe 'The amount of rent and the fees the landlord will charge and the deposits the landlord will require' (ORS 90.297(2)(a)). The written rental agreement 'must list a security deposit paid by a tenant or required by a landlord' (ORS 90.300(3)). Fair housing law limits how you set different deposits: you may not, because of a protected class such as race, sex, familial status or source of income, 'Make any distinction, discrimination or restriction against a purchaser in the price, terms, conditions or privileges relating to the sale, rental, lease or occupancy of real property' (ORS 659A.421(2)(c)). Using written, uniform deposit criteria is the cautious course. See "Disclosing Rent and Fees" and "No Security Deposit Cap".

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Oregon has no procedure for a tenant to ask for an expedited deposit refund for a fee, as some states have. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The 31-day deadline is an outer limit: you must return the unclaimed balance 'not later than 31 days after the tenancy terminates and the tenant delivers possession to the landlord' (ORS 90.300(13)), so you may account and refund sooner. You may not charge a processing or administrative fee for doing so, and you may not deduct one from the deposit: 'A landlord may not charge a fee at the beginning of the tenancy for an anticipated landlord expense and may not require the payment of any fee except as provided in this section' (ORS 90.302(1)), and a deposit claim is limited to defaults and tenant-caused damage (ORS 90.300(7)(a)). Shorter deadlines apply in a few situations the statutes name: where a tenancy ends because a utility is shut off for someone else's nonpayment, you return rent and fees 'Within four days after termination' (ORS 90.315(6)(b)(A)) and the deposit owed under ORS 90.300; where a tenancy ends because the unit is posted unsafe, the deadline is 'within 14 days of the notice of termination' (ORS 90.380(6)), and four days where the tenant ends it for a serious threat that existed at the outset (ORS 90.380(7)). An electronic refund to the tenant's bank account needs an addendum signed after the tenancy begins and the tenant has occupied the premises (ORS 90.300(13); "Return of Security Deposit" clause).

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits
bodyText: Oregon has no such thing as a nonrefundable deposit, so there is no notice that can make one lawful. A '“Security deposit” means a refundable payment or deposit of money, however designated, the primary function of which is to secure the performance of a rental agreement or any part of a rental agreement' (ORS 90.100(45)), and it 'does not include a fee' (ORS 90.100(45)). A '“Fee” means a nonrefundable payment of money' (ORS 90.100(17)). So money you call a nonrefundable deposit, cleaning deposit or move-in deposit is either a security deposit (refundable, claimable only for defaults and tenant-caused damage, and accounted for within 31 days) or a fee, and a fee is lawful only if the fee statute lists it and your written rental agreement describes it. The fee statute bars the usual up-front versions: 'A landlord may not charge a fee at the beginning of the tenancy for an anticipated landlord expense' (ORS 90.302(1)). Calling a payment last month's rent doesn't change this either: a last month's rent deposit is 'a type of security deposit, however designated' (ORS 90.100(27)). A fee charged in violation of the statute lets the tenant recover twice actual damages or $300, whichever is greater (ORS 90.302(8)). See "Fees You May Charge" for the fees you may charge and "Use of Security Deposit" clause for the deposit terms.

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Oregon has no rule requiring a separate written notice, when you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The reason is that no part of an Oregon security deposit can be nonrefundable: a security deposit is 'a refundable payment or deposit of money, however designated' (ORS 90.100(45)), and a nonrefundable payment is a fee, lawful only if the fee statute lists it and 'A fee must be described in a written rental agreement' (ORS 90.302(1)). Don't hand a tenant a receipt or notice calling any part of a deposit nonrefundable; the receipt you must give for a security deposit (ORS 90.300(2)(a)) should show it as refundable, subject to the claims the deposit statute allows. See "No Nonrefundable Deposits".

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty
bodyText: Oregon has no duty to offer, hold or give notice of a move-in or move-out inspection for ordinary tenancies, so there is no deposit penalty, such as losing the right to keep any of the deposit, for not doing so. An inspection while the tenant is still in possession is an entry, though: you may enter to inspect only after at least 24 hours' actual notice and at reasonable times, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise for a specific entry, and the tenant may deny consent but may not unreasonably withhold it (ORS 90.322(1)(f), (2)); an unlawful entry lets the tenant recover actual damages of not less than one week's rent for a week-to-week tenancy or one month's rent otherwise (ORS 90.322(8)). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no move-in or move-out inspection duty and no deposit penalty tied to one. The deposit penalty that does apply is tied to the accounting and refund: if you don't return the deposit as the statute requires, or withhold it in bad faith, 'the tenant may recover the money due in an amount equal to twice the amount' (ORS 90.300(16)) withheld without a written accounting or in bad faith ("Penalties for Deposit Mistakes"). Your written accounting must state 'specifically the basis or bases of the claim' (ORS 90.300(12)), so dated condition records and photos at move-in and move-out remain the practical way to support a damage claim ("Move-In Condition Records"). If you take part in the state's Rent Guarantee Program, its rules ask for 'move-in and move-out inspection checklists' (OAR 813-365-0030(6)) among the documents supporting a claim.

title: Utility Deposits and the Security Deposit
bodyText: Oregon has no separate rule for a utility deposit that a landlord holds, or for returning one. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. The payments the statute lists that you 'may require or accept' (ORS 90.140) include security deposits and utility or service charges, but not a separate utility deposit, and any refundable payment whose main purpose is to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit 'however designated' (ORS 90.100). So money you hold against utility bills is part of the security deposit: list it in the written rental agreement, receipt it, and account for and refund it within 31 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant delivers possession ("Return of Security Deposit" clause). Utility or service charges you bill under a written rental agreement ("Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause) are owed under the agreement, so unpaid ones can be read as a default you may claim from the deposit, like unpaid rent, and itemize in the accounting. They are not rent: a utility or service charge 'is not rent or a fee' (ORS 90.315), and unpaid utility charges support a for-cause notice, not a nonpayment-of-rent notice. Among the utility rules, a shorter deposit deadline applies only where the tenant could not get a utility before moving in because of a previous tenant's or the owner's unpaid bill and ends the tenancy: then all deposits, rent and fees come back within four days (ORS 90.315(5)(b)). Where a shutoff after move-in ends the tenancy, all rent and fees (where the tenant was responsible for the utility) or prepaid rent (where you were) come back within four days, but the security deposit follows the ordinary ORS 90.300 rules (ORS 90.315(6)(b), (7)(b)) ("No Expedited Deposit Procedure"). A deposit a utility company itself requires of the tenant is between the tenant and the utility and is governed by the Public Utility Commission's rules (for example OAR 860-021-0205), not by the landlord-tenant law.

title: Fees Must Match the Fee Statute
bodyText: Oregon handles fees for services through its closed fee list rather than a rule about whether the service is provided. A landlord 'may not require the payment of any fee except as provided in this section' (ORS 90.302), and 'A fee must be described in a written rental agreement' (ORS 90.302). The list covers only per-occurrence fees (late rent, a dishonored check, alarm tampering, early abandonment of a fixed term) and rule-violation fees after a written warning; a monthly amenity, service, trash-valet or administrative fee is not on it, and a charge for a service you don't provide fails for the same reason. A fee charged in violation of the statute lets the tenant recover 'twice the actual damages of the tenant or $300, whichever is greater' (ORS 90.302(8)); that penalty does not apply to the per-occurrence fees the statute lists, such as a late charge. Two related limits: you may charge for 'improvements or other actions that are requested by the tenant and are not required of the landlord by the rental agreement or by law' (ORS 90.302), so an optional service the tenant asks for and receives can be billed; and a utility or service charge you pass through may include only the provider's billed cost, apart from a limited markup on cable, satellite and internet service, and you 'may not hold a tenant liable for a public service charge billed to a previous tenant' (ORS 90.315). Recurring charges you set as part of the rent are rent, not fees ("What Counts as Rent"). The full list is in "Fees You May Charge".

title: Late Charge Limits
bodyText: Oregon limits late charges by structure rather than by a fixed dollar figure. You may impose one only if rent 'is not received by the fourth day of the weekly or monthly rental period for which rent is payable' (ORS 90.260) and your written rental agreement states the obligation, the type and amount, and the due dates. The amount 'may not exceed' (ORS 90.260) one of three ceilings: 'A reasonable flat amount, charged once per rental period' (ORS 90.260), meaning 'the customary amount charged by landlords for that rental market' (ORS 90.260); a reasonable daily charge from the fifth day through that rental period, where 'The per-day charge may not exceed six percent of the amount described in paragraph (a) of this subsection' (ORS 90.260); or 'Five percent of the periodic rent payment amount, charged once for each succeeding five-day period, or portion thereof' (ORS 90.260), through that rental period only. The same rule covers manufactured dwelling and floating home spaces in a park or marina, whose for-cause ground cites it; there is no separate park late-charge cap. Oregon's fixed late-fee figure, the greater of $20 or 20 percent of the monthly rent, applies only to a space 'in a self-service storage facility' (ORS 87.694), not to a dwelling. Since June 5, 2026, you may not charge a late fee if you refused a payment the tenant offered by check or another commercially reasonable method. The library's clause is "Late Charge" clause; the full rule is in "Late Charges in Oregon".

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Oregon has no statute written specifically about passing a fine a city, county or state agency imposes on you to your tenant, or about a tenant's liability for nuisance-abatement costs. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The general rules decide it. A fine pass-through is not a fee the fee statute lists, and a landlord 'may not require the payment of any fee except as provided in this section' (ORS 90.302), so a lease charge for government fines as such is not available. Where the tenant's own breach caused the fine, for example a garbage or waste violation of the tenant's duty to 'Dispose from the dwelling unit all ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste in a clean, safe and legal manner' (ORS 90.325), you may recover your actual loss as damages, because 'a landlord may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance by the tenant with the rental agreement or ORS 90.325 or 90.740' (ORS 90.401). Fines for your own duties, such as habitability and code repairs, stay with you: a lease may not have the tenant indemnify you for your own negligence (ORS 90.245), and deliberately using a lease with a term you know is prohibited and trying to enforce it can cost up to three months' periodic rent plus actual damages ("Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term"). One specific rule: the fee for removing or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm (up to $250) is not allowed if the State Fire Marshal assesses the tenant a civil penalty for the same conduct ("Fees You May Charge"). Association fines are handled in "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause. And if your good-faith attempt to evict a tenant for an act outrageous in the extreme fails in court, you 'may not be found in violation of any state statute or local ordinance requiring the landlord to remove that tenant upon threat of fine, abatement or forfeiture' (ORS 90.396) while you keep trying in good faith. Local nuisance and code ordinances may add rules.

title: Passing Local Government Charges to Tenants
bodyText: For an ordinary tenancy (not a manufactured dwelling or floating home space in a park or marina), Oregon lets you pass a local government charge through to the tenant only as a public service charge under the utility statute, and only if your written rental agreement provides for it. A '“Public service charge” means a charge imposed on a landlord by a utility or service provider, by a utility or service provider on behalf of a local government or directly by a local government' (ORS 90.315), for public services such as 'street maintenance, transportation improvements, public transit, public safety and parks and open space' (ORS 90.315) related to the unit. It 'does not include real property taxes, income taxes, business license fees or dwelling inspection fees' (ORS 90.315). You bill it like any utility charge: in writing within 30 days of the government's bill, separate from rent, with a copy of the bill or an inspection statement, and for no more than the amount billed to you ("Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause). In a month-to-month tenancy you must give 60 days' written notice before amending the agreement to add a public service charge adopted within the previous six months, and a fixed-term agreement can't be changed unilaterally. You 'may not hold a tenant liable for a public service charge billed to a previous tenant' (ORS 90.315). Because a business license or dwelling inspection fee is excluded, and the fee statute lets you charge only the fees it lists, the statutes can be read as barring you from billing a rental registration, licensing or inspection fee a city charges you to the tenant as a separate charge; you may cover your costs through the rent you set, subject to the rent-increase rules ("Statewide Rent Increase Limit"). Local ordinances may say more about their own fees.

title: No Fee for Preparing or Serving Notices
bodyText: Oregon does not let you charge the tenant a fee for preparing or serving a termination notice, or a set charge for starting an eviction. A charge like that is not on the fee statute's list, and a landlord 'may not require the payment of any fee except as provided in this section' (ORS 90.302); written as an agreed amount for the tenant's default, it is liquidated damages, which the statute also bars: 'a landlord may not charge a tenant any form of liquidated damages, however designated' (ORS 90.302), apart from the early-termination fee for a fixed term. Charging a fee in violation of the statute lets the tenant recover twice actual damages or $300, whichever is greater. Your route to the cost is the court: in an action on the rental agreement, 'reasonable attorney fees at trial and on appeal may be awarded to the prevailing party together with costs and necessary disbursements' (ORS 90.255), and that rule works both ways. One narrow exception to the fee bar: if a nonpayment eviction is dismissed because rental assistance or another payment covering the amount owed was tendered, 'Notwithstanding ORS 90.302, a landlord may charge a tenant for filing fees paid under ORS 105.130' (ORS 90.395), though paying them is not a condition of the dismissal. Don't add notice or eviction charges to a nonpayment notice; the tenant cures a nonpayment notice by paying the rent owed ("Fees You May Charge").

title: Late Charges When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule that separately bars or limits a late charge on the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The general late-charge rule applies to every tenancy: you may impose a late charge only if the rent payment 'is not received by the fourth day of the weekly or monthly rental period for which rent is payable' (ORS 90.260) and your written rental agreement sets out the charge ("Late Charges in Oregon"). Where a Housing Choice Voucher pays part of the rent, federal rules say 'The family is not responsible for payment of the portion of the rent to owner covered by the housing assistance payment under the HAP contract between the owner and the PHA' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310), and the agency's failure to pay 'is not a violation of the lease between the tenant and the owner' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310). So the cautious course is to charge any late charge only on the tenant's own share, and only when that share is late; collect a late agency payment from the agency under your contract. Oregon also protects tenants using rental assistance in nonpayment cases: a court dismisses an eviction for nonpayment if 'The landlord caused the tenant to not tender rent, including as a result of the landlord’s failure to reasonably participate with a rental assistance program' (ORS 90.395), or if rental assistance covering the amount owed is tendered. Refusing or penalizing a tenant because of a housing subsidy can also be source-of-income discrimination (ORS 659A.421).

title: Passing Property Tax Increases to Tenants
bodyText: Oregon has no statute on lease clauses that pass real property tax increases to a residential tenant, and none letting you deduct a tax share from the deposit. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The general rules decide it. Property taxes can't be billed as a utility or public service charge, because a public service charge 'does not include real property taxes, income taxes, business license fees or dwelling inspection fees' (ORS 90.315), and a tax pass-through isn't a fee the fee statute lists ("Fees You May Charge"). So any increase in what the tenant pays for the unit because your taxes went up is a rent increase, and the rent-increase rules apply (ORS 90.323 does not apply to a manufactured dwelling or floating home space in a park or marina (ORS 90.323(7)); for a month-to-month tenancy of such a space, ORS 90.600 applies instead): outside a week-to-week tenancy you 'may not increase the rent' (ORS 90.323) during the first year, without 90 days' written notice, more than once in any 12-month period, or above the statewide maximum unless an exemption applies ("Statewide Rent Increase Limit"), and the terms of a fixed term tenancy 'may not be unilaterally amended' (ORS 90.220). If your property has a local low-income rental housing tax exemption, one condition of the exemption is that 'The required rent payment reflects the full value of the property tax exemption' (ORS 307.517).

title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule giving landlords a payment, tax credit, damage guarantee or other incentive for renting to veterans. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. State housing grants that name veterans fund service organizations and projects, not individual landlords. The veterans rule that does reach you is a notice duty: 'a notice of termination of tenancy under any provision of this chapter must include the information required by ORS 408.515' (ORS 90.391), which is 'A statement that if the recipient is a veteran of the armed forces, assistance may be available from a county veterans’ service officer or community action agency' (ORS 408.515) with contact information for those offices or a statement that it can be obtained by calling 2-1-1 ("Notice Periods to End a Tenancy"). Federal or local programs (such as HUD-VASH vouchers administered by a housing authority) may offer landlord payments under their own contracts; check with the program.

title: Scheduled Rent Increases in a Lease
bodyText: For tenancies other than manufactured dwelling or floating home spaces in a park or marina, Oregon's rent-increase rules apply to every increase, including one your lease schedules in advance. 'The terms of a fixed term tenancy, including the amount of rent, may not be unilaterally amended by the landlord or tenant' (ORS 90.220), so a mid-term increase in a fixed term is possible only if the lease itself provides for it. Even then, outside a week-to-week tenancy you 'may not increase the rent' (ORS 90.323) during the first year after the tenancy begins, without written notice at least 90 days before the effective date, more than once in any 12-month period, or by more than the statewide maximum unless an exemption applies; a week-to-week increase needs seven days' written notice. A lease escalation clause can be read as not replacing the 90-day notice, which must state the amount of the increase, the new rent and the effective date ("Rent Increase Notice"). An increase above the maximum makes you liable for 'three months’ rent plus actual damages suffered by the tenant' (ORS 90.323). Oregon's retaliation statute bars 'increasing rent' (ORS 90.385) in retaliation for protected tenant acts, and it contains no exception for an increase the lease schedules, so keep scheduled increases on their stated dates and amounts. The cap figures are in "Statewide Rent Increase Limit".

title: Seasonal Rentals
bodyText: Oregon has no special rules for seasonal tenancies. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. What matters is whether the arrangement is a vacation occupancy. 'Vacation occupancy' (ORS 90.110) is outside the landlord-tenant law; it means occupancy in a dwelling unit (not a hotel or motel) where 'The occupant rents the unit for vacation purposes only, not as a principal residence' (ORS 90.100), the occupant has a principal residence elsewhere, and 'The period of authorized occupancy does not exceed 45 days' (ORS 90.100). A seasonal rental to someone who lives in the unit, or any rental longer than 45 days, is an ordinary tenancy with the usual deposit, fee, habitability, notice and eviction rules, except that a space in a recreational vehicle park for the occupant's own RV, rented for vacation purposes only by someone whose principal residence is elsewhere, can be a vacation occupancy for up to 90 days if the RV must leave the park at the end and the occupant signs the statement the statute prescribes (ORS 90.100(54)(b), renumbered (55) by Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 4). A seasonal lease with an end date is a fixed term tenancy, and if that end date falls within the first year of occupancy you may end it without cause only 'by giving the tenant notice in writing not less than 30 days prior to the specified ending date for the fixed term' (ORS 90.427), or 30 days before the date in the notice, whichever is later; without that notice, plan on the tenancy continuing ("Notice Periods to End a Tenancy"). Housing an employee whose right to occupy depends on working in and about the premises is excluded too and ends only under ORS 91.120. Stays under 30 consecutive days may be subject to transient lodging tax ("No Sales Tax on Rent").

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes, whether yearly, when rent changes or on request, and no current Oregon renter tax credit asks you to certify the rent paid. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Oregon's former homeowner and renter property tax refund program, which counted 'rent constituting property taxes' (ORS 314.033), has been repealed; today's Elderly Rental Assistance Program is a homelessness-prevention grant run through local programs, not a tax refund that needs a landlord statement. The rent-related writings you do owe are a receipt or account statement when the tenant asks for one ("Rent Receipts") and the rent-increase notice.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: You may not change the locks or otherwise shut out a tenant who is behind on rent, even if the lease says you may. 'A landlord may not recover or take possession of the dwelling unit by action or otherwise' (ORS 90.435), including by cutting heat, water, electricity or another essential service, except after abandonment or relinquishment or through the court eviction process. A lease term giving you a lockout right is unenforceable, because a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.245), and knowingly using and trying to enforce it adds a penalty of up to three months' periodic rent. If you lock out a tenant or seriously threaten to, the tenant 'may obtain injunctive relief to recover possession or may terminate the rental agreement and recover an amount up to two months’ periodic rent or twice the actual damages sustained by the tenant, whichever is greater' (ORS 90.375). You also can't hold the tenant's belongings for rent: 'Distraint for rent is abolished' (ORS 90.420). For unpaid rent, give the nonpayment notice and, if it isn't cured, file an eviction ("Nonpayment of Rent Notices"). See "No Lockouts, Utility Shutoffs or Property Seizures".

title: No Tenancy at Will Under the Landlord-Tenant Act
bodyText: For a residential tenancy under Oregon's landlord-tenant law there is no tenancy at will. A rental agreement 'is either a week-to-week tenancy, month-to-month tenancy or fixed term tenancy' (ORS 90.100), and 'If a rental agreement does not create a week-to-week tenancy, as defined in ORS 90.100, or a fixed term tenancy, the tenancy shall be a month-to-month tenancy' (ORS 90.220). So an informal or open-ended arrangement where someone lives in your unit and pays rent is a month-to-month tenancy, with the month-to-month notice rules: the tenant may end it on 30 days' written notice, and you may end it without cause on 30 days' notice only during the first year of occupancy ("Notice Periods to End a Tenancy"). The general tenancy statute in chapter 91 still describes a 'tenant at will' (ORS 91.050), ended by notice equal to the rent interval, but those chapter 91 sections (ORS 91.010 to 91.110, among others) 'do not apply to the rights and obligations of landlords and tenants governed by this chapter' (ORS 90.120). The chapter 91 rule matters only for arrangements the landlord-tenant law excludes, such as vacation occupancy or certain employee housing (which ends only under ORS 91.120).

title: Guarantors and Renewals
bodyText:
Oregon has no statute on whether a lease guarantor stays liable after the original term, and none on a guarantor's discharge, revocation or right to make you sue the tenant first. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

The one statute that applies is the statute of frauds: 'An agreement to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another' (ORS 41.580) is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, 'expressing the consideration, is in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged' (ORS 41.580). So a guaranty must be in writing, signed by the guarantor, and must state the consideration, that is, what the guarantor's promise is given for (usually your agreement to rent to the tenant).

The rest is contract law and case law, so the cautious course is to say in the guaranty itself whether it covers renewals and extensions. That matters in Oregon because a fixed term ending after the first year of occupancy 'becomes a month-to-month tenancy upon the expiration of the fixed term' (ORS 90.427) unless one of the statutory exceptions applies; a guaranty limited to the original term may not reach that continuation. Get the guarantor's written consent to a new fixed term. The library's optional clause "Guaranty" does this.

Separately, the state's Rent Guarantee Program and Housing Choice Landlord Guarantee Program can reimburse eligible landlords for some unpaid rent or damage by participating tenants; they are state programs, not lease guaranties.

title: Records You Must Give or Protect
bodyText: Oregon's records duties for ordinary tenancies are specific rather than a general ledger rule. A tenant who asks for a writing showing a payment 'is entitled to receive that writing from the landlord as a condition for making the payment' (ORS 90.140); it may be 'a receipt, statement of the tenant’s account or other acknowledgment of the tenant’s payment' (ORS 90.140) and must show the amount, the date and the landlord or property ("Rent Receipts"). You must give the tenant a copy of any written rental agreement and all amendments ("Giving Tenants a Copy of the Lease"). If you bill utilities, each bill must include the provider's bill or tell the tenant how to inspect and copy it. If you pass card or electronic payment processing fees through to the tenant (allowed since June 5, 2026 only on conditions), 'Records of fees charged to the landlord and passed through to the tenant are made available to the tenant upon written request within a reasonable time' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23). Screening charges need a receipt and, after an outside screening, a confirmation with the company's receipt. Applicant and tenant data you hold in your rental business is protected by Oregon's consumer information law: a 'covered entity' (ORS 646A.602) 'shall develop, implement and maintain reasonable safeguards to protect the security, confidentiality and integrity of personal information' (ORS 646A.622), scaled for a small business, including secure disposal; a breach of personal information (generally, a name with an unencrypted Social Security, driver license, state ID or passport number, a financial account or card number together with the code or password needed to use it, biometric data used to verify identity, a health insurance policy or subscriber number with the insurer's identifier, or medical history or health condition information; a user name with its password; or any of those without the name if it would enable identity theft) requires notice to the affected people 'not later than 45 days after discovering or receiving notification of the breach of security' (ORS 646A.604), and to the Attorney General if more than 250 people are affected, unless after an appropriate investigation you reasonably determine, and document in writing, that the people affected are unlikely to suffer harm. Since June 5, 2026, you also may not disclose a tenant's confidential information except as the 2026 act allows ("Keeping Tenants' Information Confidential").

title: Unbundled Parking
bodyText: No Oregon statute requires you, as a landlord, to rent parking separately from the unit. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Unbundling can reach you through local land-use rules instead. The state's transportation planning rules direct cities in metropolitan areas (and some urban unincorporated areas) to drop parking mandates or adopt alternatives, and one option a city or county may choose is 'A requirement that parking spaces for each residential unit in multi-unit housing developments be unbundled parking upon lease creation, lease renewal, or sale' (OAR 660-012-0445). Where a local code adopts it, 'unbundled parking' means spaces are 'rented, leased, or sold separately from the unit itself' (OAR 660-012-0005), at market rates for comparable local off-street parking, and 'The renter, lessor, or buyer of the unit must be allowed to opt out of renting, leasing, or buying the parking space' (OAR 660-012-0005). Check your city's code for multi-unit buildings. However you price parking, a recurring parking charge you set as part of the rent is rent and counts toward the rent-increase limits ("What Counts as Rent"); parking rules and towing are in "Parking Tags and Towing Agreement" clause.

title: No Truth in Renting Statement
bodyText: Oregon has no counterpart to New Jersey's Truth in Renting Act, so there is no state-prepared rights statement you must hand to tenants. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. See "Statement of Tenant Rights".

title: Claims Against a Tenant's Insurance
bodyText: For an ordinary tenancy (not a manufactured dwelling or floating home space in a park or marina, which has its own parallel rule), you 'may not' make a claim against the tenant's renter's liability insurance unless all three conditions are met: 'The claim is for damages or costs for which the tenant is legally liable and not for damages or costs that result from ordinary wear and tear, acts of God or the conduct of the landlord' (ORS 90.222); 'The claim is greater than the security deposit of the tenant, if any' (ORS 90.222); and 'The landlord provides a copy of the claim to the tenant contemporaneous with filing the claim with the insurer' (ORS 90.222). A frivolous claim against the tenant's policy lets the tenant recover actual damages plus $500, and other knowing violations of the insurance statute cost actual damages or $250, whichever is greater. You also may not 'Require that a tenant waive the insurer’s subrogation rights' (ORS 90.222), so the library offers no mutual waiver-of-subrogation clause, and a lease may not have the tenant release you from liability for your own negligence ("Lease Terms Oregon Voids"). Oregon has no statute barring a landlord or its insurer from recovering from a tenant for an accidental fire; whether the tenant is liable turns on the tenant's duty not to 'Deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises' (ORS 90.325) and on ordinary negligence law. See "Requiring Renter's Insurance".

title: Your Own Liability Insurance
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to carry liability insurance to rent out an ordinary dwelling, and there is no statewide registration that asks for proof of insurance. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Your own coverage becomes a legal condition in one situation: if you require the tenant to carry renter's liability insurance, you may do so 'only if the landlord obtains and maintains comparable liability insurance and provides documentation to any tenant who requests the documentation, orally or in writing' (ORS 90.222). The documentation may be a current certificate of coverage, given in person, by mail or by posting in a common area or office, and 'A written rental agreement that requires a tenant to obtain and maintain renter’s liability insurance must include a description of the requirements of this subsection' (ORS 90.222). The library's clause "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" does this. Lenders, associations and local registration programs may require insurance of their own.

title: Oregon's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Oregon's money limits for ordinary residential tenancies (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), whatever the lease says, as of November 2026. Manufactured dwelling and floating home spaces in a park or marina have some different figures and are not covered here. Deposits: no cap on the security deposit ("No Security Deposit Cap"); a new or increased deposit after the first year must allow the tenant 'at least three months to pay the new or increased deposit' (ORS 90.300); the written accounting and any refund are due 'within 31 days after the tenancy terminates and the tenant delivers possession' (ORS 90.300); withholding without the accounting or in bad faith lets the tenant recover 'twice the amount' (ORS 90.300) withheld. A deposit to secure a rental agreement that must be returned is due 'within five business days' (ORS 90.297), and late return adds 'a penalty equal to the greater of the deposit or an amount agreed to by the parties' (ORS 90.297). Screening charges: no more than 'the landlord’s average actual cost of screening applicants or the customary amount charged by tenant screening companies or consumer credit reporting agencies for a comparable level of screening' (ORS 90.295); 'a single applicant screening charge within any 60-day period' (ORS 90.295); violations cost 'twice the amount of any applicant screening charge paid, plus $250' (ORS 90.295). Late charges: none unless rent 'is not received by the fourth day' (ORS 90.260) of the rental period; the ceilings are a reasonable flat amount once per period, a daily charge that 'may not exceed six percent of the amount described in paragraph (a)' (ORS 90.260), or 'Five percent of the periodic rent payment amount, charged once for each succeeding five-day period, or portion thereof' (ORS 90.260). Other fees: dishonored check, 'a fee not to exceed $35' (ORS 30.701) plus any charge your bank imposed; removing or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, 'a fee of up to $250' (ORS 90.302) unless the State Fire Marshal penalizes the tenant; leaving a fixed term early without cause, 'The fee may not exceed one and one-half times the monthly rent' (ORS 90.302); rule-violation fees after a written warning, '$50 for the second noncompliance' and '$50 plus five percent of the rent payment for the current rental period' (ORS 90.302) for a third or later within a year, but up to $250 for smoking in a designated nonsmoking area or keeping an unauthorized pet capable of causing damage; cable, satellite or internet pass-through markup, 'not more than 10 percent of the utility or service charge billed to the tenant' (ORS 90.315). A fee the statute doesn't allow costs 'twice the actual damages of the tenant or $300, whichever is greater' (ORS 90.302(8)); that penalty does not apply to the fees ORS 90.302(2) allows (late rent, dishonored check, smoke or carbon monoxide alarm tampering, pet agreement violation and early termination of a fixed term), but it does apply to a rule-violation fee charged in violation of the statute. Renter's insurance you require: coverage 'may not exceed $100,000 per occurrence or the customary amount required by landlords for similar properties with similar rents in the same rental market, whichever is greater' (ORS 90.222); a knowing violation costs actual damages or $250, whichever is greater, and a frivolous claim on the tenant's policy actual damages plus $500. Rent increases: week-to-week, seven days' written notice; other tenancies, none in the first year, 90 days' written notice, once in any 12 months, and no more than the yearly maximum the state publishes, set 'as the lesser of: (A) Ten percent; or (B) Seven percent plus CPI' (ORS 90.324), unless an exemption applies; exceeding it costs three months' rent plus actual damages ("Statewide Rent Increase Limit"). Other penalties: deliberately using a lease term you know is prohibited and trying to enforce it, up to three months' periodic rent plus actual damages; a lockout or essential-service cutoff, up to two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater; ending a tenancy in violation of the qualifying-reason rules, three months' rent plus actual damages, and a qualifying-reason termination itself requires a payment of one month's periodic rent unless you own four or fewer units; knowingly disclosing a tenant's confidential information, 'an amount equal to twice the monthly rent of the tenancy or prospective tenancy' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61); failing to give a written statement of reasons for a denial, 'the applicant may recover from the landlord $100' (ORS 90.304); and tenant-portal violations, 'any damages sustained, or $100, whichever is greater' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23). Local ordinances (such as Portland's) may add limits.

title: Deposit Timing After a Victim's Release or a Perpetrator's Exclusion
bodyText: For a tenancy under Oregon's residential landlord-tenant law (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), the deposit clock does not start when a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking is released from the rental agreement under ORS 90.453 ("Early Termination by Victims"), or when a perpetrator is excluded by a lock change under ORS 90.459 ("Lock Changes for Victims") or by a court order under ORS 105.128, if other tenants stay. The statute says 'if there are any remaining tenants of the dwelling unit, the tenancy shall continue for those tenants' (ORS 90.456), and 'Any fee, security deposit or prepaid rent paid by the victim, perpetrator or other tenants shall be applied, accounted for or refunded by the landlord following termination of the tenancy and delivery of possession by the remaining tenants as provided in ORS 90.300 and 90.302' (ORS 90.456). So you keep the whole deposit, including any part the released victim or the excluded perpetrator paid, until the remaining tenants' tenancy ends and they give back possession. The ordinary deposit rule then applies: a written accounting of any claim, and a refund of the rest, 'within 31 days after the tenancy terminates and the tenant delivers possession' (ORS 90.300) ("Return of Security Deposit" clause). Apart from the cost of the lock change itself, which is at the requesting tenant's expense (ORS 90.459(2)), you may not charge the remaining tenants 'additional rent or an additional deposit or fee because of the exclusion of the perpetrator' (ORS 90.459(3)(d)); the same bar applies after a termination under ORS 90.445 (ORS 90.445(2)). Two points the statute leaves open. First, if the released victim (with any released family members) was the only tenant, no tenancy continues, so ORS 90.456 can be read as not applying, with the ordinary 31-day rule running from the end of the tenancy and the return of possession. Second, ORS 90.456 names a release under ORS 90.453 and an exclusion under ORS 90.459 or ORS 105.128, but not a perpetrator's termination by 24 hours' written notice under ORS 90.445 where the perpetrator leaves without a court order; because the other tenants' tenancy continues there too, the cautious course is to hold and account for the deposit the same way. Neither ORS 90.456 nor ORS 90.300 says how one deposit is divided among co-tenants, for example between a released victim and the tenants who stay, and no other Oregon statute or rule does. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. The cautious course is to send the written accounting to every tenant who paid part of the deposit, including a released victim at the address the victim gives you, and to refund as those tenants agree in writing; where they don't agree, take advice before paying it out. Keep what the victim gave you confidential ("Keeping Victim Information Confidential").

title: Documents a Victim May Be Asked For, Right by Right
bodyText:
For tenancies under Oregon's residential landlord-tenant law (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), the victim protections do not share one document list. What you may ask for depends on the right the tenant uses.

Release from the rental agreement ("Early Termination by Victims"). The tenant's written notice 'must be accompanied by verification' (ORS 90.453(2)(c)). Verification is one of four things: a copy of a valid protective order issued under ORS 30.866, ORS 107.095(1)(c), ORS 107.716, ORS 107.718, ORS 107.725, ORS 107.730, ORS 163.738, ORS 163.765, ORS 163.767 or ORS 163.775, or 'any other federal, state, local or tribal court order that restrains a person from contact with the tenant' (ORS 90.453(1)(c)(A)); 'A copy of a federal agency or state, local or tribal police report regarding an act of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking against the tenant' (ORS 90.453(1)(c)(B)); 'A copy of a conviction of any person for an act of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking against the tenant' (ORS 90.453(1)(c)(C)); or 'A statement substantially in the form set forth in subsection (3) of this section' (ORS 90.453(1)(c)(D)), signed by the tenant and a qualified third party. The time limit runs back from the date of the notice, not from the date of the document: the verification must show that the tenant 'Is protected by a valid order of protection' (ORS 90.453(2)(c)(A)) or 'Has been the victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking within the 90 days preceding the date of the notice' (ORS 90.453(2)(c)(B)), not counting time the perpetrator was incarcerated or living more than 100 miles from the victim's home. A protective order works for as long as it is valid, however long ago it was issued.

Damage caused by a perpetrator. A tenant is not responsible for that damage, and you 'may require a tenant to provide verification that the tenant or a member of the tenant's household is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking as provided by ORS 90.453' (ORS 90.325(4)), so the same four documents apply. The statute can be read as setting no 90-day window for this use.

Lock change ("Lock Changes for Victims"). No document is needed: 'A tenant is not required to provide verification of the domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking to initiate the changing of the locks' (ORS 90.459(1)). The exception is narrower than the release list: if the perpetrator is a tenant of the same unit, the tenant must first give you a copy of an order under ORS 107.716 or ORS 107.718, or of an order of 'any other federal, state, local or tribal court that orders the perpetrator to move out of the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.459(3)(a)). An order that only bars contact, a police report or a third-party statement is not enough for that case.

Discrimination and the eviction defense ("No Adverse Action Against Victims"). ORS 90.449 names no document, and no Oregon statute or rule lets you demand verification before you comply with it. The tenant raises the defense in court (the statutory answer form has a box for 'my status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking' (ORS 105.137(8))), and the court decides it on the evidence. Terminating a perpetrating tenant on 24 hours' notice under ORS 90.445 likewise needs no document from anyone; in a removal action, your burden of proof is 'by a preponderance of the evidence' (ORS 90.445(4)). The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no other document list.

Who may sign the statement. A qualified third party is 'a person that has had individual contact with the tenant and is a law enforcement officer, attorney or licensed health professional, an employee of the Department of Justice division providing victim and survivor services or a victim's advocate at a victim services provider' (ORS 90.453(1)(b)). The printed form's Part 2 still lists only the officer, attorney, health professional and victim's advocate; because the statement need only be 'substantially' in that form (ORS 90.453(3)), accept one signed by a Department of Justice victim-services employee too. The victim may be the tenant or a minor in the household: 'Victim' includes 'The parent or guardian of a minor household member against whom an incident related to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking is perpetrated, unless the parent or guardian is the perpetrator' (ORS 90.100(55), renumbered (56) by Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 4).

Federally assisted housing. If the unit is assisted under a covered housing program (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(a)(3)), federal law adds its own list for its eviction and termination protections: you 'may request, in writing' (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)(1)) a HUD-approved certification form, a document signed by a victim service provider, attorney or medical or mental health professional and the tenant, or a law enforcement, court or administrative record, or accept the tenant's own statement at your discretion (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)(3)), and the tenant has 'within 14 business days after the tenant receives a request in writing' (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)(2)) to provide it. Federal law does not displace Oregon law that 'provides greater protection' (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)(8)), so Oregon's lists still govern the Oregon rights. Whatever you receive stays confidential ("Keeping Victim Information Confidential").

title: Protective Order Citations Are Current in Oregon
bodyText:
Oregon has not moved or renumbered the protective-order laws its landlord-tenant victim protections point to, so none of the library's Oregon victim rows rests on a stale citation. For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, the release right accepts a copy of a valid protective order issued under ORS 30.866 (stalking protective orders sought in a civil action), ORS 107.095(1)(c) (restraining orders in a dissolution case), ORS 107.716, ORS 107.718, ORS 107.725 or ORS 107.730 (Family Abuse Prevention Act orders, ORS 107.700 to 107.735), ORS 163.738 (stalking protective orders, ORS 163.730 to 163.750) or ORS 163.765, ORS 163.767 or ORS 163.775 (sexual abuse protective orders, ORS 163.760 to 163.777), or 'any other federal, state, local or tribal court order that restrains a person from contact with the tenant' (ORS 90.453(1)(c)(A)). The lock-change rule, where the perpetrator lives in the same unit, needs an order under ORS 107.716 or ORS 107.718 or another court's order 'that orders the perpetrator to move out of the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.459(3)(a)). Every one of those sections is in force in the 2025 edition of the Oregon Revised Statutes, and no 2025 or 2026 act renumbers or repeals any of them.

The definitions behind the protections are current too: 'Domestic violence' means 'Abuse between family or household members, as those terms are defined in ORS 107.705' (ORS 90.100(12)) or abuse between partners in a dating relationship; 'Sexual assault' 'has the meaning given that term in ORS 147.450' (ORS 90.100(46)); 'Stalking' 'means the behavior described in ORS 163.732' (ORS 90.100(48)); and 'Bias crime' 'has the meaning given that term in ORS 147.380' (ORS 90.100(5)), which defines it by the bias crime offenses in ORS 166.155 and ORS 166.165. ORS 90.100 itself was renumbered from subsection (52) on by Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 4, but none of these four definitions moved.

An order Oregon's list doesn't name, such as an elder or vulnerable person abuse restraining order under ORS 124.005 to 124.040 or an out-of-state or tribal order, still counts for a release if it restrains the person from contact with the tenant. If a tenant shows you any protective order, follow its terms and the rows on each right: "Early Termination by Victims", "Lock Changes for Victims", "No Adverse Action Against Victims" and "Documents a Victim May Be Asked For, Right by Right".

A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no renumbering or repeal of these sections.
