title: No Bar on Demanding Rent for a Unit With Violations
bodyText:
Oregon has no statute or rule that bars you from demanding or collecting rent, or from serving a nonpayment notice, just because a dwelling unit has uncorrected code or habitability violations. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Some cities have their own rental housing codes; check yours.

For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, conditions affect rent in other ways:
- A unit an agency has posted as unsafe and unlawful to occupy can't be rented: you 'may not continue a tenancy or enter into a new tenancy for the dwelling unit until the landlord corrects the conditions' (ORS 90.380(2)(a)), and if the tenancy ends you must return prepaid rent for that month, prorated, within 14 days (ORS 90.380(6)) ("Posted or Unlawful Units").
- If you intentionally or negligently fail to supply an essential service and the unit becomes unsafe or unfit to occupy, the tenant may move to substitute housing after written notice and a reasonable time, 'in which case the tenant is excused from paying rent for the period of the landlord's noncompliance' (ORS 90.365(1)(c)), or may deduct the cost of substitute services or recover diminished rental value (ORS 90.365(1)(a)-(b)); these rights don't arise if the tenant, or someone on the premises with the tenant's consent, caused the condition (ORS 90.365(6)) ("Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies").
- In a nonpayment eviction or a suit for rent, the tenant may counterclaim for what you owe under the rental agreement or the landlord-tenant law, if the tenant proves that before you filed you knew or should have known of, or had actual notice of, the facts behind the counterclaim; the court may order rent paid into court, and 'If no rent remains due after application of this section and unless otherwise agreed between the parties, a judgment shall be entered for the tenant in the action for possession' (ORS 90.370(1)(b)) ("Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court").
- Since June 5, 2026, if a natural disaster affects the tenancy, the tenant does not owe rent while the unit is inaccessible or destroyed, and a unit an agency has posted as unsafe or unlawful to occupy counts as inaccessible, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise after the disaster (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21(3)) ("Tenancies After a Natural Disaster").
- A rental agreement 'may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with ORS 90.320 (1) or 90.730' (ORS 90.250): rent and the duty to keep the unit habitable go together ("Your Duty to Keep the Unit Habitable").
So you may demand rent while repairs are pending, but a tenant may set off or recover what the conditions cost them, and serving a nonpayment notice while ignoring a known habitability problem invites a counterclaim. The retaliation statute does not stop an eviction where the tenant was behind on rent when you served the notice (rent paid into court doesn't count as being behind), but it still bars a rent increase, service cut or other notice made in retaliation for a complaint.

title: Possession, Rent and Damages: Separate Actions
bodyText:
For a tenancy under Oregon's residential landlord-tenant law (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), possession and money come through separate actions.

Possession. After a valid termination notice runs out, you recover possession only by an eviction (forcible entry and detainer) action: 'the person entitled to the premises may maintain in the county where the property is situated an action to recover the possession of the premises in the circuit court or before any justice of the peace of the county' (ORS 105.110). The statutory complaint asks for 'judgment for possession of the premises, court costs, disbursements and attorney fees' (ORS 105.124(1)), and a judgment for you is 'for restitution of the premises and the costs and disbursements of the action' (ORS 105.145(1)). It doesn't award back rent or damages; the Oregon Judicial Department's FED Instructions for Landlords tell landlords to file a separate civil complaint for those ("The Eviction Court Process").

Money. Besides the termination remedies, 'a landlord may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance by the tenant with the rental agreement' (ORS 90.401(2)) or with the tenant's statutory duties (ORS 90.325). You may use the termination remedies 'simultaneously or sequentially' (ORS 90.401(1)), and 'Any right or obligation declared by this chapter is enforceable by action unless the provision declaring it specifies a different and limited effect' (ORS 90.125(2)), so you need not wait for the tenancy to end to sue for rent or damages already owed. You must mitigate: 'The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages' (ORS 90.125(1)) ("Rent Owed After a Tenant Abandons"). Attorney fees go to the prevailing party in 'any action on a rental agreement or arising under this chapter' (ORS 90.255), and an action arising under a rental agreement or ORS chapter 90 must be commenced within one year (ORS 12.125) ("One Year to Sue on a Rental Agreement").

Which court. A suit for rent or damages goes to circuit court or, up to $10,000, to a justice court, which has jurisdiction 'For the recovery of money or damages only, when the amount claimed does not exceed $10,000' (ORS 51.075(1)(a)). Both courts' small claims departments take claims up to $10,000 (ORS 46.405(3); ORS 52.750(3)). A claim of $750 or less must ordinarily be filed in small claims (ORS 46.405(2)), but one for which a statute provides attorney fees, as ORS 90.255 does, 'may be commenced and prosecuted in the small claims department or may be commenced and prosecuted in the regular department of the circuit court' (ORS 46.405(5)). ORS 90.255 can be read as such a statute.

title: No Lease-Named Agent for Eviction Papers
bodyText:
Oregon doesn't provide for a lease that names someone to accept eviction papers for the tenant, and the library offers no such clause. For a dwelling unit under ORS chapter 90, the eviction statute fixes how the tenant is served: 'Notwithstanding ORCP 10, by the end of the judicial day next following the payment of filing fees' (ORS 105.135(3)), the clerk mails the summons and complaint by first class mail 'to the defendant at the premises' (ORS 105.135(3)(a)), and the process server serves the defendant 'at the premises by personal delivery to the defendant or, if the defendant is not available for service, by attaching the summons and complaint in a secure manner to the main entrance to that portion of the premises of which the defendant has possession' (ORS 105.135(3)(b)). The notice of restitution and the writ are served the same way at the premises (ORS 105.158(2); ORS 105.161(1)). A person a lease names can't replace that method; at most, serving that person too can be read as being in addition to it. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no provision for a tenant's lease-appointed agent.

Address Confidentiality Program participants. A victim of domestic violence, a sexual offense, stalking, bias or human trafficking may enroll in the Department of Justice program, and the Attorney General then acts 'as the agent of the program participant for purposes of service of all legal process in this state' (ORS 192.822(2)); under the program's rule, 'When personal service on a Program participant is required, it may be delivered to the Address Confidentiality Program' (OAR 137-079-0210(2)) at the Department of Justice in Salem, which forwards it within three business days. Neither the eviction statute nor the program's statutes say how the two fit when the tenant's home is both the premises to be served and the address the program protects. If a tenant has told you they are a participant, the cautious course is to serve at the premises exactly as ORS 105.135(3) requires and also deliver a copy through the program, and to take advice before filing.

Your own side is different: you must disclose to the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of an owner or a person authorized to accept service of process and notices for the owner, and keep it current (ORS 90.305(1)(b), (2)) ("Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause).

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText:
Oregon has no bond a tenant can give to secure delivery of possession at the end of the term, and a lease may not use a confessed judgment to the same end: 'A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant' (ORS 90.245(1)) 'Authorizes any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement' (ORS 90.245(1)(b)). Such a term is unenforceable, and deliberately using and trying to enforce it can cost you up to three months' periodic rent on top of the tenant's actual damages (ORS 90.245(2); "Lease Terms Oregon Voids", "Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term"). This applies to tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no end-of-term possession bond.

The only bonds the eviction process uses come after a case is filed. A tenant who wants a continuance of more than two days must give 'an undertaking to the adverse party with good and sufficient security, to be approved by the court, conditioned for the payment of the rent that may accrue if judgment is rendered against the defendant' (ORS 105.140(1)), or be ordered to pay rent into court (ORS 105.140(2)) ("Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court"). A tenant who appeals a judgment for possession stays it only with a supersedeas undertaking promising not to commit waste and to 'pay the value of the use and occupation of the property for the period of possession if the judgment is affirmed' (ORS 19.335(2)). To secure the end of a tenancy, rely on the security deposit ("Use of Security Deposit" clause), the holdover rules and an eviction if the tenant stays ("The Eviction Court Process").

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText:
For a tenancy under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, a tenant facing a nonpayment eviction can stop it by paying, up to judgment, but has no statutory right to redeem after judgment.

Before judgment. 'A court shall enter a judgment dismissing a complaint for possession that is based on a termination notice for nonpayment if the court determines that' (ORS 90.395(3)) 'The tenant has tendered or caused to be tendered rental assistance or any other payment covering the nonpayment amount owed under the termination notice for nonpayment' (ORS 90.395(3)(c)). The amount is the one stated in your notice, and payment by a rental assistance program, charity or anyone else the tenant arranges counts. The case is also dismissed if you 'caused the tenant to not tender rent, including as a result of the landlord's failure to reasonably participate with a rental assistance program' (ORS 90.395(3)(b)). You can't limit how the payment comes: since June 5, 2026, 'A landlord shall allow a tenant to make payments by check or other commercially reasonable methods' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 3(1)), and you 'may not charge a late fee or terminate a tenancy based on nonpayment of rent or other charge if a landlord refuses to allow a payment offered by the tenant' that way (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 3(3)) ("Acceptable Forms of Payment" clause). After a dismissal for tender made once the case was filed, the tenant gets no prevailing party fees, costs or attorney fees (ORS 90.395(4)), and you may charge the tenant your filing fees, though paying them is not a condition of dismissal (ORS 90.395(5)) ("Nonpayment of Rent Notices").

Partial payments. You may refuse a tender 'that is for less than the full amount of rent owed or that is untimely' (ORS 90.417(1)). If you take a partial payment after a nonpayment notice, it waives the notice unless you and the tenant sign a written agreement that acceptance is not a waiver (ORS 90.417(4)(b)); no set wording is required, but the agreement must be in writing ("Accepting Rent After a Violation or Notice").

After judgment. No Oregon statute lets the tenant pay off a judgment for possession and keep the unit. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. But your own acceptance can end your right to enforce: 'A judgment may not be enforced if the parties have entered a new rental agreement or if the plaintiff has accepted rent for a period of occupancy beginning after the judgment was entered' (ORS 105.161(4)). By that wording, taking rent only for the period before the judgment can be read as not barring enforcement. If you and the tenant settle in court on a payment plan, the stipulated-agreement rules apply instead ("Settlements, Continuances and Stays in Eviction Cases").

title: No Forfeiture Election or Reinstatement After Judgment
bodyText:
Oregon has no forfeiture election and no relief-from-forfeiture rule for residential tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465. A nonpayment termination works through the notice and, after a case is filed, the tender-to-dismissal rule, not through a declared forfeiture of the lease.

- The notice is the tenant's first chance: it 'must also specify the amount of rent that must be paid and the date and time by which the tenant must pay the rent to cure the nonpayment of rent' (ORS 90.394(3)), and paying by then ends the matter ("Nonpayment of Rent Notices").
- After the notice runs and you file, the court must dismiss if the tenant 'has tendered or caused to be tendered rental assistance or any other payment covering the nonpayment amount owed under the termination notice for nonpayment' (ORS 90.395(3)(c)) at any time before judgment ("Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction").
- Once the court enters a judgment for possession, no statute reinstates the tenancy on payment. The tenancy continues only if you choose: a judgment 'may not be enforced if the parties have entered a new rental agreement or if the plaintiff has accepted rent for a period of occupancy beginning after the judgment was entered' (ORS 105.161(4)), and a stipulated agreement can let the tenant keep possession on conditions (ORS 105.145(2)) ("Settlements, Continuances and Stays in Eviction Cases").

Your notice need not say that you elect to forfeit the lease, and stating such an election adds nothing. Once your termination notice expires, the tenant no longer owes rent as such (ORS 90.220(8)(a)); a tenant who stays owes you damages for holding over (ORS 90.427(11)). Whether you can also recover rent lost for the rest of a fixed term as damages for the tenant's breach (ORS 90.401(2)), subject to your duty to mitigate (ORS 90.125(1)), is a case-law question not searched ("Rent Owed After a Tenant Abandons"). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no forfeiture-election or reinstatement rule.

title: No Benefit-Delay Defense to Eviction
bodyText:
Oregon has no eviction defense, stay or continuance for a tenant whose Social Security or other government benefit payment was delayed, reduced or stopped. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The nearest rules, for tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, are narrower:

- Rental assistance. A nonpayment case is dismissed if the tenant 'has tendered or caused to be tendered rental assistance or any other payment covering the nonpayment amount owed under the termination notice for nonpayment' (ORS 90.395(3)(c)) before judgment, or if you caused the nonpayment by failing 'to reasonably participate with a rental assistance program' (ORS 90.395(3)(b)) ("Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction"). A late benefit that arrives before judgment and covers the noticed amount therefore ends the case.
- New parents with Medicaid housing supports. Until September 28, 2027, a tenant in a nonpayment case who is the parent of a child under 12 months living in the unit, receives medical assistance and has been approved for health-related social needs housing supports, and who has given you the approval documents, may move to reschedule the trial; the court 'shall reschedule the trial to a date no sooner than 90 days and no later than 104 days from the date of the motion' (Or. Laws 2025, ch. 598, § 2(4)) if the motion is filed at least three judicial days before trial ("Settlements, Continuances and Stays in Eviction Cases").
- State service members. The court may stay the eviction of a member of the organized militia called into state active service for 30 or more days for up to 90 days where rent is $1,200 a month or less, the premises are occupied chiefly as a dwelling by the member's spouse, children or other dependents, and the member proves that the call to service materially affects the ability to pay (ORS 105.111(2)-(3)).

A federal government shutdown that delays a tenant's pay or benefits gives no Oregon defense either ("Government Shutdowns"). Housing assistance payments a landlord receives are not 'rent' for Oregon's waiver rules (ORS 90.412(1)).

title: No Cold-Weather Notice Rule
bodyText:
Oregon has no cold-weather rule: no statute or rule requires a tenant to give notice before vacating or leaving the unit during winter, or to keep the heat at a set temperature to protect pipes. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

What Oregon does provide, for tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, works all year:
- Absence notice. 'The rental agreement may require that the tenant give actual notice to the landlord of any anticipated extended absence from the premises in excess of seven days no later than the first day of the extended absence' (ORS 90.340). The library's lease carries that term ("Notice of Extended Absence" clause). If the tenant willfully fails to give it, 'the landlord may recover actual damages from the tenant' (ORS 90.410(1)).
- Entry. 'During any absence of the tenant in excess of seven days, the landlord may enter the dwelling unit at times reasonably necessary' (ORS 90.410(2)), so you can check heat and plumbing while the tenant is away ("Entering a Tenant's Home").
- Use of the systems. The tenant must 'Use in a reasonable manner all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances' (ORS 90.325(1)(e)), and is liable for damage the tenant deliberately or negligently causes (ORS 90.325(2)(b)); you must keep 'Adequate heating facilities' in good working order (ORS 90.320(1)(d)).

The library does not add a winter heat-setting or short-absence notice clause for Oregon. If you want one, word any charge for freeze damage to match the tenant's statutory fault standard, and take advice first.

title: No Rule on Extra Terms in a Notice to Vacate
bodyText:
Oregon has no rule on extra terms in a notice-to-vacate form you hand a tenant to sign, and no rule aimed at alterations made while a notice to vacate is pending. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. General rules still govern both, for tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465:

- A tenant's notice needs only to be written and timely ("Notice Periods to End a Tenancy"); you can't require the tenant to use your form. If your form adds terms, it is part of the 'Rental agreement', which 'means all agreements, written or oral' (ORS 90.100(42)), so any term in it that waives the tenant's rights is unenforceable under ORS 90.245 ("Lease Terms Oregon Voids"), and a fixed term can't be changed one-sidedly: 'The terms of a fixed term tenancy, including the amount of rent, may not be unilaterally amended by the landlord or tenant' (ORS 90.220(2)). The cautious course is to keep any move-out form to the date and forwarding address and put anything else in a separate, plainly labelled agreement.
- Your repair duty runs until the tenancy ends: 'A landlord shall at all times during the tenancy maintain the dwelling unit in a habitable condition' (ORS 90.320(1)). Cutting services to push a tenant out is barred: if a landlord 'willfully diminishes or seriously attempts or seriously threatens unlawfully to diminish services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electric or other essential service' (ORS 90.375), the tenant may recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages ("No Lockouts, Utility Shutoffs or Property Seizures"). A renovation is a qualifying landlord reason only if the premises are unsafe or unfit for occupancy, or the unit will be unsafe or unfit during the work, and only with a 90-day notice that states the reason and supporting facts (ORS 90.427(5)(a)(B), (6)(a)(A)) and, unless you own four or fewer dwelling units, a payment of one month's rent with the notice (ORS 90.427(6)) ("When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause").

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText:
Oregon's landlord-tenant statutes have no rule of their own for a tenant's bankruptcy; federal bankruptcy law decides whether you may start or continue an eviction or collect rent, and an Oregon court rule tells the trial court what to do once it learns of the bankruptcy. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no other Oregon provision.

The Oregon court rule. 'Upon notice that proceedings in an action are subject to a federal bankruptcy stay, the court must stay the action until it is shown to the court's satisfaction that the federal bankruptcy stay has been terminated or is not applicable to the action' (UTCR 7.050(1), a court rule). The court won't dismiss your eviction just because of the filing (UTCR 7.050(3)).

The federal stay. A bankruptcy petition stays 'the commencement or continuation' of a court action against the debtor (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1)) and 'any act to obtain possession of property of the estate' (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(3)), which includes the tenant's possession of the unit. Two exceptions matter for residential evictions:
- If you obtained a judgment for possession before the petition was filed, you may continue (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(22)), unless the tenant files a certification and deposits the next 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy clerk, which delays the exception for 30 days (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(l)(1)). The certification must say that 'under nonbankruptcy law applicable in the jurisdiction, there are circumstances under which the debtor would be permitted to cure the entire monetary default that gave rise to the judgment for possession, after that judgment for possession was entered' (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(l)(1)(A)). Oregon statutes give a tenant no right to cure after a judgment for possession ("Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction"), which can be read as bearing on an objection you may file (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(l)(3)).
- An eviction based on endangerment of the property or illegal use of controlled substances may proceed if you file and serve the certification the statute describes (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(23)); it takes effect 15 days later unless the tenant objects (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(m)).
Otherwise ask the bankruptcy court for relief from the stay before acting. A person injured by a willful violation of the stay 'shall recover actual damages, including costs and' attorney fees (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(k)(1)), and may get punitive damages.

The lease. A lease term that ends the tenancy because the tenant files bankruptcy or becomes insolvent is unenforceable after filing (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 365(e)(1)), so the library's lease has none. In a chapter 7 case, a residential lease the trustee doesn't assume or reject 'within 60 days after the order for relief' is 'deemed rejected' (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 365(d)(1)). Take advice before applying a bankrupt tenant's deposit or pursuing pre-filing rent.

title: Trespass Notices After Eviction and for Non-Tenants
bodyText:
Oregon has one trespass notice in its eviction law, and otherwise relies on its general criminal trespass statutes.

After an eviction. When the sheriff enforces a judgment for possession, the sheriff serves the writ 'along with an eviction trespass notice from the sheriff' (ORS 105.151(1)(b)), posted or delivered at the premises (ORS 105.161(1)). The statutory form warns: 'Trespassing or entering into or upon these premises without written consent of the landlord will result in arrest and prosecution' (ORS 105.157), and says that personal property left behind 'is in the possession of the landlord and may be redeemed by contacting the landlord' (ORS 105.157). You then handle that property as "Tenant Property After a Writ" describes.

Other people. No Oregon statute or rule sets a procedure or form for a landlord's own trespass notice barring a non-tenant from rental premises or common areas; the general trespass definitions below give a lawful direction its effect. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. The general crime applies to anyone who 'enters or remains unlawfully' (ORS 164.245(1)), which includes entering or remaining on premises not open to the public 'when the entrant is not otherwise licensed or privileged to do so' (ORS 164.205(3)(a)), failing 'to leave premises that are open to the public after being lawfully directed to do so by the person in charge' (ORS 164.205(3)(b)), and entering 'premises that are open to the public after being lawfully directed not to enter the premises' (ORS 164.205(3)(c)). So a person in charge's lawful direction not to enter, given in advance, is what makes a later entry into an open area a trespass; the statute sets no form for that direction. The 'person in charge' is whoever has lawful control 'by ownership, tenancy, official position or other legal relationship' (ORS 164.205(5)), and each apartment or rented room is a separate building (ORS 164.205(1)). So within the unit the tenant, not you, decides who is licensed to be there; in common areas you share control, and a person a tenant has invited can be read as still licensed. Second-degree criminal trespass is a Class C misdemeanor (ORS 164.245(2)); trespass in a dwelling is first-degree, a Class A misdemeanor (ORS 164.255).

Keep within chapter 90 when acting against a tenant's visitors: your access to the unit is limited ("Entering a Tenant's Home"), a visitor who moves in is handled as an unauthorized occupant ("Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants"), and you may not penalize a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking except as ORS 90.449(3) allows ("No Adverse Action Against Victims"). The library offers no barred-person clause for Oregon.

title: Owner Move-In Is a Statutory Reason, Not a Lease Reservation
bodyText:
In Oregon, owner or family move-in is a reason the statute gives you; a lease doesn't need to reserve it and can't widen it. For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465 ("When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause" has the full rules):

- Month-to-month after the first year of occupancy, and a fixed term 'on or after the expiration of the fixed term' (ORS 90.427(5)), you may end the tenancy on at least 90 days' written notice if 'The landlord intends for the landlord or a member of the landlord's immediate family to occupy the dwelling unit as a primary residence and the landlord does not own a comparable unit in the same building that is available for occupancy at the same time that the tenant receives notice to terminate the tenancy' (ORS 90.427(5)(a)(C)). The notice must state the reason and supporting facts, and you must pay one month's periodic rent with it unless you have an ownership interest in four or fewer dwelling units (ORS 90.427(6)).
- During a fixed term you may end the tenancy 'only for cause' (ORS 90.427(4)(a)), so a lease clause letting you end a fixed term early for your own or a relative's occupancy would waive the tenant's chapter 90 rights and be unenforceable under ORS 90.245(1)(a) ("Lease Terms Oregon Voids"). The library offers no owner-occupancy reservation clause for Oregon.
- During the first year of occupancy no reason is needed for a month-to-month tenancy (30 days' written notice, ORS 90.427(3)(b)); a fixed term that ends within the first year can be ended without cause only at its end, on 30 days' written notice before the ending date or the date in the notice, whichever is later (ORS 90.427(4)(b)). And in a building or property with no more than two units where you live, the owner-occupant rules in ORS 90.427(8) apply instead.

Oregon sets no minimum time the owner or family member must live in the unit afterward; the statute turns on what you intend when you give notice. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. A notice that misuses the reason exposes you to liability for three months' rent plus actual damages and gives the tenant a defense to possession (ORS 90.427(9)(a)).

title: Written Notices a Lease Can't Downgrade
bodyText:
Where Oregon's landlord-tenant law says a notice must be written, a lease can't make a verbal notice, a text or a portal message do instead. For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, except where ORS 90.300, ORS 90.315, ORS 90.425 or ORS 90.675 sets its own delivery rule, 'where this chapter requires written notice, service or delivery of that written notice shall be executed by one or more of the following methods' (ORS 90.155(1)): personal delivery, first class mail (adding three days, ORS 90.155(2)), mail plus attachment if the written rental agreement provides for it both ways, or e-mail only under a signed post-move-in addendum, and a termination notice sent by e-mail must also go by first class mail (ORS 90.155(5)). Other methods count only 'in addition to one of the service methods described in subsection (1) of this section' (ORS 90.155(3)). A lease term that lowered these requirements would waive chapter 90 rights and be unenforceable (ORS 90.245(1)(a); "Lease Terms Oregon Voids"). Delivery details are in "How to Deliver Notices".

Notices the statute requires in writing include, among others: every termination notice by you, and the tenant's notice ending a month-to-month tenancy, which must be given 'in writing not less than 30 days prior to the date designated in the notice' (ORS 90.427(3)(a)) ("Notice Periods to End a Tenancy"); nonpayment notices (ORS 90.394); rent increase notices, since you 'may not increase the rent without giving the tenant written notice' (ORS 90.323(1)); the deposit accounting (ORS 90.300(12)); a tenant's notice of your noncompliance (ORS 90.360(1)(a)) or of an essential-service failure (ORS 90.365(1)); and a victim's request for release (ORS 90.453(2)(a)).

Actual notice is different and can be informal: it may be verbal, left on an answering device, or given in writing by the listed methods (ORS 90.150), and the written rental agreement may add 'Any other method reasonably calculated to achieve actual receipt of notice, as agreed to and described in a written rental agreement' (ORS 90.150(4)) ("Agreed Method for Actual Notice" clause). Entry notices and absence notices use actual notice; termination notices never do.

title: No Good-Cause Coverage Notice; What Termination Notices Must Say
bodyText:
Oregon has a statewide for-cause rule but no separate good-cause notice: you don't have to tell tenants, at the start of the tenancy or when it ends, whether their unit is covered by or exempt from it. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no such notice.

What the termination notice itself must say, for tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465 ("When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause", "Notice Periods to End a Tenancy"):
- After the first year of occupancy, you may end a month-to-month tenancy only 'For a tenant cause and with notice in writing' under the cause statutes (ORS 90.427(3)(c)(A)) or 'For a qualifying landlord reason for termination and with notice in writing as described in subsections (5) and (6) of this section' (ORS 90.427(3)(c)(B)). A qualifying-reason notice must 'Specify in the termination notice the reason for the termination and supporting facts' (ORS 90.427(6)(a)(A)).
- A notice not renewing a fixed term for three violations must state the reason and supporting facts and follow the warning-notice rules (ORS 90.427(7)).
- A week-to-week notice, a no-cause notice ending a month-to-month tenancy during the first year of occupancy, or a no-cause notice under the owner-occupied two-unit rule 'need not state a reason for the termination' (ORS 90.427(12)(a), reaching notices under ORS 90.427(2), (3)(b), (8)(a)(B) and (8)(b)). If you choose to explain, say that the notice is given without stated cause, that the tenant has no right to cure, and that you need not prove the reason, or the explanation may give a right to cure (ORS 90.427(12)(b)).
- Every termination notice 'must include the information required by ORS 408.515' (ORS 90.391), the veterans' services information.

Exemptions work by statute, not by notice: the one-month payment doesn't apply if you own an interest in four or fewer units (ORS 90.427(6)(b)), and ORS 90.427(8) covers a building or property with no more than two units where you live.

title: Renewal Happens by Statute, Not by Lease Clause
bodyText:
In Oregon the statute does the renewing, so a lease has little room for its own automatic-renewal clause. For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465:

- After the first year of occupancy, and except in a building or on a property with no more than two units where you live (ORS 90.427(8)), a fixed term 'becomes a month-to-month tenancy upon the expiration of the fixed term, unless' (ORS 90.427(4)(c)) you and the tenant agree to a new fixed term, the tenant gives written notice at least 30 days before the ending date (or the date in the notice, if later), or you have a qualifying reason and give the required notice (ORS 90.427(4)(c)(A)-(C)). A month-to-month tenancy is one that 'automatically renews and continues for successive monthly periods on the same terms and conditions originally agreed to, or as revised by the parties, until terminated by one or both of the parties' (ORS 90.100(32)) ("When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause", "Holdover" clause).
- A fixed term ending within the first year of occupancy you may end without cause on 30 days' written notice (ORS 90.427(4)(b)); if no one gives notice and the tenant stays with your consent, the tenancy continues month to month.
- A new fixed term takes the parties' agreement. A clause signed at the start that rolls the lease into another fixed term, or that makes the tenant give more than 30 days' notice to leave at the end of the term, can be read as cutting into the tenant's statutory right in ORS 90.427(4)(c)(B), and it risks being an unenforceable waiver under ORS 90.245(1)(a). The library offers no automatic-renewal clause for Oregon; offer a new fixed term in a separate signed renewal instead.
- Rent at renewal follows the rent-increase rules: no increase in the first year, at least 90 days' written notice, no more than once in 12 months and no more than the statutory cap unless the unit's first certificate of occupancy is less than 15 years old or a regulated-affordable exemption applies (ORS 90.323(2), (5); "Statewide Rent Increase Limit"). During a fixed term, 'The terms of a fixed term tenancy, including the amount of rent, may not be unilaterally amended by the landlord or tenant' (ORS 90.220(2)).

Oregon has no reminder-notice rule for renewal clauses and no limit on how early you may ask a tenant to sign a renewal. Oregon's consumer automatic-renewal law covers a 'paid subscription or purchasing agreement' (ORS 646A.293(1)) for goods or services charged to a card or payment account; by its terms it can be read as not reaching a residential lease of real property. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no other renewal rule.

title: Who May Appear in Court for an Entity Landlord
bodyText:
If your landlord is an LLC, corporation, partnership or other entity, Oregon's general rule is that it must appear in court through a lawyer: a party 'that is not a natural person appears by attorney in all cases, unless otherwise specifically provided by law' (ORS 9.320). Two exceptions matter to landlords.

- Eviction cases. In an action for possession of a dwelling unit 'to which ORS chapter 90 applies, the plaintiff may also appear through a nonattorney who is an agent or employee of the plaintiff or an agent or employee of an agent of the plaintiff' (ORS 105.130(4)). So a property manager or employee may file and handle the eviction, and the complaint may be 'verified by an agent or employee of the plaintiff or an agent or employee of an agent of the plaintiff' (ORS 105.124(2)). The case must still be 'brought in the name of a person entitled to possession as plaintiff' (ORS 105.130(4)), meaning the owner or landlord entity, not the manager. For these actions 'attorney' also includes a licensed paralegal (associate licensee) working within the approved scope of practice (ORS 105.100).
- Small claims. 'Notwithstanding the provisions of ORS 9.320, a party that is not a natural person' may appear in the circuit court's small claims department without a lawyer (ORS 46.415(5)), and the same is true in a justice court's small claims department (ORS 52.800(2)); claims there are capped at $10,000 (ORS 46.405; ORS 52.750) ("Possession, Rent and Damages: Separate Actions").
A separate suit for rent or damages in the regular circuit or justice court department falls back under ORS 9.320, so an entity needs a lawyer there. No Oregon court rule changes these statutes: the Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no other rule.

Before an entity sues, check three things ("Landlord Registration and Rental Licensing" has the detail):
- An out-of-state LLC or corporation 'transacting business in this state without authorization from the Secretary of State may not maintain a proceeding in any court in this state until it obtains authorization' (ORS 63.704(1); ORS 60.704(1)). Owning property 'without more' is not transacting business (ORS 63.701(2)(i)), but renting it out can be read as transacting business, so register first or get advice.
- Renting under a name that isn't the owner's real and true name is doing business under an assumed business name, because carrying on business includes 'To sell, purchase or lease real estate' (ORS 648.005(3)(a)). If the name isn't registered, the owner 'shall lack standing before the courts of this state to maintain a cause of action for the benefit of the business' (ORS 648.135(1)) until it registers, which it may do at any time.
- Tenants must be able to serve you: your lease discloses the owner or agent for service of process ("Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause); see "Owners Outside Oregon: Service and Standing" for owners outside Oregon. Reporting duties that bind anyone, such as reporting unclaimed deposit refunds to the State Treasurer, apply to entity landlords too.

title: One Year to Sue on a Rental Agreement
bodyText:
Oregon gives claims under a residential tenancy a short deadline: 'An action arising under a rental agreement or ORS chapter 90 shall be commenced within one year' (ORS 12.125). It applies both ways, to your suit for unpaid rent, damages or a deposit shortfall and to a tenant's claims against you, and the clock starts when the claim accrues (ORS 12.010). Some chapter 90 sections set their own one-year clock, such as a tenant's claim for a wrongful qualifying-reason termination, which must be brought 'within one year after the tenant knew or should have known that the landlord terminated the tenancy in violation of this section' (ORS 90.427(9)(b)).

Other periods may apply to claims that don't arise under the rental agreement or chapter 90: six years for a contract or a liability created by statute, or for injury to an interest in real property (ORS 12.080), and two years for injury to the person not arising on contract (ORS 12.110(1)). Which period governs a particular claim, for example property damage pleaded as waste, can turn on case law; the cautious course is to sue within one year.

Payments and promises. A payment of principal or interest on an existing debt restarts the period: 'the limitation shall commence from the time the last payment was made' (ORS 12.240). A promise or acknowledgment restarts it only if it is 'contained in some writing, signed by the party to be charged thereby' (ORS 12.230). Whether a tenant's partial payment of back rent counts as such a payment under ORS 12.240 is not settled by the statute's text. The text can be read as saying it may. Suing on a claim you know is time-barred can be an unlawful collection practice: a debt collector may not file 'a legal action to collect' a debt 'if the debt collector knows, or after exercising reasonable diligence would know, that an applicable statute of limitations bars the collection or the collection attempt' (ORS 646.639(2)(r)) ("Collecting Money From Tenants").

Before you sue, check standing too: an unregistered foreign LLC or corporation, or an owner using an unregistered assumed business name, can't maintain the action until it registers, and registering does not 'extend any statute of limitations' (ORS 648.135(1)) ("Landlord Registration and Rental Licensing", "Who May Appear in Court for an Entity Landlord"). Service on an owner outside Oregon and the reporting of unclaimed refunds are covered in "Owners Outside Oregon: Service and Standing" and "Unclaimed Deposit Refunds".

No other Oregon statute or rule sets a separate period for a landlord's rent or damage claim: the Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none.

title: Owners Outside Oregon: Service and Standing
bodyText:
Oregon doesn't require an individual owner who lives outside the state to name an Oregon agent before renting a home or suing a tenant (entity owners are different, below), and doesn't make tenants withhold state income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found neither rule. What Oregon does require, wherever the owner lives:

- Disclosure for service. For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, you must give the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the manager and of 'An owner of the premises or a person authorized to act for and on behalf of the owner for the purpose of service of process and receiving and receipting for notices and demands' (ORS 90.305(1)(b)), and keep it current (ORS 90.305(2)). The person named need not live in Oregon. If a manager or the person who signs the rental agreement fails to make the disclosure, that person 'becomes an agent of each person who is a landlord for service of process and receiving and receipting for notices and demands' (ORS 90.305(3)). The library's lease carries the disclosure ("Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause).
- Entities. An Oregon limited liability company must 'continuously maintain in this state a registered agent and registered office' (ORS 63.111(1)), and 'Each foreign limited liability company authorized to transact business in this state must continuously maintain in this state' a registered office and a registered agent (ORS 63.721). So an out-of-state LLC that rents out Oregon property as a business does need an Oregon agent once authorized, and an out-of-state LLC or corporation transacting business here without authority 'may not maintain a proceeding in any court in this state' (ORS 63.704(1); ORS 60.704(1)) until authorized ("Who May Appear in Court for an Entity Landlord").
- Assumed business names. An owner 'not domiciled within this state' who registers an assumed business name is 'deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as agent upon whom may be served at any time any process, notice or demand required or permitted by law to be served upon them' (ORS 648.061); renting under an unregistered assumed name costs standing to sue until registered (ORS 648.135(1); "Landlord Registration and Rental Licensing").
- Time to sue and reporting. The one-year limit on claims under a rental agreement applies to you as to anyone ("One Year to Sue on a Rental Agreement"), and so does the duty to report unclaimed deposit refunds to the State Treasurer.

Oregon taxes nonresidents on Oregon rental income through their own returns; no rule makes tenants withhold from rent.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right
bodyText:
Oregon gives landlords no general right to end a tenancy after an environmental public health event or a government action that makes occupancy impossible, and the library offers no lease clause reserving one. Two statutes cover the ground instead, for tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465:

- Posted units. If, after the tenancy begins, an agency 'posts a dwelling unit as unsafe and unlawful to occupy due to the existence of conditions that violate state or local law, that materially affect health or safety' (ORS 90.380(5)), the tenant may end the tenancy immediately if the tenant didn't cause the conditions, and you may end it on 24 hours' written notice stating 'the reason for the termination' (ORS 90.380(5)(b)) only if the conditions 'Were not caused by the landlord or by the landlord's failure to maintain the dwelling' (ORS 90.380(5)(b)). You must return deposits and prorated prepaid rent within 14 days (ORS 90.380(6)) ("Posted or Unlawful Units").
- Natural disasters. Since June 5, 2026, if a declared natural disaster destroys the unit, 'the tenancy is immediately terminated and the parties are not further obligated under the rental agreement or this chapter' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21(1)), with deposits and prorated prepaid rent returned and no cleanup charge unless the tenant was responsible; no rent is owed while the unit is inaccessible, and a posted unit counts as inaccessible (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21(3)). These rules apply 'unless the parties agree otherwise following the natural disaster' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21), so a lease signed beforehand can't change them ("Tenancies After a Natural Disaster").

Any other environmental problem (contamination, a spill, smoke) leaves you with the ordinary rules: your duty to keep the unit habitable, the tenant's repair and essential-service remedies, and, after the first year of occupancy, a 90-day qualifying-reason notice for repairs that make the unit unsafe or unfit to occupy ("Fire, Casualty and Uninhabitable Units", "When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause"). A lease clause adding a landlord termination right for such events would add a cause ORS 90.427 doesn't list and risk being an unenforceable waiver (ORS 90.245(1)(a)). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no environmental-event termination rule.

title: No Double-Letting Statute
bodyText:
Oregon has no statute on double-letting (renting the same room or unit to more than one tenant) and no special rent-abatement remedy for it. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none.

The general rules still make it costly, for tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465. A tenant is a person 'entitled under a rental agreement to occupy a dwelling unit to the exclusion of others' (ORS 90.100(51)(a)(A)), and possession passes to the tenant when you give actual notice 'that the tenant has the right under a rental agreement to occupy the dwelling unit to the exclusion of others' (ORS 90.147(1)), for example by handing over the keys. Renting the same space to someone else breaks that right, and the tenant may use the remedies for your noncompliance with the rental agreement: 'the tenant may recover damages and obtain injunctive relief for any noncompliance by the landlord with the rental agreement' (ORS 90.360(2)), or give the termination notice in ORS 90.360(1) ("Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies"). If the other occupant shuts the tenant out of the unit, that is likely an unlawful exclusion: the tenant 'may obtain injunctive relief to recover possession or may terminate the rental agreement and recover an amount up to' (ORS 90.375) two months' periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater, and you must return the security deposits and prepaid rent recoverable under ORS 90.300 if the agreement ends (ORS 90.375). A second letting that excludes the tenant can be read as falling under ORS 90.375. If you can't deliver possession at the start because someone else is there, the lease's possession-delay clause applies, and you must refund the tenant's deposits if the tenancy ends (ORS 90.360(5)).

Renting rooms to several unrelated tenants under separate agreements is lawful; make each agreement say exactly which room and which shared areas it covers.

title: No Initials Requirement for Lease Terms
bodyText:
Oregon has no rule requiring a tenant to initial a lease term, or to sign or acknowledge it separately, for it to bind the tenant. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none for residential leases. Oregon also has no plain-language, type-size or boldface rule for leases ("Plain Language and Type Size").

Initials can't rescue a term the statute forbids, though. For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, the tenant may end a month-to-month tenancy 'by giving the landlord notice in writing not less than 30 days prior to the date designated in the notice' (ORS 90.427(3)(a)), and may end at the close of a fixed term after the first year of occupancy on the same 30 days' written notice (ORS 90.427(4)(c)(B)). A lease term requiring the tenant to give more notice than that can be read as cutting into those rights and risking being an unenforceable waiver, initialed or not: 'A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant' (ORS 90.245(1)) 'Agrees to waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.245(1)(a)) ("Lease Terms Oregon Voids").

Where Oregon does require a separate writing, it is a separate document, not initials in the lease. Examples: the e-mail notice addendum signed after move-in (ORS 90.155(1)(d)); the addendum, signed after move-in, for returning a deposit electronically (ORS 90.300(13)); and the unannounced-showing agreement, which must be signed while you are actively trying to sell (ORS 90.322(1)(d)(A)), 'reflected in a writing separate from the rental agreement and signed by both parties' (ORS 90.322(1)(d)(B)) and 'supported by separate consideration recited in the agreement' (ORS 90.322(1)(d)(C)). Initials remain good evidence that a tenant saw an unusual lawful term.

title: Lease Length and Signing Formalities
bodyText:
Oregon sets no maximum term for a residential lease and has no spousal-consent, homestead or community-property rule for leasing your property. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. (Oregon isn't a community-property state; its community-property statutes deal only with couples who elected into a 1943 law or acquired property elsewhere.)

The formalities that do apply turn on whether the lease runs longer than one year:
- A lease for more than a year must be in writing and signed: 'An agreement for the leasing for a longer period than one year' (ORS 41.580(1)(e)) is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or that party's lawfully authorized agent ("Written Leases and Long Terms").
- A lease longer than a year also creates an interest in real property, which can be created only 'by a conveyance or other instrument in writing, subscribed by the party creating, transferring or declaring it, or by the lawful agent of the party under written authority' (ORS 93.020(1)); only 'a lease for term not exceeding one year' (ORS 93.020(1)) is excepted. So if a property manager signs a lease of more than a year for you, give the manager written authority to do so. The statute of frauds also lists 'An agreement concerning real property made by an agent of the party sought to be charged unless the authority of the agent is in writing' (ORS 41.580(1)(f)), with no one-year limit; how that applies to a short residential rental agreement, which chapter 90 allows to be oral (ORS 90.100(42)), is not settled by the text, so the cautious course is written authority for any manager who signs leases.
- You may record a lease or a memorandum of it, acknowledged like a deed, to give notice to later buyers and lenders (ORS 93.710(1)); recording is optional.

For an ordinary residential tenancy under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, a fixed term ending after the first year of occupancy becomes month-to-month unless renewed or ended as the statute allows ("Renewal Happens by Statute, Not by Lease Clause"), and a rental agreement 'is either a week-to-week tenancy, month-to-month tenancy or fixed term tenancy' (ORS 90.100(42)).

title: Disclosing Foreclosure and Other Proceedings
bodyText:
Oregon's rule on proceedings against the property runs from you to the tenant, not the other way. For a dwelling unit 'in premises containing no more than four dwelling units' (ORS 90.310(1)), if at signing the premises are subject to an outstanding notice of default or trustee's sale, a pending foreclosure suit, a pending declaration of forfeiture or suit for specific performance of a land sale contract, or a pending tax-lien foreclosure, 'the landlord shall disclose that circumstance to the tenant in writing before the execution of the rental agreement' (ORS 90.310(1)).

If the tenant moves because of an undisclosed circumstance, 'the tenant may recover twice the actual damages or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, and all prepaid rent' (ORS 90.310(2)).

The rule doesn't apply to premises run by a court-appointed receiver (ORS 90.310(3)), and a manager who made the ORS 90.305 disclosures and didn't know of the proceeding isn't liable (ORS 90.310(4)). The library's lease carries the disclosure as "Disclosure of Pending Foreclosure or Forfeiture" clause; tenants' rights during and after a foreclosure are in "Tenants and Foreclosure".

No Oregon statute requires a tenant to tell you about, or forward, papers about a foreclosure, tax proceeding or someone else's claim to the property, and none deals with a tenant agreeing to hold under a stranger (attornment). The lease asks for that notice as a contract term ("Notice of Proceedings Against the Property" clause).

title: When the Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText:
Oregon leaves the effect of a taking on a residential lease to the lease. No Oregon statute ends the lease, reduces the rent or divides the condemnation award between you and the tenant when the government takes the property by eminent domain.

What the law does say:
- 'Private property shall not be taken for public use' without 'just compensation' (Or. Const. art. I, § 18).
- In a condemnation action brought against the record owner, 'There may be included as defendants any lessee or other person in possession and all other persons having or claiming an interest in the property' (ORS 35.245(2)), so a tenant may be a party and claim for its interest.
- A public entity acquiring property must give relocation payments and assistance to a displaced person, meaning one who moves 'as a result of' the public entity's acquisition of the real property or its written order to vacate for public use (ORS 35.500(1)), under the federal Uniform Relocation Act (ORS 35.510). Tenants who must move usually qualify; those payments are theirs.

Because the statutes are silent, the library offers an optional condemnation clause: on a total or substantial taking the lease ends when the tenant must give up possession, rent is prorated and prepaid rent and the deposit are returned; on a smaller taking rent drops in proportion; and the award belongs to you except the tenant's own relocation or personal-property payments. Prorating rent matches Oregon's rule that 'Unless otherwise agreed, rent is uniformly apportionable from day to day' (ORS 90.427(10)). Code-enforcement "condemnation" of an unsafe unit is a different thing ("Posted or Unlawful Units"). Manufactured dwelling park and marina closures caused by eminent domain have their own notice rules (ORS 90.650).

title: Leasing With Less Than Full Ownership
bodyText:
Oregon law has no usufruct (a civil-law right to use and take the fruits of someone else's property), and no Oregon statute or rule says what happens to a residential lease when a landlord who holds only a life estate or a similar limited interest loses it. Fiduciaries are different: unless the trust's terms limit it (ORS 130.720(1)), a trustee may 'Enter into a lease for any purpose as lessor or lessee ... even though the period of the lease extends beyond the duration of the trust' (ORS 130.725(9)), and a conservator acting reasonably to accomplish the purposes of the conservatorship may, without prior court approval, lease 'for a term within or extending beyond the term of the conservatorship' (ORS 125.445(11)). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no usufruct and no general rule for a lease by a holder of a limited interest.

If you lease as a life tenant or other holder of less than full ownership (a trustee or conservator acting within its statutory powers is covered above), the cautious course is to tell the tenant in writing what interest you hold and that the tenancy may end when it does, or have the remainder owner join in the lease, and take advice before signing a fixed term that could outlast your interest. Oregon's landlord-tenant rules still follow whoever holds the landlord's side: 'the holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time the tenancy terminates is responsible to the tenant for any security deposit or prepaid rent and is bound by this section' (ORS 90.300(2)(b)), and the manager and owner disclosure 'extends to and is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner or manager' (ORS 90.305(2)) ("Selling or Changing Management", "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause). Any new holder who wants the unit back must use the termination rules that apply to the tenancy ("When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause").

title: Utility Allowances and Pass-Through Limits
bodyText: Oregon has no statute on utility allowances as such (you pay a utility up to a set amount and the tenant pays the excess), but its utility-billing rule limits what you may pass through. In an ordinary residential tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), you may make the tenant pay you a utility charge billed to you only 'if a written rental agreement so provides' (ORS 90.315(4)(a)), and 'a utility or service charge may only include the cost of the utility or service as billed to the landlord by the provider' (ORS 90.315(4)(c)). The one markup allowed is up to 10 percent on cable, satellite or other video subscription service or internet access, and only if the total stays below what the tenant would pay the provider directly and the rental agreement and every bill list the markup separately (ORS 90.315(4)(c)(A)-(E)). An overage charge under an allowance plan is best treated as such a utility charge, so it follows the billing rules in "Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause: bill in writing within 30 days after you receive the provider's bill, state it separately from rent, explain how the provider assesses the charge and how you allocate it (the allowance and how the excess is worked out belong here), and include the provider's bill or offer it for inspection (ORS 90.315(4)(b)). The charge 'is not rent or a fee' (ORS 90.315(4)(e)): nonpayment can ground a for-cause termination, not a nonpayment-of-rent notice. If you break these rules, the tenant may recover 'an amount equal to one month's periodic rent or twice the amount wrongfully charged to the tenant, whichever is greater' (ORS 90.315(4)(f)). No Oregon statute or Public Utility Commission rule bars passing master-metered electricity or gas through to tenants, or sets a separate cap for resold water or sewer service; the Commission's master-meter rules only make utilities warn occupants before a shutoff ("Utility Shutoffs and Tenants"). The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. Manufactured dwelling parks and marinas follow separate billing rules (ORS 90.560 to 90.584), which this library does not draft for.

title: No Shutoffs of Utilities You Submeter or Supply
bodyText: Oregon has no separate procedure for cutting off a utility you submeter or supply to a tenant in an ordinary residential tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), and the Public Utility Commission's disconnection rules bind the utilities it regulates, not landlords. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. The general rules control, and they bar a shutoff by you. You may not recover possession by 'willful diminution of services to the tenant by interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electricity or other essential service to the tenant' (ORS 90.435). If you willfully interrupt, or seriously attempt or threaten to interrupt, heat, water, electricity or another essential service, the tenant may get an injunction or end the tenancy and recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater (ORS 90.375). So you collect an unpaid submetered charge through the lease, not by cutting service: a utility charge billed under "Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause 'is not rent or a fee', and its nonpayment 'is grounds for termination of a rental agreement for cause under ORS 90.392' (ORS 90.315(4)(e)), not for nonpayment of rent. If a service you are responsible for fails, the tenant has the essential-service remedies (ORS 90.365; "Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies"); if the utility shuts it off for your nonpayment, the tenant may pay and deduct or end the tenancy on 72 hours' notice (ORS 90.315(7); "Utilities in Your Name and Tenant Accounts"). Manufactured dwelling parks and marinas have their own submeter sections (ORS 90.560 to 90.584), under which the landlord 'is responsible for maintaining the utility or service system, including any submeter' (ORS 90.562(5)); this library does not draft for them.

title: Tenant Utility Transfers: No Cutoff Right
bodyText: No Oregon statute or rule lets you shut off, or close the account for, a utility kept in your name because the tenant has not moved it into the tenant's own name, and a lease term letting you do so would be risky. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. If you willfully interrupt heat, running water, hot water, electricity or another essential service, or seriously attempt or threaten to, the tenant may get an injunction or end the tenancy and recover up to two months' periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater (ORS 90.375), and you may not recover possession by 'interrupting or causing the interruption of heat, running water, hot water, electricity or other essential service to the tenant' (ORS 90.435). A rental agreement may not have the tenant 'waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.245(1)(a)), so a clause in which the tenant agrees to a cutoff would be unenforceable ("Lease Terms Oregon Voids"). Closing your own account so that the tenant's service stops is best treated as causing that interruption. The safer course when a tenant hasn't set up a utility the lease makes the tenant's responsibility: keep the service on, and either bill the tenant for it under a written agreement that meets ORS 90.315(4) ("Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause) or treat the failure as a breach of the lease and give a for-cause notice (ORS 90.392). If the tenant can't get service in the tenant's own name because a previous tenant or the owner owes the utility, the tenant may pay and deduct or end the tenancy (ORS 90.315(5)-(6); "Utilities in Your Name and Tenant Accounts"). Oregon also has no rule letting a court in a restraining-order case move a utility account to the protected person, and none letting a deployed servicemember suspend utilities.

title: Utility Disclosures at the Start of a Tenancy
bodyText:
Oregon's utility disclosures for an ordinary residential tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465) come from one statute, and both can sit in the lease.

First, 'The landlord shall disclose to the tenant in writing at or before the commencement of the tenancy any utility or service that the tenant pays directly to a utility or service provider that benefits, directly, the landlord or other tenants' (ORS 90.315(2)); a payment benefits others 'if the utility or service is delivered to any area other than the tenant's dwelling unit' (ORS 90.315(2)). If you knowingly fail to disclose, the tenant may recover twice the actual damages or one month's rent, whichever is greater (ORS 90.315(3)). The library's clause for this is "Tenant-Paid Utilities That Serve Others" clause.

Second, if you bill the tenant for utilities, the written rental agreement must say so, must describe any common-area charge separately, and the agreement or each bill must explain how the provider assesses the charge and how you allocate it among tenants (ORS 90.315(4)(a)-(b); "Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause).

Oregon does not require you to give a prospective or current tenant past utility bills, energy-use history or an estimate of utility costs. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

A related rule binds utilities, not you: when a regulated utility audits a rental unit at its customer's request, 'the audit shall include a heating cost estimate using average temperatures and typical lifestyles' (OAR 860-030-0005(3)(c)). Manufactured dwelling park and marina landlords give the utility information in their statement of policy instead (ORS 90.510).

title: Getting Copies of a Tenant's Shutoff Notices
bodyText: In Oregon the utility customer, not the property owner, decides who else gets shutoff notices. Each energy utility the Public Utility Commission regulates 'shall offer its customers the option to designate a third party to receive bills and notices set forth in these rules', and then sends them to that representative, 'with duplicate copies of disconnect notices also served on the customer' (OAR 860-021-0017). Regulated water utilities (OAR 860-036-1120) and wastewater utilities (OAR 860-037-0020) must offer the same choice. So a tenant who holds the account may name you to receive copies, but no statute or rule lets you, as owner, sign up on your own to be told of a tenant's pending disconnection. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The Commission's rules also make the utility warn the occupants when the billing address differs from the service address, and tell the Commission before cutting off a master-metered building ("Utility Shutoffs and Tenants"). City, county and district utilities are not under those rules. Instead, a municipal utility may not transfer a tenant's unpaid claim to you unless it notified the tenant and mailed you or your agent a copy of the notice of delinquency within 30 days after payment was due (ORS 91.255(3)), may not refuse service to a later tenant over a previous tenant's debt unless it mailed you that copy when it notified the previous tenant (ORS 91.255(4)), and, when it intends to file a lien or refuse service to a later tenant, must tell you the status of a tenant's account on request (ORS 91.255(7), (9)). See "Utilities in Your Name and Tenant Accounts". The library offers no lease clause requiring a tenant to name you: the rules make naming a third party the customer's option, so asking the tenant to do it voluntarily is the cautious course.

title: Submetered or Rebilled Electricity and Gas
bodyText: Oregon has no electricity-specific submetering disclosure for an ordinary residential tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465); electricity and gas you bill to a tenant fall under the general utility-billing rule. You may charge for them only 'if a written rental agreement so provides' (ORS 90.315(4)(a)), and the agreement or each bill must explain 'The manner in which the provider assesses a utility or service charge' and 'The manner in which the charge is allocated among the tenants if the provider's bill to the landlord covers multiple tenants' (ORS 90.315(4)(b)(B)); a submeter reading is one way to allocate. The charge may include only the provider's cost (ORS 90.315(4)(c)). The library's clause is "Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause. Whether rebilling makes you a regulated utility: Oregon defines a "public utility" to include any person that operates equipment 'for the production, transmission, delivery or furnishing of heat, light, water or power, directly or indirectly to or for the public' (ORS 757.005(1)(a)(A)), and excludes, among others, anyone providing heat, light or power 'From solar or wind resources to any number of customers' (ORS 757.005(1)(b)(C)(iii)) or 'From any energy resource to fewer than 20 residential customers so long as' only residential customers are served (ORS 757.005(1)(b)(C)(ii)). No statute or Commission rule says whether a landlord who passes a provider's electric or gas charges to tenants at cost under ORS 90.315(4) is a public utility; for manufactured dwelling parks and marinas, a landlord that complies with the facility billing sections 'is not a public utility for purposes of ORS chapter 757' (ORS 90.562(7)), and nothing equivalent covers other rentals. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The cautious course: bill only the provider's cost, as ORS 90.315(4)(c) requires, and get advice before selling electricity you generate or buying power to resell at a markup. Gas piping you own after a utility's master meter may also be subject to the Commission's pipeline safety rules, which adopt federal pipeline standards by reference (OAR 860-024-0020); check with the Commission or an advisor.

title: On-Bill Energy Loan Charges: Notice Before Signing
bodyText: If your rental property is benefited by an Oregon energy efficiency and sustainable technology loan (the state program repaid through the utility bill), you must tell the tenant before the lease is signed. 'A person entering into an agreement to sell, rent, lease or otherwise confer a right in the person's real property that is benefited by an energy efficiency and sustainable technology loan for which a loan repayment charge or other repayment obligation applies or for which a fixture filing, lien or other form of security exists shall, prior to any party signing the agreement, give notice of the loan repayment charge, repayment obligation, filing, lien or other security affecting the property to the other parties to the agreement' (ORS 470.695). A loan repayment charge is 'an amount charged to a utility customer account through on-bill financing' (ORS 470.050(18)), and an investor-owned utility's on-bill financing system must show it as a separate line item or statement on the bill (ORS 470.660(2)(b)). The statute names no form and does not say the notice must be written; give it in writing, separately from the lease and before anyone signs, so you can show it came first. The loan contract makes the borrower agree to tell anyone acquiring 'ownership of, or an interest in, the property' that the charge will move to that person's utility account unless the loan is paid off first (ORS 470.150(7)(a)); no statute or rule says whether a tenant who opens the utility account takes on the charge, so get advice before letting it sit on a tenant's account. Oregon has no other meter-based conservation charge that you must disclose to each new tenant, no rent credit for one, and no rule requiring a monthly statement of submeter readings in an ordinary tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), where a utility charge you bill may include only the provider's cost and must come with a copy of the provider's bill or an offer to inspect it (ORS 90.315(4)(b)(C), (c)). The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. Manufactured dwelling parks and marinas have their own submeter-rate and bill-posting rules (ORS 90.572; ORS 90.582); this library does not draft for them.

title: Tenant Energy Data and Building Benchmarking
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule on a utility releasing a tenant's energy usage data to you, for benchmarking or otherwise, and none that lets a lease clause authorize the release. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The Public Utility Commission's customer-information rules treat a customer's 'current or historical electricity or natural gas usage' as part of 'Proprietary customer information' (OAR 860-086-0010(6)), but they govern an electric company's transfers of that information to its competitive operations, electricity service suppliers, affiliates and aggregators under a tariff with consent procedures (OAR 860-086-0020), not releases to landlords; ask the utility what its own tariff and consent forms allow. Benchmarking duties are coming for larger apartment buildings. Oregon's building performance standard treats as a tier 2 building one with at least 35,000 square feet of floor area, not counting parking, 'that is used as a multifamily residential building' (ORS 469.275(14)(a)(A)), and 'Not later than July 1, 2028, and by July 1 every five years thereafter, an eligible building owner of a tier 2 building shall provide the department with data the department requires in rules the department adopts under subsection (1) of this section' (ORS 469.287(3)). The State Department of Energy's rules as served November 18, 2026 (OAR chapter 330, division 300) adopt the tier 1 standard and set up early-compliance incentives; no rule setting the tier 2 data requirement was found, so check the department's current rules well before 2028. If you need tenants' own usage for that reporting, the cautious course is a separate signed consent from each tenant, or whole-building data from the utility, rather than a lease clause.

title: City and District Utility Bills Left by Tenants
bodyText: Oregon's tenant-utility statute (ORS 91.255) limits how a city, county or district utility can pass a tenant's unpaid bill to you, but it does not itself give those utilities a lien (a few other statutes do, below), and no statute lets you avoid one with a lease clause or an affidavit filed with the utility. A "municipal utility" is a city, county or district that provides electricity, natural gas, domestic water, sewer, or garbage or refuse service, not a people's utility district (ORS 91.255(1)). It may not transfer a claim against a tenant to you unless it gave the tenant notice of the delinquency and mailed you or your agent, at the last address it has on file, a copy of the notice of delinquency within 30 days after payment was due (ORS 91.255(3)). It may not refuse or shut off service to a later tenant over a lien for a previous tenant's unpaid bill unless it mailed you that copy when it notified the previous tenant (ORS 91.255(4)).
