If it intends to file a lien or to refuse service to a later tenant, it must apply the same shutoff policy to tenant-occupied and owner-occupied single-family homes and must tell you the status of a tenant's account on request (ORS 91.255(6)-(9)). Other utility companies may not transfer a tenant's claim to you 'without the written consent of the owner' (ORS 91.255(2)). But 'Nothing in this section creates, expands or abridges any authority of a municipal utility to transfer a claim, based upon any contract, ordinance or lien' (ORS 91.255(10)): whether a city can lien your property depends on its charter and ordinances. One statute gives a lien directly: for a multifamily building of five or more units on a single water meter, 'the owner of the real property shall be considered the user of the water' (ORS 223.594(1)), and if the bill isn't paid and service hasn't been or won't be shut off, the municipal utility 'may place a lien on the premises' (ORS 223.594(1)). Some district statutes also let delinquent sewer charges go on the county tax roll as a lien (for example ORS 450.290(2)). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no lease-clause or affidavit route. Ask your city or district about its lien rules and keep your mailing address on file with it. See "Utilities in Your Name and Tenant Accounts".

title: Which Fire Code Applies to Your Rental
bodyText: Oregon's fire code is a model code adopted by rule: 'Effective October 1, 2025, the 2025 Oregon Fire Code which is the 2024 edition of the International Fire Code, as published by the International Code Council' (OAR 837-040-0010(2)), as amended by the Department of the State Fire Marshal, is adopted. Get the current Oregon Fire Code and the Fire Marshal's amendments, and ask your local fire authority, since the State Fire Marshal may exempt a city or district that enforces adequate regulations of its own (ORS 476.030(3)). For evaluating existing buildings, the Fire Marshal also adopts 'The fire and life safety provisions of the 2025 edition of the Oregon Structural Specialty Code and the 2025 edition of the Oregon Mechanical Specialty Code' (OAR 837-040-0140). Two limits on the Fire Marshal's rules matter to landlords: the exit-safety authority covers 'all buildings, except private residences, which are occupied for sleeping purposes' (ORS 476.030(1)(c)), and 'structural changes shall not be required in buildings built, occupied and maintained in conformity with state building code regulations applicable at the time of construction' (ORS 476.030(1)(c)). If an inspector finds a building 'especially liable to fire' and so situated or occupied as to endanger other buildings, property or human life (ORS 479.170(1)), or finds dangerous combustible material or conditions (ORS 479.170(2)), the order to repair it or remove the hazard runs against 'the owner, lessee or occupant' (ORS 479.170(3)); the Fire Marshal may close the building until it complies, and anyone injured by a failure to comply may recover actual damages from the owner or occupant (ORS 479.190). The landlord-tenant statutes set the core duties directly: safety from fire hazards, including a working smoke alarm at the start of each new tenancy, and a carbon monoxide alarm where required, are habitability items (ORS 90.320(1)(j)-(k); "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms"); you must keep an emergency exit route from each bedroom that conforms to the law in effect at occupancy or after a later renovation or change of use (ORS 90.460); and a tenant may not 'Remove, obstruct or tamper with a sprinkler head used for fire suppression' (ORS 90.325(2)(c)). Lease fire rules: "Fire Safety & Grilling" clause.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Existing Rentals
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule that makes you add fire sprinklers to an existing residential rental as a general rule. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Whether a new building or a substantial alteration needs sprinklers is set by the building codes the state adopts by reference (the Oregon Structural and Residential Specialty Codes) and the Oregon Fire Code; your building official decides at permit. Two rules can still reach an existing building. The State Fire Marshal's exit rules exempt private residences and do not require structural changes in a building built and kept to the code in force when it was built (ORS 476.030(1)(c)), but an existing building other than an institutional, group care or single-family occupancy that is a "high life hazard" for its occupants must reach 'a reasonable adequate level of exiting safety', and one approved method is 'A partial automatic sprinkler system' (OAR 837-041-0050(2)(a)); the rule's commentary says that in an apartment building a fire official 'might justifiably refuse to approve any plan that does not include significant use of automatic sprinklers' (OAR 837-041-0050(8)(e)). The finding comes with written reasons, and you then have 60 days to propose a method of improvement (OAR 837-041-0050(4)). When you convert a single-family dwelling into no more than four units, the building official may consider 'whether an automatic sprinkler system is technically feasible' and approve an alternate method (OAR 918-020-0390(3)). Sprinklers you do have are protected: a tenant may not 'Remove, obstruct or tamper with a sprinkler head used for fire suppression' (ORS 90.325(2)(c)), and your habitability duty covers safety from fire hazards (ORS 90.320(1)(j)). A rural fire protection district may by ordinance repay landlords up to 50 percent of the cost of installing fire safety systems, sprinklers included, in existing multifamily housing (ORS 478.885(2)), and a local government may not charge a system development charge for installing a residential (NFPA 13D) sprinkler system (ORS 223.301(5)).

title: No Fire Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has fire sprinklers. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The only sprinkler item in Oregon's statutory disclosure forms is the seller's question about an outdoor lawn sprinkler system in a home sale (ORS 105.464), which does not apply to rentals. Oregon has no state tax credit for a voluntary sprinkler retrofit, but a rural fire protection district may by ordinance set up a program that 'pays or repays to landlords part of the costs of installing fire safety systems in multifamily housing' (ORS 478.885(2)), up to 50 percent of the cost, and a local government may not charge a system development charge for installing a residential (NFPA 13D) sprinkler system (ORS 223.301(5)). Sprinklers and tenants: "Fire Sprinklers in Existing Rentals".

title: Code Editions Fixed by Oregon Rules
bodyText: Oregon's building and fire codes are model codes adopted by rule at a named edition, so a newer national edition does not apply until an Oregon rule adopts it. The state building code director adopts model codes, and 'Such model codes with modifications considered necessary and specialty codes may be adopted by reference' (ORS 455.110(3)). As served November 18, 2026: 'Effective October 1, 2026, the 2026 Oregon Residential Specialty Code' (OAR 918-480-0005(3)) consists of the 2024 International Residential Code, Chapters 1 through 24 and 44 with listed appendices, as amended (OAR 918-480-0005(3)(a)), with the 2023 code still accepted for plans until March 31, 2027 (OAR 918-480-0005(5)-(6)); 'Effective October 1, 2025, the 2025 Oregon Structural Specialty Code' (OAR 918-460-0010(2)) is the 2024 International Building Code with the new-construction provisions of the 2024 International Fire Code and the 2024 International Existing Building Code, as amended (OAR 918-460-0010(2)(a)); and the 2025 Oregon Fire Code is the 2024 International Fire Code as amended by the State Fire Marshal (OAR 837-040-0010(2)). For a construction project, 'Code requirements in effect at the time a plan review or permit application is filed controls the construction under the application unless the applicant agrees to be controlled by subsequent changes' (OAR 918-460-0010(4)); the residential code has the same rule (OAR 918-480-0005(4)). The landlord-tenant statutes also freeze several standards at a point in time. Plumbing, heating and electrical facilities must 'conform to applicable law in effect at the time of installation' (ORS 90.320(1)(b)), or at the time of installation for heating, wiring and required cooling (ORS 90.320(1)(d)-(e), (n)(B)); bedroom exit routes 'must conform to applicable law in effect at the time of occupancy of the building or in effect after a renovation or change of use of the building, whichever is later' (ORS 90.460(2)); and the State Fire Marshal may not require structural changes in 'buildings built, occupied and maintained in conformity with state building code regulations applicable at the time of construction' (ORS 476.030(1)(c)). So check the edition in force when the item was installed, built or renovated, not today's national edition.

title: Lighting in Common Areas
bodyText: Oregon's landlord-tenant law sets no lighting levels for halls, stairways, entries or parking areas; it covers lighting through the habitability duty and the utility-payment rules, for ordinary residential tenancies (ORS 90.100 to 90.465). A unit is unhabitable if it substantially lacks 'Electrical lighting with wiring and electrical equipment that conform to applicable law at the time of installation' and are kept in good working order (ORS 90.320(1)(e)), or 'Floors, walls, ceilings, stairways and railings maintained in good repair' (ORS 90.320(1)(h)), and 'all areas under control of the landlord' must be 'kept in every part safe for normal and reasonably foreseeable uses' (ORS 90.320(1)(f)). Light fixtures are an essential service (ORS 90.100(15)(a)(A)), and a faulty light switch is the statute's own example of a minor habitability defect a tenant may have repaired (ORS 90.368(1)(a); "Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies"). Specific lighting requirements for new construction and alterations come from the building codes adopted by reference; follow your local building official. If common-area lights are wired to a tenant's own electric service, you must disclose it in writing at or before the start of the tenancy, because a tenant's payment 'benefits the landlord or other tenants if the utility or service is delivered to any area other than the tenant's dwelling unit' (ORS 90.315(2)); a knowing failure lets the tenant recover twice the actual damages or one month's rent, whichever is greater (ORS 90.315(3); "Tenant-Paid Utilities That Serve Others" clause). If instead you bill tenants for common-area electricity, 'A utility or service charge that shall be assessed to a tenant for a common area must be described in the written rental agreement separately and distinctly' (ORS 90.315(4)(a); "Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause). No Oregon statute or rule limits this to new tenancies or to small buildings. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition) and the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026) for lighting rules in rental common areas found none beyond these.

title: Stoves and Refrigerators
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to supply a stove or refrigerator in an ordinary residential tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465): the essential-services remedy section 'does not require a landlord to supply a cooking appliance or a refrigerator if the landlord did not supply or agree to supply a cooking appliance or refrigerator to the tenant' (ORS 90.365(4)). Once you supply or agree to supply one, it is an essential service ('any cooking appliance or refrigerator supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord' (ORS 90.100(15)(a)(A))) and you must keep it in good repair (ORS 90.320(1)(i)), so if you intentionally or negligently fail to supply it, the tenant may use the essential-service remedies after written notice and a reasonable time and access for you to supply it (ORS 90.365(1)), unless you substantially supply it or are making a reasonable, good faith effort and the failure is beyond your control (ORS 90.365(3)); 'Rights of the tenant under this section do not arise if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant or a person on the premises with the tenant's consent' (ORS 90.365(6)) ("Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies"). List what you supply in the lease's appliance list ("Appliances & Equipment Included" clause). Where a tenant brings their own stove or refrigerator, nothing in Oregon law makes you maintain it.

title: Appliances You Don't Supply
bodyText: Oregon ties your repair duty to what you supply: you must keep in good repair 'Ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators' (ORS 90.320(1)(i)) if supplied or required to be supplied by you, and you need not supply a stove or refrigerator you did not supply or agree to supply (ORS 90.365(4)). No Oregon statute or rule presumes that an appliance left in the unit was supplied by you, and none requires the lease to list excluded appliances. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Whether an item a prior occupant left behind counts as supplied by you would be a question of fact, so the cautious course is to list what you supply in the lease's appliance list ("Appliances & Equipment Included" clause) and remove anything you will not maintain before the tenancy begins. Heating, plumbing, hot and cold water, electrical lighting and wiring, and any cooling the statute requires are your duty whatever the lease says (ORS 90.320(1)), and a lease may not limit your liability for your own negligence (ORS 90.245(1)(c); "Lease Terms Oregon Voids").

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Oregon has no rule requiring steam radiator covers or a radiator-cover lease rider (the topic comes from New York); heating must simply meet your habitability duty (ORS 90.320(1)(d)). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: No Balcony Inspection Program
bodyText: Oregon has no statewide program requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks or other exterior elevated parts of rental buildings. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Balconies are covered by your general habitability duty in an ordinary residential tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465): a unit is unhabitable if it substantially lacks 'Floors, walls, ceilings, stairways and railings maintained in good repair' (ORS 90.320(1)(h)), and buildings, grounds and appurtenances must be 'in every part safe for normal and reasonably foreseeable uses' at the start of the tenancy, with areas under your control kept that way (ORS 90.320(1)(f)). A balcony you know is unsafe should be repaired or closed before anyone uses it, and a tenant's balcony weight or storage rule can go in the lease ("Use of Property & Common Areas" clause). Some cities run their own rental inspection programs.

title: Window Guards, Bars and Bedroom Exits
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule requiring window guards or other fall-prevention devices in rentals, no window-guard lease notice, and no rule requiring landlords to fit release mechanisms to security bars (the quick-release rules for barred windows bind foster and care homes, not landlords). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. What Oregon does require bears on anything you put on a window, in an ordinary residential tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465). 'A landlord shall provide at all times during the tenancy a route or routes of exit from each bedroom and, if required, a secondary route of exit from each bedroom, for use during an emergency' (ORS 90.460(2)), conforming to the law in effect at occupancy or after a later renovation or change of use; if you fail, the tenant may recover actual damages and may end the tenancy on 72 hours' actual notice describing the problem, and if you don't cure within the 72 hours the tenant recovers twice the actual damages or twice the periodic rent, whichever is greater (ORS 90.460(3)). So bars, guards or locks must never block a bedroom window that serves as an emergency exit. The unit must also have 'latches for all windows, by which access may be had to the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.320(1)(L)). A tenant's portable air conditioner can be restricted in a window that 'is a necessary egress from the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.355(2)(b)(A); "Portable Cooling Devices" clause). Whether a building needs guards or opening limits on upper-floor windows is a question for the building codes adopted by reference.

title: Elevators and Other Building Facilities
bodyText: In an ordinary residential tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), any facility you supply must be kept in repair: a unit is unhabitable if it substantially lacks 'Ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, maintained in good repair if supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord' (ORS 90.320(1)(i)), and the tenant must 'Use in a reasonable manner all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances including elevators in the premises' (ORS 90.325(1)(e)). Elevators also fall under Oregon's elevator law, run by the Department of Consumer and Business Services. A person may not 'Permit or suffer an elevator to be operated, without a valid temporary operation authorization or current operating permit, on property that the person owns, controls, manages or supervises' (ORS 460.045(4)); the department inspects elevators periodically, or accepts a certified inspector's report filed within 30 days of the due date, and may have a noncompliant elevator disconnected from power, after reasonable notice unless continued operation would be an immediate hazard (ORS 460.125(1)(a), (3)); a business that installs, alters, repairs or maintains elevators needs an elevator contractor license and the worker an elevator license (ORS 460.045(1), (2)), and installing or altering an elevator also needs a department installation permit (ORS 460.045(3)). Elevators in private residences are exempt except for the initial installation permit and inspection (ORS 460.035(4)(j)). Pools and spas have their own rules ("Pools and Spas at Rentals"). Oregon has no product-safety or consumer-protection statute that puts a separate duty on you for facilities such as automatic garage door openers. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. List the facilities you supply in the lease ("Appliances & Equipment Included" clause).

title: No Waterbed Statute
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals: nothing requires you to allow them, sets an extra deposit or insurance for them, or prescribes how they are installed. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. So it is a lease term: the library's Oregon use-of-property clause requires your prior written consent for a waterbed or other water-filled furniture ("Use of Property & Common Areas" clause). A rule you adopt about them must meet Oregon's conditions for landlord rules (ORS 90.262; "House Rules"). Any extra charge must fit Oregon's closed list of fees (ORS 90.302; "Fees You May Charge"), and a tenant may not 'Deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or knowingly permit any person to do so' (ORS 90.325(2)(b)), but is not responsible for damage from acts of God or from a perpetrator's conduct relating to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking (ORS 90.325(3)).

title: Asbestos in Rental Buildings
bodyText: Oregon regulates asbestos work at rentals through the Department of Environmental Quality, but has no rule requiring you to tell tenants about asbestos. Before a demolition or renovation, 'the owner or operator of a demolition or renovation activity must have an accredited inspector complete a survey' (OAR 340-248-0270(1)), and keep the survey report on site during the work (OAR 340-248-0270(2)); the owner or operator includes 'a person who owns, leases, operates, controls, or supervises the facility undergoing demolition or renovation' (OAR 340-248-0010(35)). Demolition and renovation of residential buildings with four or fewer units built after January 1, 2004 are exempt from the survey (OAR 340-248-0250(1)(c)), and projects removing less than three square feet or three linear feet are exempt from the licensing, notification and survey rules if removing asbestos is not the main purpose, the work is part of a needed repair and the removal methods meet the Oregon OSHA construction asbestos standard; a project may not be split up to qualify (OAR 340-248-0250(1)(f)). By statute, 'an owner or operator of a facility containing asbestos shall require only licensed contractors to perform asbestos abatement projects' (ORS 468A.715(1)), unless your own trained and certified employees do the work (ORS 468A.715(2)). The do-it-yourself exemption is for an owner who occupies a single-unit private residence and does the work personally (OAR 340-248-0250(1)(a); ORS 468A.755(1)); and work outside a residence skips the notification rule only 'if the residence is not a rental property, a commercial business, or intended to be demolished' (OAR 340-248-0250(1)(b)). So at a rental, use licensed contractors and follow the Department's abatement notification rule (OAR 340-248-0260). For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, asbestos does not count as an 'imminent and serious threat' that lets a tenant end the tenancy on 48 hours' notice (ORS 90.365(2)), and it is not a 'minor habitability defect' the tenant may fix and deduct (ORS 90.368(1)(b)); your general habitability duty still applies (ORS 90.320(1)). No statute or rule requires an asbestos disclosure to a tenant or applicant. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Oregon OSHA adopts the federal asbestos standards by reference (OAR 437-002-0360(2); OAR 437-003-0001(25)(a)).

title: Tenant Cooperation With Pest Treatment
bodyText: Oregon has no bed-bug-specific rules on reporting, unit preparation or treatment costs, but its general tenant-duty statute requires cooperation. In an ordinary residential tenancy (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), the tenant must keep the areas under the tenant's control free from rodents and vermin 'as the condition of the premises permits and to the extent that the tenant is responsible for causing the problem' (ORS 90.325(1)(b)), and 'The tenant shall cooperate to a reasonable extent in assisting the landlord in any reasonable effort to remedy the problem' (ORS 90.325(1)(b)). Your side is the habitability duty: buildings and grounds must be free of rodents and vermin at the start of the tenancy, and areas under your control kept that way (ORS 90.320(1)(f); "Bed Bugs and Pests"). Entry for inspection or treatment follows the ordinary rule: at least 24 hours' actual notice and reasonable times, unless an emergency or the tenant's written repair request applies (ORS 90.322(1)(b)-(c), (f)); the tenant may deny a particular entry by actual notice (ORS 90.322(1)(f)), but 'A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent from the landlord to enter' (ORS 90.322(2); "Entering a Tenant's Home"). A lease term asking the tenant to report suspected pests promptly and follow reasonable preparation instructions is lawful, but the library has no Oregon pest-cooperation clause yet; if you charge a tenant for treatment, limit it to an infestation the tenant deliberately or negligently caused or knowingly permitted another person to cause (ORS 90.325(2)(b)), and never for one resulting from an act of God or from a perpetrator's conduct relating to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking (ORS 90.325(3)), and remember a fee outside Oregon's closed list is barred (ORS 90.302; "Fees You May Charge"). Pest control operators' reports of bedbug treatment sites to public health authorities are kept confidential (ORS 192.582(2)). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no bed-bug-specific tenant duty.

title: No Pesticide Notice Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule requiring you, or your pest control company, to give tenants advance notice of a pesticide application or other pest treatment at a rental. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The notice that does apply is the entry notice: to enter a unit for treatment you must give at least 24 hours' actual notice and come at a reasonable time, unless it is an emergency or the tenant asked for the work in writing (ORS 90.322(1)(b)-(c), (f); "Entering a Tenant's Home"). Pesticide notice statutes exist for other settings: schools must give written notice of proposed pesticide applications to, at a minimum, parents and guardians of minor students, adult students, administrators, faculty and staff, generally at least 24 hours ahead (ORS 634.740(1), (3)), and a homeowners association must tell an owner, on request, when it plans to apply pesticide to the owner's lot and how to opt out (ORS 94.763(2)); that right belongs to you as owner, not to your tenant. Product labels and the Department of Agriculture's applicator rules govern how a pesticide is applied, and giving tenants the product name and any re-entry or ventilation instructions with your entry notice is a sensible practice, not a legal requirement.

title: Hazardous Contamination: No General Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Apart from former illegal drug manufacturing sites, Oregon has no statute or rule requiring you to tell a tenant about hazardous-substance contamination at a rental, or to put a recorded environmental use restriction into the lease. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The drug-lab rule is a bar, not a disclosure: 'no person shall transfer, sell, use or rent any property knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe it was used as an illegal drug manufacturing site' unless it has been determined fit for use (ORS 453.867(1)), and a lease made in violation is voidable by the tenant (ORS 453.867(2); "Drug Lab Contamination"). For cleanup sites, the Department of Environmental Quality may rely on 'Institutional controls' (ORS 465.315), which its rules define as 'a legal or administrative tool or action taken to reduce the potential for exposure to hazardous substances', including use restrictions (OAR 340-122-0115(33)); no rule found requires an owner to pass those restrictions on to tenants. If a recorded restriction limits how the property may be used (for example, no digging or no well use), the cautious course is to tell tenants and adopt it as a written rule. Contamination does not change the habitability duty: the buildings and grounds must be safe and the water supply safe to drink to the extent you control it (ORS 90.320(1)(c)(D), (f)). Related rows: "Lead-Based Paint", "Drinking Water Wells (from 2027)", "Flood Plain Notice and Insurance".

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule requiring you to disclose defective (corrosive or imported) drywall to a tenant. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. A defect that affects the unit is handled under your habitability and repair duties (ORS 90.320(1); "Your Duty to Keep the Unit Habitable").

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: Oregon has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65: you need not post or give tenants a warning about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared-Meter Disclosures
bodyText: Of the three pre-lease disclosures some states require (former military ordnance sites, a pending demolition, and shared utility meters), Oregon requires only the utility one, for ordinary residential tenancies (ORS 90.100 to 90.465). Shared meters: 'The landlord shall disclose to the tenant in writing at or before the commencement of the tenancy any utility or service that the tenant pays directly to a utility or service provider that benefits, directly, the landlord or other tenants' (ORS 90.315(2)), which covers a tenant-paid meter that also serves common areas or other units; a knowing failure lets the tenant recover twice the actual damages or one month's rent, whichever is greater (ORS 90.315(3); "Tenant-Paid Utilities That Serve Others" clause). Ordnance: Oregon has no disclosure duty for former military training or ordnance sites ("Military Installations Nearby"). Demolition: Oregon has no duty to tell an applicant that you have applied to demolish the building. If you later end a month-to-month tenancy, or a fixed-term tenancy on or after the end of its term, because you intend to 'demolish the dwelling unit or convert the dwelling unit to a use other than residential use within a reasonable time' (ORS 90.427(5)(a)(A)), you must give at least 90 days' written notice stating the reason and supporting facts and, unless you have an ownership interest in four or fewer residential dwelling units subject to the chapter, pay one month's periodic rent with the notice (ORS 90.427(6); "When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause"). Some cities add relocation rules of their own. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no ordnance or pre-lease demolition disclosure.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Oregon has no statute or rule requiring you to tell a tenant about public shoreline or beach access rights, coastal erosion or tsunami zones affecting a rental. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Oregon's ocean shore is held for public use: it is state policy 'to forever preserve and maintain the sovereignty of the state heretofore legally existing over the ocean shore of the state from the Columbia River on the north to the Oregon-California line on the south so that the public may have the free and uninterrupted use thereof' (ORS 390.610(1)), and public rights in it are vested in the state (ORS 390.610(3)), so do not describe the ocean shore in front of a coastal rental as private to your tenants. The seller's disclosure form asks about damage from 'beach movements' (ORS 105.464), but that form applies to sales, not rentals. Flood-zone duties for rentals are covered in "Flood Plain Notice and Insurance".

title: Recording a Lease Is Optional in Oregon
bodyText: Oregon never requires you to record or register a residential lease, and there is no state lease registry. Recording is optional: an instrument creating 'a leasehold interest' (ORS 93.710(1)), or a memorandum of it, that is signed by the person from whom the interest passes and acknowledged like a deed 'may be indexed and recorded in the records of deeds of real property in the county where such real property is located' (ORS 93.710(1)). If you record, the recording 'constitutes notice to third persons of the rights of the parties under the instrument irrespective of whether the party granted such interest or estate is in possession of the real property' (ORS 93.710(1)). Oregon's recording act makes an unrecorded 'other agreement or memorandum thereof affecting the title of real property' 'void as against any subsequent purchaser in good faith and for a valuable consideration' who records first (ORS 93.640(1)); whether an ordinary residential lease is such an agreement, and whether a tenant's possession gives a later buyer notice anyway, are questions only case law settles. Recording changes nothing between you and your tenant: no right or duty under the residential landlord and tenant law (ORS chapter 90) depends on it. A lease for longer than one year must be in writing and signed (ORS 41.580(1)(e); ORS 93.020(1); "Written Leases and Long Terms"). For a lease of one year or less, recording is rarely worth the cost; for a long lease or one with a purchase option, the tenant may ask to record a memorandum, which must contain the items ORS 93.710(3)(a) lists. Oregon also has no statewide rental registration program for ordinary rentals ("Landlord Registration and Rental Licensing"); some cities run their own. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no statute or rule requiring a residential lease to be recorded or registered.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: Oregon has no state-published rights and responsibilities guide that you must give a tenant before signing or at renewal, and no rule requiring the tenant to sign an acknowledgment of one. For ordinary residential tenancies (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), Oregon also requires no state summary of tenant rights ("Statement of Tenant Rights"); particular notices instead carry their own required wording, each covered by its own row. The one state-prescribed rights handout is for manufactured dwelling parks and marinas: the facility landlord 'shall provide the applicant, purchaser or tenant a copy of an informational handout regarding rights of tenants and landlords when a tenant is selling a manufactured dwelling or floating home in a facility, in a form prescribed by the Housing and Community Services Department' (ORS 90.525(6)). This library does not draft for facilities. Some cities require their own handouts. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none.

title: No State Limit on Renting Homes in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: No Oregon statute limits renting a home in a single-family zone to an owner who lives on the lot, and Oregon's lot-division program for middle housing does not make you live in one of the units, set a minimum rental term or exclude housing a tenant recently occupied. State law runs the other way. Cities over 2,500 people and counties over 15,000 must allow at least one accessory dwelling unit for each detached single-unit dwelling in urban single-unit zones, and the local siting and design rules they may apply do 'not include owner-occupancy requirements of either the primary or accessory structure or requirements to construct additional off-street parking' (ORS 197A.425(1)(b)(B)). The one carve-out lets local governments regulate 'vacation occupancies, as defined in ORS 90.100, to require owner-occupancy or off-street parking' (ORS 197A.425(2)). Larger cities and counties must allow every middle housing type (duplexes through cottage clusters and townhouses) on lots zoned for residential use, and smaller cities a duplex (ORS 197A.420(2); ORS 197A.420(3)). The middle housing land division statute lists the conditions a city may impose, and a city 'May not subject an application to approval criteria except as provided in this section' (ORS 92.031(4)(c)); none of them concerns owner occupancy, renting or earlier tenants (ORS 92.031(2)-(4)). A recorded covenant that allows a single-unit dwelling but bars middle housing or an accessory dwelling unit cannot be enforced (ORS 93.277(1)). The compiled text limits this to instruments executed on or after January 1, 2021 (ORS 93.277(2)(a)), but a 2025 act in effect since July 17, 2025 says 'ORS 93.277 applies to instruments executed before, on or after January 1, 2021' (Or. Laws 2025, ch. 476, § 8); the two disagree on older covenants, so take advice before relying on either for a covenant recorded before 2021. From January 1, 2027, the protection is limited to land within an urban growth boundary, where such a covenant is void and unenforceable (ORS 93.277, version operative January 1, 2027; Or. Laws 2025, ch. 476, §§ 7a, 12). Oregon's rent-control preemption reaches only an ordinance 'which controls the rent that may be charged for the rental of any dwelling unit' (ORS 91.225(2); "Local Rent Control Is Preempted"); it says nothing about who may rent a home. Many cities and counties have short-term rental and vacation-occupancy rules. Separately, from January 1, 2027, very large institutional real estate investors may not buy a single-family residence unless an exception applies (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 64 (HB 4128), § 2); that limits buying, not renting. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no state limit on renting homes in single-family zones.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Oregon zoning law reaches accessory dwelling units (ADUs), but not the lease itself: renting an ADU is an ordinary residential tenancy under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, with the same rules as any other dwelling unit. Cities over 2,500 people and counties over 15,000 'shall allow in areas within the urban growth boundary that are zoned for detached single-unit dwellings the development of at least one accessory dwelling unit for each detached single-unit dwelling, subject to reasonable local regulations relating to siting and design' (ORS 197A.425(1)(a)), and those regulations do 'not include owner-occupancy requirements of either the primary or accessory structure or requirements to construct additional off-street parking' (ORS 197A.425(1)(b)(B)). So a local rule there may not make you live on the lot as a condition of having, or renting, the ADU or the main house. Local governments may still regulate 'vacation occupancies, as defined in ORS 90.100, to require owner-occupancy or off-street parking' (ORS 197A.425(2)), so short-term rental of an ADU may be restricted locally; local rules are not covered here. In rural residential zones a county may, but need not, allow one ADU on a lot of at least two acres, and 'A county may not allow an accessory dwelling unit allowed under this section to be used for vacation occupancy, as defined in ORS 90.100' (ORS 215.495(3)); the county may add its own restrictions (ORS 215.495(7)). No Oregon statute sets a minimum rental term for an ADU. If your city or county gives you a property tax exemption for a new ADU, during the exemption the unit must be 'Used as the occupant's primary residence' (ORS 307.590(3)(b)(A)) and 'Not rented out for consideration as transient lodging for any duration' (ORS 307.590(3)(b)(B)). Two tenancy rules often matter for ADUs. If the unit is on the same property as your primary residence and the property has no more than two dwelling units, after the first year of occupancy you may end a month-to-month tenancy without cause on at least 60 days' written notice (ORS 90.427(8)(a)(B); "When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause"). And the statewide rent-increase limit does not apply while 'The first certificate of occupancy for the dwelling unit was issued less than 15 years from the date of the notice of the rent increase' (ORS 90.323(5)(a); "Statewide Rent Increase Limit"); the 90-day notice rules still apply. Oregon's rent-control preemption (ORS 91.225) reaches only local rent control, not ADU rules. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no other state rule on leasing an ADU.

title: No Health-District Rental Regulations
bodyText: Oregon has no rule requiring you to give a tenant a health district's rental regulations on request, or to refer a tenant to a health district. Oregon's local public health authorities (a county, 'A health district formed under ORS 431.443' (ORS 431.003(7)(b)), or an intergovernmental entity) have no general rental-housing regulations addressed to landlords in the statutes or rules; one state health rule does reach a rental through them: when screening or other evidence shows that occupants may have elevated lead levels, or that a dwelling presents a serious risk of lead exposure, the owner must let lead investigators of the Oregon Health Authority or 'the local health department having jurisdiction' into all parts of the dwelling, if access is requested during regular working hours and the investigators show identification and credentials (OAR 333-095-0020; "No State Lead Notice Beyond the Federal Disclosure"). Your health and sanitation duties come from the habitability statute instead: at the start of the tenancy, the premises must be 'clean, sanitary and free from all accumulations of debris, filth, rubbish, garbage, rodents and vermin' (ORS 90.320(1)(f)), along with the rest of the habitability list ("Your Duty to Keep the Unit Habitable"). A tenant may also turn to a city or county code enforcement office, and if a government posts the unit as unsafe to occupy, the condemned-unit rules apply ("Posted or Unlawful Units"). Some cities and counties run housing-code programs. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none.

title: No State Lead Notice Beyond the Federal Disclosure
bodyText: Oregon adds no lead notice, certificate or packet of its own to the lease. For housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet apply ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause; "Lead-Based Paint"). Oregon's lead statute describes that federal duty, which 'Requires that sellers and landlords of residential housing constructed before 1978 notify buyers and tenants of known lead-based paint hazards' (ORS 431A.350(3)(c)(A)), but adds no state form. Two other lead rules can reach you during a tenancy, neither tied to the lease. First, the Oregon Health Authority has adopted the federal renovation rules by reference, including the federal subpart on residential property renovation (OAR 333-070-0200(2)), so renovation work covered by those rules carries the federal pre-renovation information requirements; that text is federal and is not restated here. Second, if blood-lead screening or other evidence suggests occupants are exposed to lead, the Authority may inspect, and 'The owner(s) and occupant(s) of any such dwelling or premise shall allow access to authorized lead investigators of the Division or of the local health department having jurisdiction' (OAR 333-095-0020) during regular working hours; it is the Authority, not you, that 'may notify such occupants of the hazards' (OAR 333-095-0030). Lead-based paint alone does not give a tenant the 48-hour termination right, because the threat it requires 'shall not include the presence of radon, asbestos or lead-based paint' (ORS 90.365(2)), and a minor habitability defect 'Does not mean the presence of mold, radon, asbestos or lead-based paint' (ORS 90.368(1)(b)). For the certification rules on lead work, see "No Lead-Safe Building Certificate; Who Must Be Certified for Lead Work". A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no state lead notice for the lease.

title: No Lead-Safe Building Certificate; Who Must Be Certified for Lead Work
bodyText: Oregon has no lead-safe certificate to attach to a lease and no periodic lead-safe certification or registration of older rental buildings. What Oregon certifies is the firms and people who do lead work. A firm 'may not perform or offer to perform a renovation for compensation unless the firm is certified as provided under ORS 431A.355' (ORS 431A.358(2)) by the Oregon Health Authority, and 'A contractor may not perform lead-based paint renovation in this state unless the contractor is a certified lead-based paint renovation contractor' (ORS 701.510(2)) licensed by the Construction Contractors Board. Abatement, inspection and risk assessment (lead-based paint activities) need their own certifications and licence (ORS 431A.358(1); ORS 431A.358(3); ORS 701.510(1)). If you renovate your own rental yourself: under the contractor licensing law a contractor works 'for another' (ORS 701.005(5)(a)), the law exempts 'A person performing work on a property that person owns or performing work as the owner's employee, whether the property is occupied by the owner or not' (ORS 701.010(7)), and the Board's renovation rule reaches a contractor 'unless such contractor is exempt from the board's licensing requirements' (OAR 812-007-0300). So the Board's licence can be read as not reaching an owner, or the owner's employee, working on the owner's own rental (a reading, not a settled rule). The Health Authority's firm certification is a separate question: it turns on the federal definitions of a firm and of renovation, which Oregon adopts (ORS 431A.353(2); ORS 431A.353(5)). The cautious course: treat paint-disturbing renovation, repair or painting in a rental built before 1978 as work for a certified firm with a certified renovator, whether you do it yourself or hire it out. If you knowingly hire an uncertified firm where certification is required, the Authority may order you to get a risk assessment and abate or control the hazards it finds (ORS 431A.363(3)); a person who violates the certification law or its rules, or fails to obey such an order, faces civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation per day (ORS 431A.363(1)), and if you do not comply on time the Authority may do the work and charge you its costs (ORS 431A.363(4)-(5)). See "Lead-Based Paint" and "No State Lead Notice Beyond the Federal Disclosure". The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no lead-safe certification of rental buildings.

title: No Code Variance Notice to Tenants
bodyText: Oregon has no state health or sanitary code for ordinary rentals under which a landlord gets a variance, and no rule requiring you to give tenants, or attach to the rental agreement, a notice of any variance, exception or waiver. Oregon's habitability standards are in the landlord-tenant act itself (ORS 90.320(1); "Your Duty to Keep the Unit Habitable"), and they can't be waived: a rental agreement 'may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with ORS 90.320 (1) or 90.730' (ORS 90.250). The state building code has its own waiver and modification procedures (for example, the accessibility appeals process in ORS 447.250), but none of them requires a notice to tenants. Cities with their own housing codes may grant variances under local rules. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: Oregon has no rule requiring you to tell a tenant whether a certificate of occupancy is required or valid for the unit, or to give the tenant a copy, and no rule barring rent for a period the unit is occupied without one. A certificate of occupancy matters in the tenancy law in one place: the statewide rent-increase limit does not apply if 'The first certificate of occupancy for the dwelling unit was issued less than 15 years from the date of the notice of the rent increase' (ORS 90.323(5)(a)). If you rely on that exemption to raise rent above the limit, your rent-increase notice must state the 'Facts supporting the exemption authorized by subsection (5) of this section, if the increase is above the amount allowed in subsection (2)(d) of this section' (ORS 90.323(3)(c)), so say when the first certificate of occupancy was issued ("Statewide Rent Increase Limit"). If a government posts a unit as unsafe or unlawful to occupy, the condemned-unit rules apply instead ("Posted or Unlawful Units"). Cities and counties issue certificates of occupancy under the state building code and may run rental licensing programs. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no certificate-of-occupancy disclosure.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice or Placement Rule
bodyText: Oregon has no single-family occupancy notice, no rule presuming that a tenant lacks lawful occupancy unless the rental agreement is notarized or signed by a licensed agent, and no font-size or first-page placement rule for lease disclosures. Oregon sets no type-size or readability standard for residential leases at all ("Plain Language and Type Size"). A tenant's right to occupy rests on the rental agreement, written or oral, and an eviction runs through the court process for possession (ORS 105.100 to 105.168), not through a presumption from how the lease was signed. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: Disclosing Condemnation and Code Orders
bodyText: Oregon's disclosure rule for inspection and condemnation orders is in the condemned-units statute ("Posted or Unlawful Units"). If an agency has posted the unit as unsafe and unlawful to occupy, you may not continue or start a tenancy until you correct the conditions (ORS 90.380(2)(a)). If an agency has given you written notice that the unit is unlawful, but not unsafe, to occupy, you may not start a new tenancy until you correct the conditions; you avoid liability to the new tenant for breaking that rule only 'if, prior to the commencement of the tenancy, the landlord discloses to the tenant that the dwelling unit has been determined to be unlawful to occupy' (ORS 90.380(3)(c)). That disclosure 'must be in writing, include a description of the conditions that led to the agency's determination and state that the landlord is obligated to correct the conditions before entering into a new tenancy' (ORS 90.380(3)(d)), with a copy of the agency's notice attached, and it does not excuse the agency's penalties or your habitability duties (ORS 90.380(3)(e)). You may not take a deposit to secure a rental agreement for a posted or noticed unit without first making that disclosure to the applicant (ORS 90.380(4)(a)). The library offers no clause for the disclosure. No other Oregon statute or rule requires you to disclose open inspection or code-enforcement orders to tenants. In a city of more than 300,000 people, the code official must notify you in writing when your premises may cause tenant relocation, and you may not terminate a rental agreement because you received that notice except for the reasons in ORS 90.385(4) (ORS 90.465(3)-(4)). Manufactured dwelling parks and marinas have their own rule, which this library does not draft for: a landlord required to close the park or marina by eminent domain or agency order must notify tenants in writing 'no later than 15 days after the landlord receives notice of the exercise of eminent domain or of the agency order' (ORS 90.645(9); ORS 90.671(7)). The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no other disclosure duty.

title: No Special District Statement in the Lease
bodyText: Oregon has no rule requiring a lease to state that the property lies in a special district, economic improvement district, enterprise zone or urban renewal area, or that the tenant knows of and will comply with district laws, charges or plans. Oregon's special districts (such as water, sanitary, fire and park districts listed in ORS 198.010) and its urban renewal and economic improvement districts levy taxes and assessments on the property, not on tenants, and their statutes set no statement for residential leases. If you want a tenant to bear such a cost, build it into the rent: Oregon's fee statute says a landlord 'may not require the payment of any fee except as provided in this section' (ORS 90.302(1); "Fees You May Charge"), and it has no category for district taxes or assessments. A 'public service charge' (ORS 90.315(1)(b)(A)), meaning a charge imposed on you by a utility or service provider or by a local government for municipal services and public resources such as street maintenance, transit, public safety or parks, but not real property taxes, income taxes, business license fees or dwelling inspection fees (ORS 90.315(1)(a), (1)(b)), is the exception: outside manufactured dwelling and floating home facility tenancies, if the written rental agreement so provides, you may pass through such a charge billed to you for a public service to the tenant's unit or to a common area available to the tenant, under the utility-billing rules, and it is then not rent or a fee (ORS 90.315(4)(a), (4)(e); "Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause); for a month-to-month tenancy, a charge adopted in the previous six months needs 60 days' written notice before you amend the agreement to add it (ORS 90.315(4)(d)(A)). Pending special assessments are a question on the seller's property disclosure statement for sales (ORS 105.464), not on a lease. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: Duties That Depend on How Many Units You Own
bodyText: Oregon tiers a few landlord duties by how many units you own or how many are on the property; read each limb of a threshold together (both must be met where the statute says 'and'). By units you own: when you end a tenancy after the first year for one of the landlord reasons (demolition, renovation, owner or family move-in, sale to an owner-occupant), you must pay the tenant one month's rent, but the payment rules 'do not apply to a landlord who has an ownership interest in four or fewer residential dwelling units subject to this chapter' (ORS 90.427(6)(b); "When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause"). By the property: the foreclosure disclosure applies to 'premises containing no more than four dwelling units' (ORS 90.310(1); "Disclosure of Pending Foreclosure or Forfeiture" clause); the recycling duty to a landlord 'who has five or more residential dwelling units on a single premises' in a city with multifamily recycling service (ORS 90.318(1); "Recycling Notice" clause); and if the unit is on the same property as your primary residence 'and the building or the property contains not more than two dwelling units', you may end a month-to-month tenancy after the first year without cause on 60 days' notice (ORS 90.427(8); "Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit"). Fair housing: Oregon has no counterpart to the federal exemptions for an owner of three or fewer single-family houses or an owner-occupied building of up to four units (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)); the only Oregon small-owner exemption reaches the renting of space within a single-family residence that the owner 'actually maintains and occupies' as the owner's primary residence where all occupants share some common space, and only for sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and familial status (ORS 659A.421(8); "Oregon Fair Housing Classes"). Construction liens: the notice of right to a lien that protects owners is not needed from someone who supplies labor, labor and material, or rented equipment for a 'commercial improvement', and only an owner-occupied building of up to four units counts as a 'Residential building' (ORS 87.021(3)(b)); so on a rental you don't live in, the statute can be read as letting a lien arise without that advance notice. Buying homes: from January 1, 2027, an institutional real estate investor (one owning 2,500 or more single-family residences that pools investor funds and manages $1 billion or more) may not buy a single-family residence unless an exception applies, such as one that 'Is occupied by a tenant as defined in ORS 90.100' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 64, § 2(1)(c)), or one listed for sale for at least 90 consecutive days, with a notarized disclosure to the seller and the Department of Justice (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 64 (HB 4128), §§ 1-2). The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no other duty tiered by the number of units a landlord owns.

title: Student Housing and the Landlord-Tenant Act
bodyText: Oregon's landlord-tenant law treats student housing as an exclusion question, not a separate set of duties. The act does not govern 'Residence at an institution, public or private, if incidental to detention or the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar service, but not including residence in off-campus nondormitory housing' (ORS 90.110(1)), nor 'Occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in the portion of a structure operated for the benefit of the organization' (ORS 90.110(3)), unless the arrangement was 'created to avoid the application of this chapter' (ORS 90.110). So a dormitory a school provides as part of its educational service falls outside the act, but off-campus housing that is not a dormitory stays inside it. If you privately own or manage apartments rented to students, you are an ordinary landlord: the rent-increase limit, the for-cause rules after the first year of occupancy and every other rule of ORS 90.100 to 90.465 apply as for any tenant ("Who the Landlord-Tenant Act Covers"). Whether a privately owned building that a school master-leases and runs as a dormitory is 'Residence at an institution' (ORS 90.110(1)) is not settled by statute; case law would decide it, so the cautious course is to treat its occupants as tenants. Oregon sets no student-specific lease terms, deposits or notices; a school that provides student housing has its own duties (for example, giving new students vaccine information, ORS 433.281), which do not bind private landlords. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no other student-housing rule for landlords.

title: No Work Card for Senior Housing Staff; Housing for Older Persons
bodyText: Oregon has no work card or state background-check requirement for staff of 55-or-older or 62-or-older housing. Oregon's age-restricted housing law is a fair housing exemption: Oregon's ban on familial status discrimination 'does not apply to familial status distinction, discrimination or restriction with respect to housing for older persons' (ORS 659A.421(7)(a)), which means housing provided under a state or federal elderly program, housing 'Intended for, and solely occupied by, persons 62 years of age or older' (ORS 659A.421(7)(b)(B)), or housing intended for at least one person 55 or older per unit where at least 80 percent of the dwellings are so occupied and the owner or manager publishes and follows policies showing that intent (ORS 659A.421(7)(b)(C)). The federal Fair Housing Act has the same exemption, with HUD's verification rules for 55-or-older housing (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b)(2)). The exemption covers familial status only; every other protected class still applies. Housing for older persons is also outside the rule that lets tenants run a family child care home (ORS 90.358(7)). State background checks apply to licensed care settings (such as adult foster homes and room and board facilities), not to ordinary senior apartments. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no work card rule.

title: Housing an Employee
bodyText: If you house an employee whose right to live there depends on the job, Oregon's landlord-tenant act does not govern the arrangement: it excludes 'Occupancy by an employee of a landlord whose right to occupancy is conditional upon employment in and about the premises' (ORS 90.110(7)), unless the arrangement was 'created to avoid the application of this chapter' (ORS 90.110). Such an employee 'may only be evicted pursuant to ORS 105.100 to 105.168' (ORS 91.120) after at least 24 hours' written notice of the termination of employment or 'a notice period set forth in a written employment contract, whichever is longer' (ORS 91.120), and that rule 'does not create the relationship of landlord and tenant' (ORS 91.120). So you must still go to court for possession; you may not lock the employee out. Oregon requires no signed disclosure of occupancy and vacating conditions and no offer of a rental agreement when the job ends, but put the housing terms, including any longer notice period you agree to, in a written employment agreement, because ORS 91.120 reads the notice period from it. If the employee instead rents under a rental agreement whose occupancy does not depend on the job (for example, an ordinary tenant who also works for you), the employee is a tenant and every rule of ORS 90.100 to 90.465 applies; whether an arrangement is 'conditional upon employment' (ORS 90.110(7)) is a question of fact. Any housing you own, rent or control and an employee occupies is also subject to the employer-housing access rules: you may not restrict access by government officials, health and service providers or invited guests (ORS 659A.253(1)), house rules on use and occupancy bind them only if reasonable and posted at least three days before enforcement (ORS 659A.256), and you may not evict an employee for complaining or for inviting such visitors (ORS 659A.259(1)). Housing provided to farm or reforestation workers can be a farmworker camp with its own registration, posting and operator rules (ORS 658.705 to 658.850), which this library does not draft for. The same 24-hour rule applies when a tenant's own live-in employee must leave (ORS 91.122). Oregon has no rule on filing a rent agreement for a sponsored or guest worker. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no other employee-housing rule.

title: No Duty to Disclose Nearby Sex Offenders
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to tell a tenant or applicant that a registered sex offender lives on or near the property, or to point tenants to the registry. Oregon's real property statute lists among the 'incidents that are not material facts to a real property transaction' (ORS 93.275(1)) 'The fact or suspicion that a sex offender registered under' (ORS 93.275(1)(d)) Oregon's registration statutes 'resides in the area' (ORS 93.275(1)(d)). A lease can be read as a real property transaction, and on that reading the presence of a nearby registrant is not a fact you must disclose (the statute does not define the term). The same list covers a death or crime on the property and an occupant's blood-borne infection (ORS 93.275(1)(a)-(c)), and you may not disclose that 'an occupant or owner of the real property has or died from a blood-borne infection' (ORS 659A.145(10)). For screening and the facility rule on level three offenders, see "Registered Sex Offenders". The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no disclosure duty.

title: Program Inspections in Subsidized and Voucher Tenancies
bodyText: Oregon has no special rule for subsidized housing when a tenant refuses a program inspection, and no rule letting you refuse a voucher or subsidized tenancy because of the program's inspection. The general access rules apply. 'A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent from the landlord to enter' (ORS 90.322(2)), and you may enter to inspect on at least 24 hours' notice at reasonable times ("Entering a Tenant's Home"). 'If the tenant refuses to allow lawful access, the landlord may obtain injunctive relief to compel access or may terminate the rental agreement under ORS 90.392' (ORS 90.322(7)), with the tenant's usual right to cure a for-cause notice, and may recover actual damages. If a government agency requires you to enter and you can't after a good-faith effort that follows the access rules, 'the landlord may not be found in violation of any state statute or local ordinance due to the failure' (ORS 90.322(6)). On the program side, Oregon tells housing authorities to facilitate landlord participation by 'Ensuring timely inspection of dwelling units and prompt processing of tenant applications and tenant-based assistance payments to landlords' (ORS 456.390(3)(a)), and federal rules make the housing authority, not you, inspect a voucher unit before the lease term and at least every two years (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.405(a)-(b)). Refusing an applicant because the applicant uses a voucher or other housing assistance is source-of-income discrimination (ORS 659A.421(1)(d); ORS 659A.421(2)(a); "Source of Income"). Oregon's statute does not say whether refusing because of the inspection requirement itself is refusing because of source of income; the cautious course is not to refuse or delay a voucher tenancy over the inspection. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no subsidized-inspection rule.

title: No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Oregon has no state fact sheet on pets and eviction, and no rule requiring you to give a tenant with a dog or cat any pet information sheet with the lease. Two pet rules touch eviction instead. If a tenant keeps a pet the rental agreement doesn't allow and the pet is 'capable of causing damage to persons or property' (ORS 90.405(1)), you may give a written notice that the tenancy ends on a date at least 10 days later unless the tenant removes the pet (ORS 90.405(1); "Pets" clause). And if a tenant leaves pets behind as abandoned property, you may 'Allow an animal control agency to remove any abandoned pets or livestock' (ORS 90.425(7)(b)(B)); if the agency won't, 'the landlord shall exercise reasonable care for the animals given all the circumstances' (ORS 90.425(7)(b)(B)) and may give them to an organization willing and able to care for them, such as a humane society. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: No Plain-Language Statement for Leases
bodyText: Oregon has no plain-language statute for residential leases: no readability test, no required statement of consumer restrictions listing the tenant's waivers, and no state preapproval of lease forms ("Plain Language and Type Size"). Oregon does have a voluntary plain-language review for consumer contracts: a seller or extender of credit may submit a consumer contract to the Department of Justice, which certifies it if it meets standards such as using 'words that convey meanings clearly and directly' (ORS 180.545(1)(a)), and the contract may then say 'The form of this contract meets Oregon plain language guidelines' (ORS 180.550). That program covers written contracts 'to the value of $50,000' (ORS 180.540(3)) involving real estate, goods or services as the unlawful trade practices law defines them, and that definition says '“Real estate” does not cover conduct covered by ORS chapter 90' (ORS 646.605(6)(b)(A)). So a residential rental agreement governed by ORS chapter 90 can be read as falling outside it. Even where it applies, certification 'is not an approval of the contract's legality or legal effect' (ORS 180.555(2)), and you may not claim your contract meets Oregon's plain-language guidelines unless the Department has certified it (OAR 137-020-0100(5)). Nothing in Oregon law requires the lease to list the rights a tenant gives up; instead, a lease term waiving a tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant act is barred and unenforceable (ORS 90.245(1)-(2); "Lease Terms Oregon Voids"). The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain no other plain-language rule for leases.

title: No Minimum Type Size for Leases
bodyText: Oregon sets no minimum type size for a printed residential lease, and no rule keeps a small-print lease out of evidence ("Plain Language and Type Size"). Type-size rules in Oregon law apply to other documents, such as certain consumer credit and condominium disclosures, not to leases. Make the lease readable anyway: a court can refuse to enforce an unconscionable term ("Unconscionable Lease Terms"), and a lease of more than one year must be in writing and signed (ORS 41.580(1)(e); "Written Leases and Long Terms"). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: Association Documents and Condominium Leases
bodyText: Oregon does not require a lease of a condominium unit or a planned-community home to disclose the association's obligations or documents to the tenant, to carry an owner's or tenant's statement that it knows the association documents, or to be copied to the association's board. Whether association rules bind your tenant depends on the governing documents ("Condominium and HOA Rules"; "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause). Two Oregon rules still matter. First, if you want the tenant to pay association assessments, you must set out 'the assessment requirement in the written rental agreement at the commencement of the tenancy' (ORS 90.302(7)(f)(C)) and give the tenant a copy of the assessment 'before or at the time the landlord charges the tenant' (ORS 90.302(7)(f)(D)), along with the statute's other conditions. Second, a long lease from a condominium developer is treated as a sale: in the condominium act a sale by a developer includes 'a lessee's interest in a unit for more than three years or less than three years if the interest may be renewed under the terms of the lease for a total period of more than three years' (ORS 100.005(32)), and a developer must give a purchaser the condominium disclosure statement (ORS 100.705(2)) and copies of the declaration and bylaws (ORS 100.725(1)). A developer is the declarant or a person that acquires an interest from one 'for the primary purpose of resale' (ORS 100.005(15)), so an owner who simply rents out a unit is not covered; if you are a developer leasing a unit for more than three years, follow the developer sale rules and take advice. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found no other association disclosure duty for leases.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: Oregon has no counterpart to California's Tenant Protection Act lease notice; Oregon's rent-increase limit and for-cause rules apply without any lease notice ("Statewide Rent Increase Limit"; "When You May End a Tenancy Without Cause"). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Exemption Notice
bodyText: Oregon has no counterpart to California's Tenant Protection Act exemption notice; the only exemption statement Oregon requires is in a rent-increase notice above the limit, which must state the 'Facts supporting the exemption authorized by subsection (5) of this section' (ORS 90.323(3)(c); "Statewide Rent Increase Limit"); for a month-to-month tenancy of a manufactured dwelling or floating home facility space, the notice must state the facts supporting the ORS 90.600(3) exemption instead (ORS 90.600(2)(c)). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: No Sunset on Oregon's Rent and Eviction Limits
bodyText: Oregon has no counterpart to the California Tenant Protection Act's sunset; Oregon's rent-increase limit and for-cause rules carry no repeal date (ORS 90.323; ORS 90.324; ORS 90.427; "Statewide Rent Increase Limit"). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

title: No Communal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: Oregon has no counterpart to the territorial rules requiring government approval of a lease of communal or native-owned land; no Oregon statute or rule requires a state officer to approve, or voids, a residential lease of land held by a tribe, and leases of land held in trust for a tribe may be subject to federal rules. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none.

title: Caring for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText: Oregon gives you no special right to enter a rental to feed, check on or remove a tenant's animal while the tenancy lasts, and no rule that makes you an animal's owner after you feed or shelter it for a set number of days. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain neither. During a tenancy under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, the general entry rule applies ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause, "Entering a Tenant's Home"): you give at least 24 hours' actual notice and enter only at reasonable times, and you may not enter if the tenant, after receiving the notice, denies consent, unless another limb applies, and 'A landlord has no other right of access except' (ORS 90.322(5)) by court order, during an absence of the tenant of more than seven days, or after abandonment or relinquishment. In an emergency you may enter 'without consent of the tenant, without notice to the tenant and at any time' (ORS 90.322(1)(b)). The statute's example is a repair problem, but '“Emergency” includes but is not limited to' (ORS 90.322(1)(b)) that example, so an animal in real distress may be an emergency. If you enter in the tenant's absence, give the tenant actual notice within 24 hours of the fact, date and time of the entry, the nature of the emergency and the names of the persons who entered (ORS 90.322(1)(b)). During any absence of the tenant of more than seven days, you 'may enter the dwelling unit at times reasonably necessary' (ORS 90.410(2)). Otherwise, reach the tenant and get agreement to that specific entry (ORS 90.322(1)(f)), or call animal control or the police: where there is probable cause of neglect or abandonment, a peace officer, 'after obtaining a search warrant or in any other manner authorized by law, may enter the premises or motor vehicle where the animal is located to provide the animal with food, water and emergency medical treatment and may impound the animal' (ORS 167.345(2)).
