After the tenancy ends, a pet left behind is governed by ORS 90.425 ("Property Left Behind After a Tenancy"), which applies to ordinary and facility tenancies alike, once one of its triggers is met: for example, the tenancy has ended and you reasonably believe the tenant left the property with no intention of claiming it, or you received possession from the sheriff (ORS 90.425(2)). After giving the written notice, you must store the tenant's property with reasonable care, except that you may 'Allow an animal control agency to remove any abandoned pets or livestock' (ORS 90.425(7)(b)(B)). 'If an animal control agency will not remove the abandoned pets or livestock, the landlord shall exercise reasonable care for the animals given all the circumstances, including the type and condition of the animals' (ORS 90.425(7)(b)(B)), and you may give them 'to an agency that is willing and able to care for the animals, such as a humane society or similar organization' (ORS 90.425(7)(b)(B)). Oregon's cruelty laws turn on custody, not a day count: animal neglect is failing 'to provide minimum care for an animal in such person’s custody or control' (ORS 167.325(1)(a)), and animal abandonment is leaving 'a domestic animal or an equine at a location without providing minimum care' (ORS 167.340(1)). So once you take a tenant's animal into your care, give it food, water and shelter until animal control or a shelter takes it. For rabies control only, an 'Owner' includes a person 'who harbors an animal or who has it in the care of the person' (ORS 433.340(2)). For the dog-control laws, a 'Keeper' is 'a person who owns, possesses, controls or otherwise has charge of a dog' (ORS 609.035(5)), and where a county or city dog control program applies, a keeper of a dog that has its permanent canine teeth or is six months old must license it 'within 30 days after the person becomes keeper of the dog' (ORS 609.100(1)). The library offers no lease clause letting you or a caretaker the tenant names into the unit to care for an animal, because a standing right of that kind would add an access right that ORS 90.322(5) does not give. ORS 90.322 does not cover a space in a manufactured dwelling park or marina (ORS 90.322(3)); those tenancies have their own rules.

title: No Oregon Rule on Guests Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText: No Oregon statute or rule lets a tenant take in people displaced by a wildfire, flood or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy terms, and none limits how you apply those terms to displaced guests. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. So for a tenancy under ORS 90.100 to 90.465 your ordinary guest terms ("Guest Policy" clause, "Guest Policy (14-Day Limit)" clause) and occupancy rules ("Occupancy Limits") apply in a disaster as at any other time. A guest is not a tenant: 'Tenant' 'Does not mean a guest or temporary occupant' (ORS 90.100(51)(c)). If you want to let a displaced person stay longer without making them a tenant, Oregon's tool is a temporary occupancy agreement: 'the landlord, tenant and proposed temporary occupant must enter into a written temporary occupancy agreement that describes the temporary occupancy relationship' (ORS 90.275(1)). You may screen the person for conduct or a criminal record, but you 'may not screen the proposed temporary occupant for credit history or income level' (ORS 90.275(5)); the tenant may end the arrangement at any time, and you only for a material violation (ORS 90.275(3)) ("Temporary Occupancy Agreements"). Oregon's 2026 disaster rule deals with the tenant's own tenancy when a natural disaster destroys the unit or makes it inaccessible, not with guests (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 108, § 21, added to ORS 90.100 to 90.465 and effective June 5, 2026, compiled number pending; "Tenancies After a Natural Disaster"). Check any local emergency order before acting on a guest violation during a declared emergency.

title: Emergency Contacts and Tenant Confidentiality
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to collect an emergency contact from a tenant or to give tenants an emergency or after-hours number. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. What you must give the tenant in writing at or before the start of the tenancy is the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent for service of process and notices (ORS 90.305(1); "Manager and Owner Disclosure" clause), kept current (ORS 90.305(2)). No statute requires the lease to carry a management website or a social-services hotline; the help notice Oregon does require goes with a nonpayment termination notice or summons, not the lease: 'A landlord shall deliver a copy of the notice posted on the website of the Judicial Department under ORS 105.136' (ORS 90.395(2)). If you do ask for an emergency contact, handle it under Oregon's confidential-information law (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61, § 2, effective June 5, 2026, added to ORS chapter 90, compiled number pending; "Keeping Tenants' Information Confidential"). 'A landlord may not make a disclosure of confidential information relating to a tenant' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61), former tenant, applicant or household member, and the protected list includes a 'Phone number' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61), an 'Electronic mail address' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61) and 'Medical records or records related to disability' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61). The exceptions include disclosure 'With the separate written consent of the individual' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61) and 'As necessary to share a phone number or electronic email address for repair, maintenance or utilities or services as defined in ORS 90.315 (1)' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61). A knowing violation lets the individual recover 'an amount equal to twice the monthly rent of the tenancy or prospective tenancy' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61). Collecting a contact's name and number is not a disclosure, but telling the contact about the tenant (for example a hospitalization) or passing on the tenant's number or e-mail may be. The cautious course is a short signed form, separate from the lease, in which the tenant names the contact and says what you may tell that person and when (the act requires the consent to be separate, so a lease clause cannot supply it). Whether the contact's own phone number is information 'relating to a tenant' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61) is not settled, so treat it as confidential too. For the narrower case of a sole tenant's death, the lease can name the person you should contact, because Oregon gives rights in the tenant's abandoned property to 'Any person designated in writing by the tenant to be contacted by the landlord in the event of the tenant’s death' (ORS 90.425(21)(a)(C)) ("Contact Person if Tenant Dies" clause).

title: No Oregon Duty to Screen Rental Staff
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to run background checks on your maintenance staff, on-site managers or other employees, including those with keys or access to units, and sets no rule on whom you may employ in apartment work. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. If you choose to screen, Oregon's general employment rule applies to you as an employer: 'It is an unlawful practice for an employer to exclude an applicant from an initial interview solely because of a past criminal conviction' (ORS 659A.360(1)), which includes requiring an applicant to disclose a conviction on the application or before the initial interview (ORS 659A.360(2)), though 'nothing in this section prevents an employer from considering an applicant’s conviction history when making a hiring decision' (ORS 659A.360(3)). A separate rule covers licensed property managers, not your employees: 'An applicant for a property manager license must submit to a background check, except an applicant who is currently licensed as a real estate broker or principal real estate broker or who is eligible for renewal of such licenses' (OAR 863-024-0015(1)), which 'includes a criminal background check' with fingerprints (OAR 863-024-0015(2)), and the license 'may be granted only to an individual who is trustworthy and competent to conduct professional real estate activity in a manner that protects the public interest' (ORS 696.022(6)(a)). Screening is still sensible risk management for anyone who will hold keys, and every entry your staff make must follow the entry rules ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause, "Entering a Tenant's Home"); the lease key terms are in "Keys" clause. Federal consumer-reporting rules apply if you use a screening company's report to make a hiring decision; they are not covered here.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging Requirements in Oregon
bodyText: For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465 (not manufactured dwelling park or marina spaces, ORS 90.462(11)), Oregon's tenant charging rule is ORS 90.462, summarized in "Electric Vehicle Charging": 'A tenant may submit an application to install an electric vehicle charging station for the personal, noncommercial use of the tenant' (ORS 90.462(1)), and you 'may prohibit installation or use of a charging station installed and used in compliance with this section only if the premises do not have at least one parking space per dwelling unit' (ORS 90.462(2)). You must approve a completed application 'within 60 days after the tenant submits the application unless the delay in approving the application is based on a reasonable request for additional information' (ORS 90.462(3)); you may require an application, your architectural standards, reasonable review and permitting charges and reasonable restrictions that do not significantly raise the cost or cut the performance of the station (ORS 90.462(4)). The station must be installed and removed by at least a licensed journeyman electrician (ORS 90.462(5)); a hard-wired pedestal station must be 'a certified electrical product' (ORS 90.462(9)), and the owner of any other station that is not one must keep renter's liability insurance of at least $100,000 covering it and name you as an additional insured (ORS 90.462(10)). The tenant pays installation, electricity and damage from the station (ORS 90.462(6)). New buildings: the state building code must require newly constructed multifamily buildings with five or more dwelling units (and commercial and mixed-use buildings) to include 'provisions for electrical service capacity at no less than 20 percent of the vehicle parking spaces in the garage or parking area for the building' (ORS 455.417(2)); townhouses are excluded (ORS 455.417(3)(b)). The code rule took effect July 1, 2022 (OAR 918-460-0200), and cities within a metropolitan area must require capacity 'to serve 40 percent of all vehicle parking spaces' (OAR 660-012-0410(3)) for new buildings of five or more units. Selling charging to tenants: Oregon has no tax on electricity sold through a charger and no weights-and-measures registration for chargers. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. The device-license requirement covers only instruments 'specified in ORS 618.141' (ORS 618.121), a list of scales and fuel meters with no electricity category, although the general definition of 'Weights and measures' (ORS 618.010) excludes only 'meters for the measurement of electricity, gas or water when operated in a system of a public utility' (ORS 618.010), so ask the State Department of Agriculture before billing by the kilowatt-hour. You do not become a public utility by charging vehicles: 'public utility' does not include a person 'that furnishes natural gas, electricity, ethanol, methanol, methane, biodiesel or other alternative fuel to any number of customers for use in motor vehicles and does not furnish any utility service described in paragraph (a) of this subsection' (ORS 757.005). Oregon's cash-acceptance law 'does not apply to' (ORS 659A.410) 'Electric vehicle charging stations' (ORS 659A.410). Separately, from June 5, 2026, 'A landlord shall allow a tenant to make payments by check or other commercially reasonable methods' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 3(1)) and 'may not require a tenant to make payments by debit card, credit card, electronic check, tenant portal or any other form of electronic payment' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 3, added to ORS chapter 90, compiled number pending), so if you bill tenants for charging, offer a nonelectronic way to pay (whether the rule reaches a pay-at-the-charger sale is not settled). A separate rule, ORS 91.265, covers commercial tenants, not residential ones.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging in Shared Parking
bodyText: Oregon's tenant charging right is tied to the tenant's own space: a tenant may apply to install a station 'in, or near, a parking space assigned to the tenant or the dwelling unit of the tenant' (ORS 90.462(1)), for 'the personal, noncommercial use of the tenant' (ORS 90.462(1)). You may refuse only where 'the premises do not have at least one parking space per dwelling unit' (ORS 90.462(2)); otherwise you may set reasonable restrictions on installation and use that do not 'Significantly increase the cost of the charging station' (ORS 90.462(4)(d)(A)) or 'Significantly decrease the efficiency or performance of the charging station' (ORS 90.462(4)(d)(B)), and require your architectural standards (ORS 90.462(4)(b)). If the combined charging load needs new electrical capacity, 'the landlord may assess the cost of the additional improvements to each tenant that has installed, or will install, a charging station' (ORS 90.462(7)). The rest of the rule is in "Electric Vehicle Charging". ORS 90.462 says nothing more about unassigned or common parking than its 'or the dwelling unit of the tenant' limb (ORS 90.462(1)), which can be read as letting a tenant without an assigned space apply for a station near the tenant's unit; Oregon has no statute or rule on chargers you provide for shared use by residents (access, scheduling, fees or allocation). The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. Those are matters for your rules, which must meet ORS 90.262 ("House Rules"), and any charging fee must fit Oregon's closed fee list or be priced as a utility or service charge ("Fees You May Charge"). Condominium owners and planned-community lots have their own charger rules (ORS 100.627; ORS 94.762), and ORS 90.462 does not apply to manufactured dwelling park or marina spaces (ORS 90.462(11)).

title: A Tenant's Charging Station When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: Under ORS 90.462 (tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465; not facility spaces, ORS 90.462(11)), a tenant's charging station belongs to the tenant: 'Unless a landlord and tenant negotiate a different outcome, a charging station installed under this section is deemed to be the personal property of the tenant' (ORS 90.462(8)). It 'must be installed and removed by a person that holds a license' (ORS 90.462(5)) as at least a journeyman electrician, and the tenant pays 'The cost of damage to the premises that results from the installation, use, maintenance, repair, removal or replacement of the charging station' (ORS 90.462(6)(b)). Oregon has no residential rule letting you require removal, capped wiring or restoration when the tenancy ends. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. Compare the commercial rule, where 'Upon termination of the rental agreement, the landlord may require the tenant to' (ORS 91.265(7)(c)) remove the station, cap wires and conduit and restore the premises; ORS 90.462 has no such term. A station the tenant leaves behind after the tenancy ends can be read as the tenant's personal property, so handle it under the abandoned-property procedure (ORS 90.425; "Property Left Behind After a Tenancy") rather than keeping it. Because the statute lets you 'negotiate a different outcome' (ORS 90.462(8)), you may agree in writing that the station stays and becomes yours, or that the tenant removes it on leaving; the library offers no clause for that, because the terms (price, transfer, removal and who pays) depend on the deal, so take advice before writing your own. The rest of the rule is in "Electric Vehicle Charging".

title: Hunting and Fishing on Leased Farmland
bodyText: Oregon has no statute that gives a tenant of rented farmland hunting or fishing rights, or that keeps those rights with the owner unless the lease grants them in writing; who may hunt on the land is a matter for your lease. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. Oregon's hunting-trespass law lets a tenant in possession give permission: 'No person shall hunt upon the cultivated or enclosed land of another without first obtaining permission from the owner or lawful occupant thereof, or the agent of such owner or occupant' (ORS 498.120(1)), and 'No prosecution shall be commenced under this section except upon written complaint filed with a magistrate' (ORS 498.120(1)). So if you lease out farmland and want to keep or control hunting, say so in the lease, because the statute can be read as letting your tenant, as lawful occupant, permit it otherwise. One wildlife rule does keep a hunting privilege with the owner: landowner preference tags for deer, elk and pronghorn go only to a 'Landowner', defined as a person or entity that 'holds title in trust or in fee simple to 40 or more contiguous acres of land' (OAR 635-045-0002(42)), who names the tag recipients (OAR 635-075-0005(2)), so a farm tenant cannot register for them. If either of you lets the public hunt or fish on the land free of charge, Oregon's recreational-use law limits liability, and it treats 'a tenant, a lessee, an occupant' (ORS 105.672(4)(a)) as an owner: an owner who permits recreational use 'is not liable in contract or tort for any personal injury, death or property damage that arises out of the use of the land for recreational purposes' (ORS 105.682(1)), except for intentional injury (ORS 105.682(2)) and subject to the charge rules in ORS 105.688. A lease of farmland is not a residential tenancy under ORS 90.100 to 90.465 except as to any dwelling unit rented with it, so ORS chapter 90 can be read as not governing the hunting terms.

title: Renting Furnished in Oregon
bodyText:
Oregon has no statute or rule for furnished rentals: nothing requires an inventory or condition statement for furniture, a separate furniture deposit, or a duty to supply or repair furniture. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

The general rules apply. The tenant may not 'Deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or knowingly permit any person to do so' (ORS 90.325(2)(b)), but 'A tenant is not responsible for damage that results from' (ORS 90.325(3)) acts of God or a perpetrator's conduct relating to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking. The deposit may be used 'To repair damages to the premises caused by the tenant, not including ordinary wear and tear' (ORS 90.300(7)(a)), and any money you hold as security for furniture is a security deposit under ORS 90.300, not a fee ("Fees You May Charge").

Appliances you supply must be kept 'in good repair if supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord' (ORS 90.320(1)(i)), and you need not supply a stove or refrigerator you did not agree to supply (ORS 90.365(4)); list them under "Appliances & Equipment Included" clause.

If you rent furnished, use the optional furnishings clause ("Furnishings (Furnished Rentals)" clause), which lists the items and charges the tenant only for damage the tenant is at fault for.

Short furnished stays may fall outside chapter 90 altogether: 'Transient occupancy in a hotel or motel' (ORS 90.110(4)) and 'Vacation occupancy' (ORS 90.110(6)) are excluded. In a manufactured dwelling park or marina, a landlord may not unreasonably restrict a tenant 'in choosing a fuel supplier, furnishings, goods, services or accessories' (ORS 90.525(1)).

title: No Statutory Guest Right in Oregon Rentals
bodyText:
Oregon gives tenants in ordinary rentals (ORS 90.100 to 90.465) no general statutory right to have guests, visitors, caregivers or suppliers that the lease cannot limit, in buildings of any size; but for a tenant with a disability, refusing 'to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when the accommodations may be necessary to afford the individual with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling' (ORS 659A.145(2)(g)) is unlawful discrimination, so a guest limit may have to yield for a needed live-in or visiting caregiver. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

Guests are not tenants: 'Tenant' 'Does not mean a guest or temporary occupant' (ORS 90.100(51)(c)). Reasonable guest terms in the lease or your rules are allowed ("Guest Policy" clause, "Guest Policy (14-Day Limit)" clause), and a rule adopted under ORS 90.262 must meet that section's conditions ("House Rules").

A longer stay can be handled by a written temporary occupancy agreement (ORS 90.275; "Temporary Occupancy Agreements").

You may not charge a guest fee: 'A landlord may not charge a fee at the beginning of the tenancy for an anticipated landlord expense and may not require the payment of any fee except as provided in this section' (ORS 90.302(1)), and no guest or visitor fee is on that list ("Fees You May Charge"). A fee charged in violation lets the tenant recover 'twice the actual damages of the tenant or $300, whichever is greater' (ORS 90.302(8)); that penalty does not apply to the per-occurrence fees listed in ORS 90.302(2), such as late rent fees.

Don't use guest rules to punish a tenant who has complained or organized: retaliatory 'decreasing services' (ORS 90.385(2)) includes 'Intentionally and unreasonably interfering with and substantially impairing the enjoyment or use of the premises by the tenant' (ORS 90.385(2)(b)).

If you allow guest parking, the towing rules require you to post signs and say how guest vehicles are identified (ORS 90.485; "Towing at a Rental").

Tenants in a manufactured dwelling park or marina have statutory rights to meet in each other's homes and to invite speakers (ORS 90.750(2); ORS 90.755(1)); those rules don't apply to other rentals.

title: Home Businesses in Oregon Rentals
bodyText:
In an Oregon rental under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, the starting rule is that 'Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy the dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit' (ORS 90.340), so you may restrict or permit business use in the lease ("Residential Use Only" clause).

The one exception is family child care: 'a landlord may not prohibit the tenant’s use of a dwelling as a family child care home if' (ORS 90.358(1)) the home 'is certified under ORS 329A.280 or registered under ORS 329A.330' (ORS 90.358(1)(a)) and 'The tenant has notified the landlord of the use' (ORS 90.358(1)(b)).

You must 'take reasonable steps to cooperate' (ORS 90.358(2)) with that use; you may still require advance payment for modifications you are not otherwise required to make, and prohibit a use that zoning, association documents or Early Learning Council rules don't allow (ORS 90.358(4)); you may choose one of two liability protections (ORS 90.358(5); "Family Child Care Home Conditions" clause); retaliation for the use is barred (ORS 90.385(1)(f)); and the rule does not apply to housing for older persons (ORS 90.358(7)).

For zoning, 'A family child care home is considered a residential use of property for zoning purposes' (ORS 197.671(2)(a)).

Oregon has no statute that makes any other home-based business a permitted use as against a lease, or that requires the lease to spell out a home-business restriction. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none.

Home occupations are a zoning question for the city or county: a county 'may allow, subject to the approval of the governing body or its designate, the establishment of a home occupation and the parking of vehicles in any zone' (ORS 215.448(1)), with limits in farm and forest zones, and city codes set their own rules.

title: No Oregon Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: Oregon does not require you to adopt a key-control policy, keep a key log, limit or record which employees hold master or unit keys, or rekey locks between tenants, whatever the size of the building. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. What Oregon does require: the unit must have 'Working locks for all dwelling entrance doors and latches for all windows, by which access may be had to the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.320(1)(L)) and a means of unlocking them and reaching the common areas the tenant uses, including at least one means other than a tenant portal (ORS 90.320(1)(m) as amended by Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23, § 6, effective June 5, 2026; "Locks and Keys", "Smart Locks and App-Based Entry"). A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking may ask for the locks to be changed (if the perpetrator is a co-tenant, only after giving you a court order requiring the perpetrator to move out, ORS 90.459(3)(a)), and you 'shall promptly change the locks to the tenant’s dwelling unit at the tenant’s expense or shall give the tenant permission to change the locks' (ORS 90.459(2)) ("Lock Changes for Victims"). Every entry with a key, by you or your staff, must follow the entry rules (ORS 90.322; "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause), and abusing access or using it to harass is barred (ORS 90.322(2)). Handing over or getting back keys can matter legally: delivery of possession 'may be implied by actions such as the landlord’s delivery of the keys to the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.147(1)), but your receipt of keys at the end is not by itself acceptance of a surrender (ORS 90.148). Lease terms on keys and lost-key charges are in "Keys" clause. A written key-control policy and rekeying between tenants are good practice, not legal duties; Oregon also sets no employee-screening duty ("No Oregon Duty to Screen Rental Staff").

title: Smart Locks and App-Based Entry
bodyText: Oregon regulates smart locks and app-based entry through the habitability list, not a separate statute. For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, the unit must have 'Working locks for all dwelling entrance doors and latches for all windows, by which access may be had to the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.320(1)(L)). Since June 5, 2026, it must also have 'A means of unlocking locks under paragraph (L) of this subsection' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23) 'and of unlocking or otherwise accessing all common areas or common facilities of the premises to which the tenant has access, such as an access code or a fob, key card or other tangible key which must include at least one means other than a tenant portal' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23). A 'Tenant portal' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23) is 'any electronic application, software, website or digital platform provided by or on behalf of a landlord that a tenant, applicant or prospective applicant uses in connection with applying for, establishing, maintaining or terminating a tenancy' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 23). So an app-only smart lock is not enough: give every tenant at least one non-portal way in (a code, fob, card or key) for the unit and every common area the tenant may use ("Locks and Keys", "Tenant Portals"). The 2025 edition of ORS 90.320(1)(m) still prints the earlier text (an app system plus 'at least one alternative means of access' (ORS 90.320(1)(m))), which the 2026 act replaced for agreements entered into before, on or after June 5, 2026. Oregon has no landlord-tenant statute or rule on smart-lock entry logs or access data (the general Oregon Consumer Privacy Act, ORS 646A.570 to 646A.589, can reach entry logs and biometric data only for a business that, in a calendar year, controls or processes the personal data of 100,000 or more Oregon consumers, or of 25,000 or more while deriving 25 percent or more of its annual gross revenue from selling personal data, ORS 646A.572(1)(a)(A)-(B)), and none letting a domestic-violence survivor ask a landlord that manages connected-device or app accounts to cut off another person's access. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. For a victim, the lock-change rule applies, and changing an access code or reissuing credentials can be read as the practical equivalent: on request you 'shall promptly change the locks to the tenant’s dwelling unit at the tenant’s expense or shall give the tenant permission to change the locks' (ORS 90.459(2)) ("Lock Changes for Victims"). Entry through a smart lock is still entry: the ORS 90.322 notice and consent rules apply ("Landlord's Right of Entry" clause). A tenant's phone number and e-mail held in an access app are confidential information under Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61, § 2 ("Keeping Tenants' Information Confidential").

title: Police, Crime-Free Programs and Tenant Calls for Help
bodyText: Oregon has no general statute requiring you to cooperate with police, join a crime-free housing program or add a crime-free lease addendum, no state chronic-nuisance (calls-for-service) rule for rentals, and no general rule protecting a tenant who calls the police. A state nuisance-abatement law does reach rentals: any place where unlawful drug activity, prostitution or commercial gambling occurs, any place found unfit for use as an illegal drug manufacturing site and not decontaminated and certified fit within 180 days, and any place used for listed animal-cruelty or animal-fighting activity is a nuisance (ORS 105.555(1); ORS 105.597), and the Attorney General, a district attorney, a county or city attorney or a person residing or doing business in the county may sue to enjoin it (ORS 105.560(1)) after at least 10 days' notice to the owners of record (ORS 105.565(1)). If the complaint asks for it, the court may close the place for up to a year (ORS 105.580(2)), but enters no order against an owner acting in good faith who had no knowledge of the nuisance or has been making reasonable efforts to abate it, has not been in contempt of court in the proceedings, and will make best efforts to abate it immediately and keep it from being a nuisance for a year (ORS 105.580(3)). The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none of those three. City ordinances (for example chronic-nuisance programs) may apply; check yours. If an ordinance requires you to remove a tenant on threat of a fine, abatement or forfeiture, state law protects a good-faith effort: if your good-faith attempt to end the tenancy for an act outrageous in the extreme fails in court, you 'may not be found in violation of any state statute or local ordinance requiring the landlord to remove that tenant upon threat of fine, abatement or forfeiture as long as the landlord continues to make a good faith effort to terminate the tenancy' (ORS 90.396(5)). Three state rules do touch police involvement. First, you may not act against a tenant 'Because of criminal activity relating to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking in which the tenant or applicant is the victim, or of any police or emergency response related to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking in which the tenant or applicant is the victim' (ORS 90.449(1)(c)); the one exception lets you end a victim's tenancy after a written warning about the perpetrator's conduct if the tenant lets in a perpetrator who is an actual and imminent threat to others on the premises, or lets the perpetrator live in the unit as an unauthorized occupant (ORS 90.449(3)); a violation lets the tenant recover 'up to two months’ periodic rent or twice the actual damages sustained by the tenant or applicant, whichever is greater' (ORS 90.449(4)(a)) and gives a defense to eviction ("No Adverse Action Against Victims"). Second, retaliation is barred where the tenant 'has performed or expressed intent to perform any other act for the purpose of asserting, protecting or invoking the protection of any right secured to tenants under any federal, state or local law' (ORS 90.385(1)(g)). Third, on a court order for a pen register or trap and trace device, a 'landlord, custodian or other person shall furnish the investigating law enforcement agency forthwith with all information, facilities and technical assistance necessary' (ORS 165.669(1)) if the order directs it, is 'reasonably compensated' (ORS 165.669(3)) and is protected from suit for complying (ORS 165.669(4)). Police entry into a tenant's home is a matter for warrants and the tenant's consent, not your entry right: you have 'no other right of access' (ORS 90.322(5)) beyond ORS 90.322, which can be read as barring you from letting officers in on your own authority except as the law otherwise allows. Before giving police a tenant's personal details, check the confidential-information rule: disclosure is allowed 'As required by a court order or judicial warrant or subpoena but not an administrative warrant or subpoena' (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61) ("Keeping Tenants' Information Confidential"). Criminal conduct by a tenant is handled under the termination statutes ("Criminal Activity" clause, "24-Hour Terminations").

title: Parking Rules, Charges and Notice
bodyText: Oregon has no special notice rule for parking: nothing requires parking rules to be delivered before the lease is signed or under a set heading, requires the lease to say whether parking is provided or what it costs, limits the vehicle information you may ask for, or ties a parking permit to the lease term. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. The general rules do the work for tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465. A parking rule binds the tenant only if, among other conditions, 'The tenant has written notice of it at the time the tenant enters into the rental agreement, or when it is adopted' (ORS 90.262(1)(f)), and a rule adopted later that 'works a substantial modification of the bargain' (ORS 90.262(2)) needs the tenant's written consent; in a fixed term, the terms, 'including the amount of rent, may not be unilaterally amended' (ORS 90.220(2)) ("House Rules"). Any parking charge must be in the written rental agreement as rent or a permitted fee (ORS 90.302(1)); a fee for 'Parking violations' (ORS 90.302(3)(b)(E)) is allowed only for a second or later noncompliance within a year after a written warning and is capped at $50, then $50 plus five percent of the current rent (ORS 90.302(3)(a)). Towing has its own conditions ("Towing at a Rental", "Parking & Vehicle Requirements" clause): towing from a reserved, unassigned space for lack of a tag requires written agreements that, among other things, 'Specify whether guest parking is allowed' (ORS 90.485(3)(c)(C)) ("Parking Tags and Towing Agreement" clause); and you 'may not have a motor vehicle removed under this section because the vehicle’s registration has expired or is otherwise invalid' (ORS 90.485(7)), so Oregon has no posted-notice period for registration tows because it bars them. An inoperable vehicle may be towed only after a prominent notice affixed at least 72 hours before (ORS 90.485(6)). You 'may not require that a tenant display a nonremovable tag, sticker or other device on a motor vehicle that might reveal or indicate to the public the premises where the tenant resides' (ORS 90.263). The tower must have the facility owner's signed authorization at the time of the tow (ORS 98.854(2)).

title: Political Canvassing and Signs in Oregon Rentals
bodyText: For ordinary rentals (ORS 90.100 to 90.465), Oregon has no statute that gives candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or canvassers access to your building or common areas, or that protects a tenant's political signs or door-to-door political canvassing. A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms found none. Two rules still limit you. You may not retaliate because 'The tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants’ union or similar organization' (ORS 90.385(1)(c)), and retaliatory 'decreasing services' (ORS 90.385(2)) includes 'Unreasonably restricting the availability of or placing unreasonable burdens on the use of common areas or facilities by tenant associations or tenants meeting to establish a tenant organization' (ORS 90.385(2)(a)) ("Tenant Organizing"). Any rule you adopt on signs, canvassing or common-area use must meet ORS 90.262 ("House Rules"), and display rules are covered in "Flags, Signs and Religious Displays". The broader political-access rights apply only to tenants renting a space for a manufactured dwelling or floating home in a facility (and rented lots in a park converted to a planned community subdivision, ORS 90.643(3)(b)(M)-(N)): no rule may 'infringe upon the right of a person who rents a space for a manufactured dwelling or floating home to invite public officers, candidates for public office or officers or representatives of a tenant organization to appear and speak upon matters of public interest in the common areas or recreational areas of the facility' (ORS 90.755(1)), 'The landlord shall allow the tenant to place political signs on or in a manufactured dwelling or floating home owned by the tenant or the space rented by the tenant' (ORS 90.755(2)), and tenants may canvass one another (ORS 90.750(3)), subject to reasonable rules.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: Oregon has no statute that gives a tenant a right to display religious or cultural items (such as a mezuzah on a doorframe, a holiday display or a cultural flag), and none that limits your rules on them as such. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. Fair housing law is the real limit. You may not, 'because of the race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, marital status, familial status or source of income of any person' (ORS 659A.421(2)), 'Make any distinction, discrimination or restriction against a purchaser in the price, terms, conditions or privileges relating to the sale, rental, lease or occupancy of real property' (ORS 659A.421(2)(c)); federal law likewise bars discrimination 'in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling' (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b)) because of religion or national origin. So a display rule must be neutral and applied evenly: a rule that singles out religious or cultural items, or is enforced against one faith's items but not others, invites a discrimination claim ("Oregon Fair Housing Classes"). A display rule is also an ordinary rule that must meet ORS 90.262, including that 'It applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner' (ORS 90.262(1)(c)), and a rule adopted mid-tenancy that substantially modifies the bargain needs the tenant's written consent (ORS 90.262(2)) ("House Rules"). A small item on a doorframe may raise the alterations clause rather than a display rule ("No Alterations" clause). Flags and signs generally are covered in "Flags, Signs and Religious Displays".

title: What an Oregon Tenant May Not Do
bodyText:
Oregon lists what a tenant may not do in ORS 90.325(2), for ordinary tenancies (ORS 90.100 to 90.465).

A tenant may not:
- '(a) Remove or tamper with a smoke alarm, smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm as described in ORS 105.842 or 479.300' (ORS 90.325(2));
- '(b) Deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or knowingly permit any person to do so' (ORS 90.325(2));
- or '(c) Remove, obstruct or tamper with a sprinkler head used for fire suppression' (ORS 90.325(2)).

But 'A tenant is not responsible for damage that results from' (ORS 90.325(3)) acts of God or conduct by a perpetrator relating to domestic violence, sexual assault, bias crime or stalking, and you may ask for verification of the latter under ORS 90.453 (ORS 90.325(4)).

Two related limits: 'A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent from the landlord to enter' (ORS 90.322(2)), and 'Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy the dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit' (ORS 90.340).

A material violation of ORS 90.325 is a ground for a for-cause termination notice (ORS 90.392(2)(b)), which the tenant can defeat by curing a curable violation by the date in the notice (ORS 90.392(4)), except that there is no right to cure substantially the same violation repeated within six months of an earlier notice (ORS 90.392(5)(a)), and alarm tampering can carry the fee allowed by ORS 90.302(2)(c) ("Alarm Tampering Fee" clause).

The tenant's affirmative duties are in "Tenants' Duties Under Oregon Law"; the lease clause restating the prohibited acts is "Prohibited Acts by Tenant" clause.

title: Limits on How the Property Is Used
bodyText: For tenancies under ORS 90.100 to 90.465, the default is that 'Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy the dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit' (ORS 90.340), so the lease may limit the purposes for which the property is used; the library's clause is "Residential Use Only" clause, which keeps the statutory family child care exception (ORS 90.358; "Home Businesses in Oregon Rentals"). Oregon has one old statute that voids a rental used for an unlawful purpose, limited to gambling: 'No person shall let or rent any house, room, shop or other building, or any boat, booth, garden or other place, knowing or having reason to believe it will be used for gambling purposes' (ORS 91.240(1)); such rental contracts 'are void between the parties' (ORS 91.240(2)); and if a lessee or occupant uses the place for gambling, the lessor 'upon discovery thereof, may avoid and terminate such lease or contract of occupancy' (ORS 91.240(3)). For a residential tenancy, recover possession through the eviction process in ORS 105.100 to 105.168 on a proper termination notice rather than treating the lease as automatically void. Apart from that, no Oregon statute or rule makes a lease void or annulled when the premises are used for a prohibited purpose. The Oregon Revised Statutes, the Oregon Administrative Rules, the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026, the 2026 Uniform Trial Court Rules and the statewide eviction forms contain none. Criminal use is handled by termination instead: acts 'outrageous in the extreme' (ORS 90.396(1)(f)) on or near the premises, including prostitution or promoting prostitution and the unlawful manufacture, delivery or possession of a controlled substance (ORS 90.396(1)(f)(A)-(B)), allow a 24-hour termination notice ("24-Hour Terminations", "Criminal Activity" clause); other misuse is a for-cause ground (ORS 90.392(2)). Separately, places used for prostitution, gambling for profit, drug activity or listed marijuana offenses, uncleaned former drug-manufacturing sites, and places used for listed animal-cruelty or animal-fighting activity are nuisances (ORS 105.555(1); ORS 105.597) that a public attorney or any person residing or doing business in the county may sue to abate after at least 10 days' notice to the owners of record (ORS 105.560(1); ORS 105.565(1)). If the complaint asks for it, the court may order the premises closed for one year unless released sooner (ORS 105.580(2)), but 'The court, if satisfied of an owner’s good faith, shall enter no order of abatement as to that owner' (ORS 105.580(3)) if the owner had no knowledge or has been making reasonable efforts to abate, has not been in contempt, and will make best efforts to abate the nuisance immediately and prevent it for a year.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Oregon Leases
bodyText: The library does not offer an arbitration clause for Oregon leases. Oregon's arbitration act makes 'An agreement contained in a record to submit to arbitration any existing or subsequent controversy arising between the parties to the agreement is valid, enforceable and irrevocable except upon a ground that exists at law or in equity for the revocation of a contract' (ORS 36.620(1)). The landlord-tenant act, though, says a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant 'Agrees to waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter' (ORS 90.245(1)(a)). Its one exception lets the parties include 'a provision for informal dispute resolution' (ORS 90.220(5)), and informal dispute resolution 'does not include mandatory mediation or arbitration' (ORS 90.100(24)). Whether a binding arbitration term agreed before any dispute waives the tenant's chapter 90 remedies (the court action for possession under ORS 105.100 to 105.168, counterclaims under ORS 90.370, attorney fees under ORS 90.255), and whether the Federal Arbitration Act (FEDERAL: 9 U.S.C. § 2) would override that reading, is a question only Oregon courts can settle. The stakes are real: 'If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by the landlord to be prohibited and attempts to enforce such provisions, the tenant may recover in addition to the actual damages of the tenant an amount up to three months’ periodic rent' (ORS 90.245(2)). The library offers an arbitration clause only where a state's law allows it and no statute penalizes using a prohibited term, so it offers none for Oregon. What you can use: a lease clause for voluntary consultation or voluntary mediation ("Informal Dispute Resolution" clause). Separately from any lease term, a circuit court must refer most civil actions where 'The only relief claimed is recovery of money or damages' and no party claims more than $50,000 to court-annexed arbitration (ORS 36.405(1)(a)). Statutory arbitration of tenancy disputes exists only for manufactured dwelling park and marina space tenancies (ORS 105.138; ORS 90.767), which have their own rules. A landlord who still wants a pre-dispute arbitration clause should take legal advice first.

title: Habitability Rules Oregon Does Not Have
bodyText:
Oregon's habitability rule is short and firm: 'A landlord shall at all times during the tenancy maintain the dwelling unit in a habitable condition' (ORS 90.320(1)), the tenant's remedies are the ones in ORS 90.360 to 90.368, plus the counterclaim in an action for possession based on nonpayment of rent, or in an action for rent (ORS 90.370), and accepting rent does not waive the duty ("Collecting Rent Means Keeping the Unit Habitable"). Many rules other states add are absent in Oregon for ordinary tenancies (ORS 90.100 to 90.465):
- No presumption that you breached because a unit has a code violation or an unabated citation ("No Oregon Presumption on Habitability or Repair Time"), and no lease statement of fitness or agreed condition ("No Required Oregon Lease Statement on Habitability").
- No rule that repair promises be in writing or carry a completion date ("Promises to Clean, Repair or Improve in Oregon"), and no right for either side to end the tenancy because repairs would cost too much ("No Oregon Right to End a Lease Because Repairs Cost Too Much").
- No rent escrow for repairs and no small-landlord opt-out notice ("No Small-Landlord Opt-Out From Oregon Repair Remedies"); no bar on demanding rent just because a code violation is uncorrected, apart from the posted-unit rules ("No Bar on Demanding Rent for a Unit With Violations"; "Posted or Unlawful Units"); no rule splitting a rent reduction between a subsidized tenant and the subsidy ("Subsidized Rent When an Oregon Unit Is Unfit").
- No state rule on who clears snow or keeps up the yard ("Snow and Ice Removal in Oregon"; "Yard, Landscaping and Irrigation Work in Oregon"); the tenant takes on such tasks only by a separate writing that meets ORS 90.320(2) ("Tenant Maintenance Tasks Agreement" clause).
- No smoke-drift rule or smoke-drift waiver ("No Smoke-Drift Waiver in an Oregon Lease").
- No general sprinkler retrofit duty, balcony inspection program, window-guard rule, steam radiator cover rule or pest-treatment notice ("Fire Sprinklers in Existing Rentals"; "No Balcony Inspection Program"; "Window Guards, Bars and Bedroom Exits"; "No Radiator Cover Rule"; "No Pesticide Notice Rule for Rentals"), and no separate shutoff procedure for a utility you submeter ("No Shutoffs of Utilities You Submeter or Supply").
A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026 and the 2026 court rules found none of them. Cities may have their own housing codes and inspection programs.

title: Landlord Questions Answered Outside Oregon's Landlord-Tenant Act
bodyText:
Some landlord questions are answered, or confirmed absent, outside ORS chapter 90:
- Squatters. Oregon has a squatter remedy. A squatter is a person occupying a dwelling unit 'who is not so entitled under a rental agreement or who is not authorized by the tenant to occupy that dwelling unit' (ORS 90.100(47)(a)); the landlord-tenant act doesn't govern 'Occupancy by a squatter' (ORS 90.110(5)), but you may recover possession through the court eviction process 'after giving the person 24 hours' written notice of the termination of the occupancy' (ORS 91.140); the notice must give the date and time to vacate and state that the cause is the person's status as a squatter (ORS 91.140) ("Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants").
- Receipts. Any tenant who asks is entitled to a writing showing a payment, cash or not (ORS 90.140(2); "Rent Receipts"). Only a licensed property manager has a cash-specific rule: 'A property manager must prepare a legible written receipt for any cash funds received under a property management agreement' (OAR 863-025-0060(1)).
- Registration before an eviction. Oregon has no statewide landlord registration or rental license for ordinary rentals, so none is a condition of a possession judgment ("Landlord Registration and Rental Licensing"); city programs may differ. Standing rules outside chapter 90 can still stop a suit: an out-of-state LLC or corporation transacting business here without authority 'may not maintain a proceeding in any court in this state' (ORS 63.704(1); ORS 60.704(1)), and renting under an unregistered assumed business name costs standing until you register (ORS 648.135(1)) ("Who May Appear in Court for an Entity Landlord"; "Owners Outside Oregon: Service and Standing"). Whether renting homes is transacting business for that rule is not settled by the statutes; the cautious course is to register first.
- Also confirmed absent outside chapter 90: a maximum lease term or spousal-consent rule ("Lease Length and Signing Formalities"); a contamination, drywall, chemical-warning or shoreline disclosure ("Hazardous Contamination: No General Disclosure Duty"; "No Defective Drywall Disclosure"; "No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule"; "No Shoreline Access Disclosure"); a certificate-of-occupancy or special-district statement ("No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure"; "No Special District Statement in the Lease"); a lead-safe building certificate ("No Lead-Safe Building Certificate; Who Must Be Certified for Lead Work"); a single-family-zone leasing limit ("No State Limit on Renting Homes in Single-Family Zones"); and a veterans' landlord incentive ("No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans").
A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026 and the 2026 court rules found none of them.

title: Other Rules Oregon Does Not Have
bodyText:
Beyond habitability ("Habitability Rules Oregon Does Not Have") and the points answered outside the landlord-tenant act ("Landlord Questions Answered Outside Oregon's Landlord-Tenant Act"), these rules some states have are absent in Oregon for ordinary tenancies (ORS 90.100 to 90.465):
- Deposits: no posted deposit standards, separate nonrefundable-deposit notice, expedited refund procedure or inspection-notice penalty, and no separate rule for a utility deposit you hold ("No Deposit Standards Disclosure"; "No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice"; "No Expedited Deposit Procedure"; "No Inspection-Notice Penalty"; "Utility Deposits and the Security Deposit").
- Rent and charges: no rule on passing government fines or property tax increases to the tenant, no property-tax statement, no separate limit on late charges on a subsidy's share, and no separately rented parking requirement; any charge still has to fit the closed fee list (ORS 90.302(1)) ("Passing Government Fines to Tenants"; "Passing Property Tax Increases to Tenants"; "No Property Tax Rent Statement"; "Late Charges When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent"; "Unbundled Parking").
- The lease document: no initials or separate-signature rule, type-size rule, plain-language statute, state rights guide or truth-in-renting statement, and no guarantor-renewal rule ("No Initials Requirement for Lease Terms"; "No Minimum Type Size for Leases"; "No Plain-Language Statement for Leases"; "No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide"; "No Truth in Renting Statement"; "Guarantors and Renewals").
- Ending a tenancy: no seasonal-tenancy rules, possession bond, forfeiture election, benefit-delay defense, cold-weather notice, lease-named agent for eviction papers, rule on extra terms in a notice-to-vacate form, good-cause coverage notice or landlord termination for an environmental event ("Seasonal Rentals"; "No End-of-Term Possession Bond"; "No Forfeiture Election or Reinstatement After Judgment"; "No Benefit-Delay Defense to Eviction"; "No Cold-Weather Notice Rule"; "No Lease-Named Agent for Eviction Papers"; "No Rule on Extra Terms in a Notice to Vacate"; "No Good-Cause Coverage Notice; What Termination Notices Must Say"; "No Environmental-Event Termination Right").
- Occupancy and conduct: no double-letting statute, statutory guest right, disaster-guest rule, political-access or religious-display right, furnished-rental rules, waterbed rule, pet fact sheet, parking-rules notice or crime-free addendum mandate ("No Double-Letting Statute"; "No Statutory Guest Right in Oregon Rentals"; "No Oregon Rule on Guests Displaced by a Disaster"; "Political Canvassing and Signs in Oregon Rentals"; "Religious and Cultural Displays"; "Renting Furnished in Oregon"; "No Waterbed Statute"; "No Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet"; "Parking Rules, Charges and Notice"; "Police, Crime-Free Programs and Tenant Calls for Help").
- Management: no key-control or employee background-check mandate, no rule on utilities left in your name, no energy-data release rule and no special rule for a refused subsidy inspection ("No Oregon Key-Control Mandate"; "No Oregon Duty to Screen Rental Staff"; "Tenant Utility Transfers: No Cutoff Right"; "Tenant Energy Data and Building Benchmarking"; "Program Inspections in Subsidized and Voucher Tenancies").
Cities may have their own rules on some of these points.

title: Where Oregon Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText:
Several Oregon rules apply only if, or unless, the written rental agreement says so; a silent lease takes the default. For ordinary tenancies (ORS 90.100 to 90.465):
- Rent: 'Unless otherwise agreed, rent is payable at the dwelling unit' (ORS 90.220(7)(a)) ("Rent Payment" clause); rent in installments of less than a month needs a 'written agreement' (ORS 90.417(3)) ("Rent Paid in Installments" clause); and 'Unless otherwise agreed, rent is uniformly apportionable from day to day' (ORS 90.427(10)).
- Charges: every fee 'must be described in a written rental agreement' (ORS 90.302(1)) ("Fees for Repeated Rule Violations" clause; "Alarm Tampering Fee" clause); you may bill utility or service charges only 'if a written rental agreement so provides' (ORS 90.315(4)(a)) ("Utility Charges Billed by Landlord" clause); renter's liability insurance may be required only 'in a written rental agreement' (ORS 90.222(1)) ("Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause).
- Deposits: a carpet-cleaning deduction regardless of the tenant's own cleaning needs a written term (ORS 90.300(7)(c)(A)(iii)), and 'A last month's rent deposit does not limit the amount of rent charged unless a written rental agreement provides otherwise' (ORS 90.300(10)) ("Last Month's Rent Deposits").
- Use and absence: 'Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy the dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit' (ORS 90.340) ("Residential Use Only" clause), and you can recover actual damages for an unannounced absence of more than seven days only 'If the rental agreement requires' notice (ORS 90.410(1)) and the tenant willfully fails to give it ("Notice of Extended Absence" clause).
- Notices: an added notice method counts only 'as agreed to and described in a written rental agreement' (ORS 90.150(4)) ("Agreed Method for Actual Notice" clause; "Service of Notices by Mail and Attachment" clause).
Optional clauses the library offers for Oregon, each off unless you choose it: "Service of Notices by Mail and Attachment" clause, "Agreed Method for Actual Notice" clause, "Place of Payment for Nonpayment Notices" clause, "Rent Paid in Installments" clause, "Carpet Cleaning Deduction" clause, "Fees for Repeated Rule Violations" clause, "Alarm Tampering Fee" clause, "Entry for Yard Maintenance" clause, "Family Child Care Home Conditions" clause, "Parking Tags and Towing Agreement" clause, "Criminal Activity" clause, "Contact Person if Tenant Dies" clause, "Informal Dispute Resolution" clause, "No Cannabis Growing" clause, "Repair Contact and Approved Repairers" clause, "Guaranty" clause, "Furnishings (Furnished Rentals)" clause and the condemnation clause "Condemnation". Declined, each with its own row: binding arbitration, contractual interest, a holdover premium, a casualty-termination clause, jury and exemption waivers and a temporary occupancy agreement ("Arbitration Clauses in Oregon Leases"; "Interest on Money a Tenant Owes"; "Premium Holdover Rates (Barred)"; "Fire, Casualty and Uninhabitable Units"; "Jury Trial Waivers (Not Offered)"; "Waiving Exemptions From Collection (Not Offered)"; "Temporary Occupancy Agreements"). Three things belong in a separate writing, not the lease: the e-mail notice addendum signed after the tenant moves in (ORS 90.155), an agreement to show the unit without notice (ORS 90.322(1)(d)) and consent to release confidential information (Or. Laws 2026, ch. 61, § 2).
Option to purchase. Oregon has no lease-option or rent-to-own statute for homes (no special early-exercise right, cure period or bar on forfeiting an option payment). Until the option is exercised the tenant stays a tenant: 'A tenant who holds but has not exercised an option to purchase the dwelling unit is not a purchaser' (ORS 90.110(2)), so chapter 90 applies in full. The seller's property disclosure statement does 'not apply to a leasehold in real property' (ORS 105.465(1)(b)); for property with one to four dwelling units (and some condominium, timeshare and owner-sited manufactured dwelling property) a seller owes it, unless the buyer says the property won't be the buyer's or family's residence (ORS 105.465(1)(a)), 'to each buyer who makes a written offer to purchase real property in this state' (ORS 105.465(2)), and a buyer who gets it may revoke the offer within five business days unless the buyer has waived that right in writing (ORS 105.475(1)). Whether exercising a written option is such an offer is not settled by the statutes; the cautious course is to deliver the statement before the tenant exercises. Oregon's lease-purchase law covers personal property only (ORS 646A.120(5)). A search of the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition), the Oregon Administrative Rules (as served November 18, 2026), the Oregon Constitution, Oregon Laws 2025 and 2026 and the 2026 court rules found no lease-option statute.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Oregon departs from the uniform rule on checks marked 'paid in full'. Cashing a check or other instrument marked 'paid in full', 'payment in full', 'full payment of a claim' or similar, or one sent with a statement to that effect, does not settle the claim or stop you collecting the rest unless you, personally or through an officer or employee with actual authority to settle claims, agree in writing to accept that amount as full payment (ORS 73.0311). So you may cash a tenant's short check marked paid in full and still collect the balance, as long as you sign nothing accepting it as full payment. Separately, Oregon's landlord-tenant law lets you accept a partial payment of rent, and sets when doing so affects a termination notice for nonpayment (ORS 90.417; see "Accepting Rent After a Violation or Notice").

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Oregon's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the chapter, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (ORS 90.130). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
